strengths: PERF-E1's core fix genuinely landed: computeGraphProjection now reads each entity/claim exactly once (N+M+S, never N×M) and is HEAD-gated through the same well-tested CanonicalQueueCache the stage drains use (pipelineProjections.ts:392), with a reference-equality no-op path in the store so an idle tick does no restamp, no save and no push.

PERF-E3 — the 'hangs during ingest' mechanism — is properly closed: Connect's whole link/orphan/dedup tail is skipped outright on an unchanged HEAD (connectStage.ts:1572), each queued node is byte-stable-prefiltered OFF the lock before any lock hold (connectStage.ts:1589), and captures got a real two-lane priority Mutex (stageLock.ts:212) wired to Orchestrator.capture, watchRun, intakeRun and researchRun.

PERF-E4 landed cleanly and was improved beyond the recommendation: promote applies only the git diff --name-status delta (staging.ts:136) AND drains no longer promote directly — they request() a debounced, cap-bounded coalescing promoter, so Obsidian's watcher sees occasional bursts instead of a continuous stream.

The lock discipline itself is sound where it counts: no lock.run section anywhere awaits a Copilot/LLM call — every stage prepares cognition off-lock in its own worktree and takes the lock only for the commit/advance. That is the single most important structural property in this domain and it holds.

PERF-E6's incremental audit read is a well-engineered fix: per-file byte offsets with a torn-tail guard so a mid-append line is never silently lost, and an unchanged file costs exactly one fs.stat (activityIndex.ts:220).

The Ask latency path closed almost completely: process-wide RecallClient reuse ends the per-question CLI-server leak (ipc.ts:516), tool calls now serve from SQLite/FTS5 with a composite search tool, history is capped at 10 turns × 2 KB, tool results are windowed to 32 KB with an honest truncation note, and kb:askProgress pushes live tool-call progress.

The renderer poll layer is now one correct primitive: createVisibilityPoll (shell/visibilityPoll.ts) pauses on window-background AND ancestor .view.hidden, self-stops on detach, and geometrically backs off a rejecting target — fixing R1, R2, R9 and R15 in one place rather than five hand-rolled idioms.

#511's keyed rendering is real where it was applied: Ask patches the transcript incrementally instead of re-marked-ing every prior turn, and Activity/Explore/Health repaint scoped regions (activityView.ts:201/226/254, exploreView.ts:204/209) rather than the whole container.

Every fix carries an explicit, honest comment naming the issue number, the mechanism and — where a tradeoff was accepted — the tradeoff (e.g. the priority lane's documented starvation caveat, sparse-checkout's silent-drop landmine). This is unusually good provenance for a perf wave.
open_questions: Is `.kb/cache/library.db` (21.1 MB for a 4.7 MB corpus) intentionally storing every body three times — entities.body, claims.body/source_files.body, and the fts_bodies virtual table? An FTS5 `content=` external-content table would remove the duplicate at the cost of a join. Not a defect, but the 4.5× amplification will matter at a year vault and nobody appears to have measured it.

The graph projection's backlink map is EMPTY on the real test vault: all 10,719 wikilinks in entities/ point at `sources/.../source.md`, so `[[entities/...]]` never matches. That means the entire backlink precompute (and Health's orphan detection, which reports every entity as an orphan) is computing over a graph with zero entity↔entity edges. Is Connect's link-promotion actually producing entity-to-entity `[[wikilinks]]` in practice, or is the expensive machinery running on a structurally empty input? This is a correctness question for the Reliability/Product lane but it invalidates any perf benchmark of the backlink path.

Should the four maintained projections also stop when the vault has no pending work at all, not just when no window is open? Graph + Connect's sweep now genuinely track mutation; status/review/today do not. A single 'canonical HEAD moved OR a stage is busy' gate could collapse the entire idle loop to one cheap fs read per store per tick — but that is a design decision about how stale a tray-mode status readout may be.

Nightly CI has been red every day since 2026-07-13 and its report-red filer errors before it runs, so no perf regression would ever be filed. Is there an owner for re-greening it before v0.1.0-rc.1, and should a cheap idle-compute assertion (git-spawn count, entities/ read count over 60s on a fixture) be added to that lane once it is green?

`libraryIndexRuntime.ts` deliberately never closes its sqlite store on vault switch ('a tracked fast-follow'). At one open handle per root that is genuinely negligible, but combined with PERF-9's per-read HEAD spawn it suggests the index lifecycle was never wired to the pipeline at all. Is the advance-seam hook (the deferred fast-follow) still planned, or has lazy-on-read become the intended design?

domains.label: ux
domains.title: User experience: install, configure, use
domains.verdict: The strongest-executed domain in the repo — dense, consistent loading/empty/error/warming state discipline across all 17 view modules, a genuinely well-designed guided first-run and macOS TCC permission flow — undermined by an unfinished distribution/install story (unsigned, unnotarized, no updater, zero user-facing guidance) and several settings/affordances that promise a capability the UI doesn't actually deliver (hotkey change, dismiss-restore).
domains.summary:
This domain is where the project's engineering discipline is most visible. Every one of the 10 rail views goes through the same shared vocabulary — `paintSkeleton`/`skeletonFragmentHtml` on mount, a bounded `withTimeout`/`loadGraphWithWarming` read, a calm `.load-warming` face distinct from the alarming `.load-face-error` face, a retryable `renderLoadError`, and a shared `emptyState()` primitive for the zero-data case. I verified this file-by-file (loadGuard.ts + 10 view modules) rather than trusting the summary claim, and it holds: Today/Explore/Health additionally get the "still preparing, not broken" warming face for their heavier full-graph reads, and Reviews/Settings/Sources/Agents-hub/Watched-folders all wire skeleton→error→empty correctly. `WARMING_AFTER_MS` shows as an "unused export" in the knip report, but that's a false alarm — it's consumed as `loadGraphWithWarming`'s own default parameter inside the same file, not by an external importer, so the warming face genuinely fires.

The first-run flow is calibrated exactly to the brief's ask for "simple flows simple, complexity progressive": `setupFlow.ts`'s three post-vault-creation steps (model → optional sample seed → 4-card tour) are each independently skippable and non-blocking — a hung model-catalog fetch or a failed sample-seed degrades to a calm note and lets Continue proceed regardless. The macOS TCC folder-permission flow (`permissionGate.ts`, #56's shipped mitigation) is a real pre-prompt → probe-write → Blocked-with-Retry loop, with an actual "Open System Settings" deep link and a closed retry loop — not a dead end. Reviews' set-aside recovery genuinely answers "why did this fail, and what can I do": each card shows the failure reason plus stage, with optimistic Retry/Dismiss and an honest reconcile-with-error-banner on failure. The banned-lexicon scrub ("KB"/generic "vault" in user copy) is clean across every user-visible string I sampled. Dark mode, the global ⌘K search, and reduced-motion are all real and cross-platform-wired (the ⌘K handler checks both `metaKey` and `ctrlKey`).

Where it falls short is less about any individual view and more about the edges: distribution and a few settings affordances that were fully built on the backend but never got a UI. The install story is the most consequential: `forge.config.ts` and `release.yml` both explicitly document that macOS builds ship unsigned by default (`KB_OSX_SIGN` is opt-in, and the release workflow's own comment says "no such [signing] secrets exist in this repo yet"), Windows' `MakerSquirrel({})` carries no code-signing config either, there is no auto-updater, and there is zero README/LICENSE/CHANGELOG at the repo root and no docs link anywhere in the app (I read `aboutPanel.ts`'s `CREDITS` line and Settings' entire footer — neither carries a URL). For a project whose only release workflow has run once and failed, this is exactly the kind of gap the severity rubric calls release-blocking for a first public pre-release: a clean-machine user hits Gatekeeper's "damaged" dialog with literally nothing in the product or repo telling them what to do.

Several other findings are "backend built it, UI never surfaced it" gaps I could confirm precisely: the quick-capture global hotkey (`quickCaptureAccelerator`) has a complete, live-reactive IPC round-trip (`setInstanceSettings` → `setAccelerator`) but Settings hardcodes/re-sends `'Alt+Space'` unchanged with a comment admitting "isn't edited here yet" — meaning a Windows user whose OS reserves Alt+Space for the native system menu has no in-app way to pick a different one. Health's dismiss button's own tooltip promises a finding is "restorable later," and the backend genuinely supports `dismissed:false` as a restore, but zero call sites in the shell ever send it — there is no "view dismissed" affordance anywhere. Explore's radial graph nests individually keyboard-focusable `role="button"` nodes inside an outer `<svg role="img">`, a documented ARIA anti-pattern where AT browse-mode can treat the whole graphic as one flat image. The main window's `titleBarStyle: 'hiddenInset'` is applied unconditionally even though it's macOS-only per Electron's own contract, so the exact double-title-bar problem the code comments say was fixed for macOS is plausibly never addressed for the equally-targeted Windows build. Finally, of the three nightly e2e specs that have been red for 7 weeks, I could directly confirm two are stale-selector drift, not real regressions: `.activity-empty` and `.ask-citations .cite-ref` are both structurally absent from current source (the views now use the shared `.viz-empty` primitive and `.ask-refs`/`.ask-ref` respectively) — meaning the only automated coverage of two real UX flows this domain cares about has been uninformative since the refactors landed.

strengths: Every rail-reachable data view shares one loading/warming/error/empty vocabulary (loadGuard.ts) with zero exceptions found across 10 views — a real, verified consistency, not an aspirational claim.

Guided first-run (setupFlow.ts) is calibrated to 'simple flows simple, progressive disclosure': every step independently skippable, and every async call (model catalog, sample seed) degrades to a calm note rather than blocking Continue.
The macOS TCC folder-permission flow (permissionGate.ts, #56) is a genuinely complete pre-prompt→probe→Blocked-with-Retry loop with a real deep link to System Settings, not a dead-end warning.

Reviews' set-aside recovery shows the actual failure reason per item plus a working Retry/Dismiss with honest optimistic-then-reconcile-on-failure behavior — a real answer to 'why did it fail, what can I do.'
The banned-lexicon scrub (no 'KB'/generic 'vault' in user-visible copy) is clean across every string sampled in shell/qcap.
Dark mode, ⌘K global search, and reduced-motion are all real, cross-platform-wired (⌘K checks both metaKey and ctrlKey), not cosmetic scaffolding.
Quick Capture degrades per-platform affordance-by-affordance (screenshot/selection buttons stay hidden entirely when unsupported) rather than showing dead controls.
Obsidian compatibility is shipped thoughtfully: a curated, non-destructive .obsidian/ config scaffold ships with every new vault (VAULT-5/6).
open_questions: Does the third nightly-red e2e assertion (jobs.e2e.ts's '.sidebar .nav-group' toHaveText 'Manage') actually fail on the selector text, or does it fail earlier (missing packaged build / different root cause) — the current NAV_VIEWS/railHtml markup looks structurally correct on static inspection, so this needs an actual e2e run to confirm, which was out of scope for this review.

Is there a product decision to eventually sign+notarize macOS builds and code-sign the Windows Squirrel installer, or is unsigned-only an accepted interim state for as long as the app stays pre-release/internal? This materially changes whether UX-1 is truly release-blocking today versus a known, deferred cost.
Is the Guidance surface / 'you' card (noted as unscheduled in prior design work) intended to eventually host the in-app help link UX-8 is missing, or is that a separate concern?

domains.label: latent
domains.title: Latent bugs, time bombs & risks
domains.verdict: Structurally careful but carrying real, already-detonating time bombs: one confirmed unbounded disk leak (3.3 GB / 185 orphaned git worktrees in the live vault, ~92% of its footprint), a shipped Electron with a published advisory, no Content-Security-Policy anywhere, and a hand-rolled YAML/frontmatter layer that provably breaks on CRLF and on ordinary filenames.
domains.summary:
This domain splits cleanly into "the disciplined half" and "the half nobody has looked at since main went dormant on 2026-07-13."

The disciplined half is genuinely good, and it is not decoration. Both append-only JSONL sinks rotate (`devlog.ts` 5 MB × 5, `tracing.ts` 8 MB × 3) with the #256 OOM lesson written into the comment. Crash capture has the right semantics — `uncaughtException` records then exits (preserving Node's contract), `unhandledRejection` records loudly without tearing the app down. Path containment is centralized, symlink-safe (realpath of the deepest existing ancestor), and explicitly distinguishes rel-containment from id-validation so callers can't collapse the two; conversation ids are ULID-validated before any path is built. The SSRF defense is the real layered kind: a static `isAllowedUrl` gate before any socket, plus an `http.Agent({lookup})` that refuses the connection when *any* resolved address is non-public — DNS-rebinding-safe, not a hostname regex. Job scheduling derives "due" from the job's own journal timestamps at a fixed interval, so there is no cron string, no local-time arithmetic, and therefore no DST or timezone bomb — a class of bug this app simply doesn't have. Model resilience is three-deep: probe the live CLI catalog, walk an ordered preference list, and fall to `--model auto` per call with a WARN. Packaging has *real* CI assertions for both native modules (`better_sqlite3.node` and `fsevents` under `app.asar.unpacked/`), and the fuse set is conservative (RunAsNode off, node-CLI inspect off, asar integrity + only-load-from-asar on). Two userData JSON stores write tmp+rename. Across 46k prod LOC there are 0 TODO/FIXME, 2 eslint-disable, 10 `any`.

The undisciplined half is where the bombs are, and one has already gone off. `EPHEMERAL_STAGES` in `canonicalAdvance.ts:74` is `['archive','claims','connect','decompose','consolidation']` — **`compose` is missing**, yet `composeStage.ts:40` sets `STAGE = 'compose'` and line 343 creates ephemeral worktrees through the same path. The reaper's name regex therefore never matches a `compose-<ULID>` directory, and `pruneStaleWorktreeBranches` skips the branches because they're still checked out. The live vault at `~/kb-test-1` holds **185 leaked `compose-*` worktrees totalling 3.3 GB** — out of a 3.6 GB vault, i.e. ~92% of it — with `.git` at 123 MB and only 14 admin entries in `.git/worktrees` against 185 directories on disk. The code's own comment predicts exactly this outcome ("each new item gets slower as the leak grows — eventually starving the pipeline"). It went undetected for three months because every cleanup call is `.catch(() => {})` (lines 179–182), so the leak produced zero log lines.

Untrusted-content handling is the second cluster. There is **no CSP at all** — `index.html` carries only a charset meta, and no `onHeadersReceived` handler sets one — while 71 `innerHTML` sites render vault/LLM-derived strings behind exactly one `DOMPurify.sanitize` call (`askView.ts:26`) and a hand-rolled `esc()`. The renderer holds the full 74-channel `kb:*` bridge, so a sanitizer bypass is an escalation, not a defacement. Shipped `electron` is 42.2.0 with a published advisory fixed in 42.11.2 (a patch bump) and nine patch releases of Chromium fixes behind. Usefully, the audit is much less scary than its headline: of 46 advisories, exactly **two reach the shipped bundle** (electron, dompurify) — `js-yaml` is a devDependency used only by `eval/runner/loader.ts`, with zero imports under `app/src`, and `npm audit fix` would *downgrade* electron-forge 7→6.

Which leads to the third cluster: because there is no YAML library in prod, frontmatter is hand-rolled — and it is provably wrong in two ways I verified in-session. `deriveSourceTitle`'s `/^---\n([\s\S]*?)\n---/` returns **null** on CRLF input; with Git-for-Windows' default `core.autocrlf=true` and no `.gitattributes` written at vault init, every checkout into the staging worktree on Windows makes every source's frontmatter invisible to the pipeline. And `scalar()` (`sourceDoc.ts:9`) only quotes on `[:#'"\n]` or edge whitespace, so a file named `[draft] notes.md` emits `title: [draft] notes.md`, which js-yaml rejects outright ("bad indentation of a mapping entry") — Obsidian's Properties panel, the exact surface PRIN-24 exists to serve, shows a parse error for that note. `*ref`, `- item`, `{a}`, `null` and `yes` all mis-parse too.

Rounding out: the app-level log is 99.84% telemetry noise (36,037 `mem.sample` of 36,094 lines, 5,215,838 bytes — 99.5% of the rotation threshold) with zero boot or crash events, so the sink built for boot forensics will rotate real errors out under sampler pressure; the `kb-app`→`Vellum` rename moved `app.getPath('userData')` with no migration (both dirs still exist on this machine); the process-wide RecallClient is created once and never health-checked; the SDK is pinned at `1.0.0-beta.7`; and the nightly `report-red` auto-filer — the safety net for all of this — cannot even start, because it has no checkout step under a workflow-level `working-directory: app`.

strengths: Both append-only JSONL sinks actually rotate and the rationale is encoded: devlog.ts (5 MB × 5) and tracing.ts (8 MB × 3), with the #256 'unrotated spans.jsonl drove the heap to OOM' lesson written into writeSpanLine's comment. Growth-over-time was thought about, not assumed away.

Crash capture has correct, deliberate semantics (crashCapture.ts): uncaughtException records a synchronous breadcrumb then exits (preserving Node's crash-on-uncaught contract), while unhandledRejection records loudly but does NOT tear down the app — and the choice is documented as a KB-Lead-flagged decision rather than an accident.

Path containment is centralized and symlink-safe (pathContainment.ts): realpath of the deepest EXISTING ancestor with the non-existent tail re-appended, so a committed symlink can't look contained and then be followed out. It also explicitly refuses to conflate Class A (rel-containment) with Class B (id charset validation).

The SSRF defense is the real layered kind, not a hostname regex: isAllowedUrl gates before any socket, and makeSsrfSafeLookup is wired into the http(s) Agent so a public-looking name that RESOLVES to a private/loopback/metadata IP is refused at connect time (DNS-rebinding-safe). Empty resolution also throws.

Job scheduling derives 'due' from the job's own journal timestamps at a fixed interval (jobScheduler.ts isJobDue) rather than a cron string in local time — so the whole DST / timezone / clock-skew bug class simply does not exist here, and schedules survive restarts with no separate timer state.

Model resilience is three-deep and honest: probeAcceptedModels against the live CLI catalog, selectPreferredModel over an ordered list with a 'degraded' verdict, and runWithModelFallback retrying once on `--model auto` ONLY for an unavailable-model rejection — never masking auth/content/network failures behind a model swap.

Native-module packaging has actual CI assertions, not just config: ci.yml asserts better_sqlite3.node AND fsevents are present under app.asar.unpacked/ on every PR (and again on macOS), which is a genuine generalization of the #540 class rather than a one-off fix.

Electron fuses are set conservatively in forge.config.ts: RunAsNode off, EnableNodeOptionsEnvironmentVariable off, EnableNodeCliInspectArguments off, cookie encryption on, asar integrity validation on, OnlyLoadAppFromAsar on.

Both userData JSON stores write via tmp + rename (writeJsonAtomic, reused by appConfig after BUG-13/#518), and every read path is null-tolerant — a corrupt conversation file is skipped rather than breaking the whole list.

The reaper's design instinct is right even though its list is wrong: EPHEMERAL_WT_NAME is an explicit allowlist with a written rationale for why a shape-match ('-<26 chars>$') would be latent data loss against job-<ulid> worktrees. Allowlist-over-denylist for a destructive guard is the correct call.

Prior-review issues closed without a linked PR did in fact land as code: #505 (single-walk graph projection), #506 (devlog tail read + researcher due-check memo), #507 (priority lock lane, off-lock connect precheck), #508 (least-squares leak slope, sparse checkout), #513, #514 (process-wide RecallClient), #515 (boundedGit + before-quit flush), #518 (atomic appConfig write), #528 (deciderScaffold) are all present and annotated on main.

Hygiene metrics are unusually clean for a 46k-LOC codebase built in ten weeks: 0 TODO/FIXME, 2 eslint-disable, 10 `any`, and comments that record *why* a guard exists (with issue numbers) rather than restating the code.
open_questions: Root cause of the compose-worktree leak beyond the missing allowlist entry: 185 directories exist on disk but only 8 have `.git/worktrees` admin entries, so most were partially torn down (admin entry gone, files left) rather than never cleaned. Was `git worktree remove --force` failing on these nested-in-staging worktrees, or did `fs.rm` fail? Both are silently caught, so the transcript is gone — a repro under load would settle whether the allowlist fix alone is sufficient.

Is Windows actually a shipped target for the first pre-release? MakerSquirrel is configured and nightly.yml runs a Windows e2e leg, but #56 (macOS TCC) is the only platform MUST and signing is macOS-only. The CRLF finding (RISK-4) is release-blocking if yes and deferrable if no — this needs an explicit product call, not an inference from the maker list.

Where do real users' vaults live? WAL-mode SQLite plus a git repo inside an iCloud Drive / Dropbox / OneDrive folder (the default home for Obsidian vaults) is a corruption surface the code does not currently consider. Related: should `.kb/cache/` move out of the vault entirely so the vault stays knowledge-only and sync-safe?

Is `@github/copilot-sdk` beta.7 → 1.0.x a supported upgrade, and does the app want a declared minimum `copilot` CLI version? The probe's own comment records that accepted model ids differ between CLI 0.0.373 and 1.0.62, but nothing enforces a floor.

Was the memory sampler's `mem.sample`-at-info level a deliberate choice (trend data is the point) or an oversight? The answer decides between lowering the level and giving the sampler its own sink file — both are one-line changes but they serve different intents.

Does the vault need a size/health budget at all? 3.6 GB for 336 sources is dominated by the leak, but even post-fix the vault carries a 21 MB index, a 2.1 MB graph projection, 1.5 MB of spans and 2.2 MB of pipeline log inside `.kb/cache/`. A user-visible disk readout would have surfaced this in week one.

domains.label: platform
domains.title: Platform support (macOS / Windows / Linux)
domains.verdict: macOS (the primary target) is genuinely well-engineered for platform quirks (TCC, PATH, signing, tray/Dock lifecycle); Windows is formally a "must" (STACK-3) but has never once produced a working packaged build in ~7.5 weeks of daily CI, and a second, independent, unmitigated defect (CRLF line endings breaking the frontmatter parsers) would break the core pipeline on a very common Windows git config even if packaging were fixed; Linux is an unverified bystander (makers registered, never built) that happens to boot under xvfb by accident of a different job.
domains.summary:
This domain splits sharply into "macOS: cared for" and "Windows/Linux: assumed, unverified, actively broken in two independent ways." macOS gets real engineering investment: SPEC-0034's TCC/signing work is substantially built and verified (MACOS-3/5/6 marked verified by an empirical signed-build run), the tray/Dock dual-lifecycle (QCAP-8) is intentional and tested, PATH resolution (resolvePath.ts) correctly recovers a GUI process's login-shell PATH with Windows-aware PATHEXT-style suffix fallback (resolveExecutable tries `.exe/.cmd/.bat` on win32), watched-folder ingestion uses chokidar's native per-OS backends (fsevents/inotify/ReadDirectoryChanges, no polling) with symlink-following disabled, and the entity-filename sanitizer (entityFileName) thoughtfully strips path-hostile characters, control bytes, and leading/trailing dots — explicitly citing "Windows hazards" in its own doc comment. All 14 process.platform call sites in prod code gate cleanly (darwin-only TCC/screenshot/selection-capture, win32-only PATH no-op and PATHEXT fallback) with sensible degrade-not-crash behavior everywhere checked.

But the two "must"/committed non-macOS platforms don't hold up under direct verification. First, Windows packaging is completely dead: every nightly e2e-matrix run since the workflow's first execution on 2026-07-13 through today (2026-09-04 — roughly 53 consecutive days) fails at the "Package the app" step itself, before e2e even runs, with an identical node-gyp error rebuilding better-sqlite3's native binding: `Error: Could not find any Visual Studio installation to use`, despite the runner's own log showing VS Enterprise IS present (@electron/node-gyp's VS-detection script hits `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER` and can't parse a newer VS version string). This directly falsifies STACK-3 ("app packages for macOS and Windows," Verify: none-yet) and — since release.yml's build job runs the identical `npm run package` step on the identical windows-latest matrix entry, and better-sqlite3 postdates release.yml's one and only run (2026-06-28, before the SQLite index landed) — a real `git tag v*` push today would almost certainly reproduce the same failure, meaning the Release workflow's Windows artifact is untested and very likely broken too. Second, independent of packaging, a CRLF line-ending defect would break the pipeline's own markdown parsers on any Windows machine using Git for Windows' own recommended default (`core.autocrlf=true`): I verified directly (`node -e`) that the non-multiline regex idiom used throughout the doc parsers, e.g. `/^id:\s*(.+)$/`, fails to match a line with a trailing `\r` (JS's `.` excludes CR as a line terminator), and this exact idiom recurs in connectDoc.ts's parseEntityNode (id/kind/name — all three required, so the whole entity throws), claimsStage.ts (kind/name/subject/status/confidence), connectStage.ts, mergeNodes.ts, and recallTools.ts — roughly 87 `.split('\n')`-based line parsers across 56 prod files use this general style. The trigger is real: `ensureStagingWorktree` performs an actual `git worktree add` checkout of the `staging` branch — the pipeline's own operational root — and neither the app repo nor a newly-created vault (`vault.ts`'s scaffold, which writes `.gitignore`/README but never `.gitattributes`) ever forces LF, so a checkout on an autocrlf=true machine would smudge every existing tracked markdown file to CRLF before the very next parse.

Beyond those two headline defects, I found a cluster of smaller but concrete platform gaps. There is no `app.requestSingleInstanceLock()` anywhere; combined with QCAP-8 (never quit on window-all-closed on macOS) and a background pipeline whose canonical-writer serialization is explicitly an in-process `Mutex` only ("the engine runs in-process, so a single shared Mutex instance... IS that serialized writer" — stageLock.ts's own comment), a double-launch would run two uncoordinated processes against the same vault git repo. `entityFileRel`'s within-kind collision guard does exact string comparison on the `taken` Set, so two entities whose names differ only by case (e.g. "Apple"/"apple") are never flagged as colliding, yet resolve to the same path on both shipped platforms' default case-insensitive filesystems (macOS APFS, Windows NTFS) — silent data loss, verified by direct code reading, untested. `entityFileName` has no Windows reserved-device-name guard (CON/PRN/AUX/NUL/COM1-9/LPT1-9). `build/icon.ico` has never existed despite forge.config.ts's own comment describing exactly where the packager needs it, and despite full multi-resolution PNG source art already sitting in `brand/assets/icon/png/` — nobody ever ran it through an ico packer. Linux is the least-verified: no nightly/CI job has ever run `npm run make` on a Linux runner (release.yml's build matrix is `[macos-latest, windows-latest]` only), so MakerDeb/MakerRpm — both registered in forge.config.ts — have never once executed; and the one CI path that would validate an actual xvfb-launched Linux boot (ci.yml's dispatch-only `snapshots` job) has itself never been dispatched with `update_snapshots=true` in this repo's history, so the two committed `*-linux.png` baselines have unverified CI provenance. Finally, the observed userData-directory drift ('kb-app'/'KB-App'/'vellum'/'Vellum' all coexisting under Application Support, already noted this session) has zero migration code anywhere and would manifest identically — but guaranteed, not filesystem-dependent — on Linux's strictly case-sensitive `~/.config/`.

strengths: macOS TCC/signing (SPEC-0034) is the one platform area with real spec depth and empirical verification: MACOS-3 (stable signing identity) and MACOS-5 (TCC grant propagates to spawned git/copilot subprocesses) are marked verified from an actual DEV-2 signed-build run, not just claimed.

resolvePath.ts is genuinely platform-careful: recovers the login-shell PATH via `$SHELL -ilc` for GUI-launched processes (fixing the classic Finder/Dock stripped-PATH problem), is a correct no-op on win32 ("no-op on Windows (different model)", app/src/main/resolvePath.ts:95-97), and resolveExecutable (line 111-113) tries `.exe/.cmd/.bat` PATHEXT-style suffixes on win32 — this is the kind of cross-platform CLI-discovery code that's easy to get wrong and here it's correct and unit-tested.

chokidar watch config (watchScheduler.ts) uses each OS's native backend (fsevents/inotify/ReadDirectoryChanges — no usePolling) with followSymlinks:false and non-recursive depth:0 for v1, and moveOriginalToArchive (watchConnectors.ts) already handles the EXDEV cross-device rename case with a copy-then-unlink fallback.

entityFileName (connectDoc.ts:62-68) is a thoughtful cross-platform filename sanitizer: strips path separators, wikilink-significant chars, C0 control bytes, drops leading/trailing dots and spaces with an explicit "Windows hazards" comment, and caps length — clearly platform-aware design even where it has gaps (case-folding, reserved names).

Quick Capture's two macOS-exclusive richer input modes (screenshot capture via `screencapture`, selection-read via AppleScript) degrade cleanly rather than half-working: both are gated on process.platform === 'darwin', and the renderer hides the screenshot button cluster entirely off-macOS (`if (ctx.screenshotSupported) shots.hidden = false;`) rather than showing a broken affordance.

e2e/packagedApp.ts correctly resolves the platform-specific packaged-binary path for all three OSes (darwin .app bundle, win32 .exe, linux binary) — the e2e harness itself is platform-honest even though the CI matrix around it has gaps.
The macOS Dock+tray dual-lifecycle (QCAP-8, lifecycle.ts) is a small, pure, unit-tested function (`shouldQuitOnWindowAllClosed`) with a clear one-line policy, not scattered platform conditionals.
open_questions: Does the Windows packaging failure (PLAT-1) reproduce with a pinned/newer @electron/rebuild or by explicitly setting GYP_MSVS_VERSION/vcvars — i.e. is this a one-line CI fix or does it need a deeper native-toolchain workaround? I could not test this without running `npm run package`, which was out of scope for this session.

Does the obsidian://open?path= URI actually round-trip correctly with a Windows absolute path's backslashes once percent-encoded (citationLink.ts's obsidianOpenUri), or does Obsidian's URI handler require forward slashes on Windows too? I found no test or code comment addressing this and could not verify on a real Windows/Obsidian install.

Is Linux genuinely a committed v1 target, or is it carried in forge.config.ts (MakerDeb/MakerRpm) more speculatively than STACK-3 (which only names macOS and Windows) implies? This materially changes whether PLAT-7/PLAT-8 are scope gaps or correctly-deprioritized nice-to-haves — worth a product-owner ruling rather than treating both as equally urgent.

Does maker-rpm's `rpmbuild` dependency actually exist on GitHub's ubuntu-latest runner image today? I did not run `npm run make` (out of scope), so PLAT-7's exact first-failure mode on Linux is inferred from the total absence of any prior run, not directly observed.

Global-shortcut (Quick Capture's hotkey) and Tray/AppIndicator behavior under a Wayland-only Linux session are both well-known rough edges for Electron generally; I could not verify Vellum's specific behavior there since no Linux runtime CI exists at all (this is really the same root gap as PLAT-7/PLAT-8, not a separate finding).

domains.label: headless
domains.title: Headless-run, daemon readiness & provider (Copilot/BYOA) surface
domains.verdict: Unstarted at the architecture level (RFC #531 is 0% implemented — no daemon, no utilityProcess, no localhost transport) but standing on a genuinely well-engineered, electron-free provider/concurrency substrate that materially de-risks the eventual work.
domains.summary:
This domain splits cleanly into two halves that should not be graded the same way. The provider/BYOA surface — model resolution, concurrency, egress security, researcher scheduling — is some of the most careful engineering in the repo: an AIMD adaptive-concurrency controller that classifies rate-limit vs content errors and backs off only on real throttling (copilotAdaptive.ts), a per-stage-reservation semaphore that prevents the observed BLOCKED-Claims starvation pathology (copilotConcurrency.ts, SCALE-3), a model-resolution ladder that probes the live CLI's accepted catalog instead of trusting a hardcoded pin (copilotModelProbe.ts, ORCH-28), and a genuinely hardened egress path for the Web researcher — static allowlist THEN a custom DNS-rebinding-safe connect-time lookup (researchFetch.ts) — that goes well beyond a token gate. All of this is unit-tested (28-30 tests per module) and matches its specs closely. Jobs and researchers (SPEC-0023/0028) both run as restart-safe, single-flight, audit-derived-due schedulers that never block live capture (JOBS-3/5, ORCH-17/18), verified directly in code, not just spec prose.

The other half — headless-run itself, the subject GitHub #531 exists to plan — is untouched: zero commits reference headless/daemon/utilityProcess since the RFC was filed on 2026-07-12, and main hasn't moved since 07-13. The engine-purity claim the RFC rests on is real and actually stronger than advertised: not just src/kb (0 electron imports across 165 files) but main/pipeline.ts and main/pipelineLifecycle.ts — the actual production startPipeline() orchestration layer — are ALSO 100% electron-free, with only 3 app.getPath() call sites in the whole main tier. A daemon bootstrap could therefore call the real production code path directly rather than reimplementing wiring, a better starting position than the RFC's own framing ("the eval runner proves it") suggests — but the eval runner (eval/runner/actions.ts) is NOT that bootstrap: it hand-wires Orchestrator/ConnectStage/ClaimsStage directly, skips JobScheduler/ResearcherScheduler entirely, and is invoked via `vitest run`, not a standalone binary. There is no headless entry point today at all — `npm start` (electron-forge start) is the only way to run the app.

Every piece Phase A needs is either present-but-unguarded or absent: the 71 request/response + 3 push channels are genuinely serializable (zero function-typed fields in any payload before the KbApi interface), and a direct diff of preload.ts vs ipc.ts channel names confirms today's parity is correct — but by hand, with no test, which is exactly the acceptance criterion #531 names before Phase A can safely promote ipc.ts's handler bodies. Phase B (utilityProcess isolation) has a concrete, verifiable motivation still live in the code: startTelemetry's uncaughtException handler force-exits the whole main process, and since the engine still runs in that same process, any uncaught exception anywhere in orchestration takes the open window down with it. Phase C (localhost daemon) has zero groundwork — no net.createServer/http.createServer/WebSocket anywhere in src/main or src/kb.

A closer look at "can it run unattended" surfaces a real, verifiable gap the RFC doesn't mention: shouldQuitOnWindowAllClosed returns true for every platform except darwin, so on Windows/Linux the entire process — pipeline, jobs, researchers, quick-capture — dies the moment the last window closes; only macOS's Dock+tray dual-model (QCAP-8) keeps it alive. "Headless-run is a ratified product requirement" is therefore true today only on one of three desktop platforms, and even there it stops the instant the user actually quits — there is zero use of Electron's Notification API anywhere, so a Review awaiting a decision (a research depth-escalation, a job disposition) surfaces nowhere except the passive tray status line, which only reports whole-pipeline stalls, not individual pending decisions.

The most concrete, independently verified finding is a partially-landed closed issue: #514 promised (as explicit acceptance criteria) moving background-decider prompts from CLI argv to stdin/temp-file and capping every tool result at 32KB (with a 5MB-source truncation test). The process-leak fix, progress push, honest Quick-tier, and priority-reserved semaphore slot from that same issue are all genuinely implemented and verified in code — but the prompt-size-bound half is not: every one of the six thin deciders still embeds the full, unbounded source text into a single `execFile('copilot', ['-p', prompt, ...])` argv argument, and recallTools.readSource/readNode return whole files via an untruncated cache, in contrast to recall.ts's own conversation history, which DID get the promised windowing (MAX_HISTORY_TURNS=10, MAX_HISTORY_TURN_CHARS=2000). This is exactly the "closure ≠ landed code" pattern the review brief asked to check for, caught here with a specific, citable gap rather than a general suspicion.

strengths: AIMD adaptive concurrency controller (copilotAdaptive.ts) correctly distinguishes rate-limit signatures from truncated-JSON content errors (including the subtle 'position 429' false-positive class already caught by QD-2/#357) so it only backs off on real throttling — a pure, deterministic, well-tested state machine.

The concurrency semaphore (copilotConcurrency.ts) implements a genuine no-starvation reservation (SCALE-3) plus an interactive-priority lane with bounded timeout (ASK-16) — directly fixes the observed live BLOCKED-Claims pathology SPEC-0048 documents, and is exercised by ~30 unit tests.

Model resolution (copilotModelProbe.ts, ORCH-28) probes the live CLI's actually-accepted catalog rather than trusting a hardcoded pin, with an ordered preference ladder, per-stage tiering, and a visible (never silent) degradation signal — directly responsive to the 'claude-opus-4 hard-rejected pre-flight' regression it documents fixing.

Web-researcher egress defense (researchFetch.ts) is real defense-in-depth: a static allowlist (isAllowedUrl) THEN a custom DNS lookup wired into the http(s) Agent that re-validates the RESOLVED address at connect time, closing the DNS-rebinding hole a static host check alone would miss.

JobScheduler and ResearcherScheduler are both restart-safe (audit/journal-derived 'due' checks, no fragile persisted timer state), single-flight-guarded, and run concurrently with live capture without blocking it (JOBS-3/5, ORCH-17/18) — verified directly in the scheduler code, not just asserted in spec prose.

The KbApi wire contract is cleanly serializable today (no functions/classes in any payload type) and channel-name parity between preload.ts and ipc.ts is currently correct by direct diff — a real, if currently unguarded, head start on #531 Phase A.

Provider-surface code is unusually well self-documented with root-cause commit history embedded in comments (e.g. copilotModel.ts's account of the gpt-5.5 unpinned-model regression), making the design intent auditable without archaeology.
open_questions: Is there an actual, confirmed `workiq` CLI / `@workiq/cli` npm package the team has installed and tested end-to-end, or is the M365/WorkIQ researcher still entirely unverified against a real server? The code's own comments suggest the latter but this could not be checked against the npm registry from this sandboxed, offline environment.

Given main has been dormant 7 weeks with #531 untouched, is headless-run still an active near-term priority, or has it been implicitly deprioritized behind the SPEC-0061 functional rethink? The spec index doesn't say.
Should 'headless-run' be explicitly re-scoped to macOS-only in the spec until Phase C lands, given the current Windows/Linux behavior (DAEMON-3) contradicts the stated cross-platform requirement?

domains.label: release
domains.title: Release readiness of the de-facto beta (main @19bb68f) & release-blocker triage
domains.domain: Release readiness of the de-facto beta (main @19bb68f) & release-blocker triage
domains.verdict: Buildable but never once executed end-to-end: a private v0.1.0-rc.1 dry run fails at the first gate for a trivial reason (package.json is still 0.1.0), and a public release is additionally blocked by unsigned/un-notarized artifacts, the still-open TCC MUST (#56), and missing LICENSE/CHANGELOG/release-notes machinery.
domains.summary:
The release lane is real, small, well-commented and unit-tested — and has never run. Zero tags, zero GitHub releases, and exactly one Release workflow run ever (28308929235, 2026-06-28): a 0-second "workflow file issue" failure on a branch push of a draft workflow later superseded by #560/#569. The first real tag is therefore an untested path.

I walked that path by running the gates. The verify job would PASS on 19bb68f: I fetched the commit's real check-runs with the same gh api call the workflow makes and ran verifyRequiredChecks.mjs against it — all three ruleset contexts (typecheck · lint · unit (ubuntu-latest), secret scan, package build-check (ubuntu-latest)) are present and green, exit 0. ci.yml runs on push to main, so squash-merge commits genuinely carry required checks; the biggest structural risk I expected is not a problem. But `node tagVersion.mjs v0.1.0-rc.1` exits 1 — package.json is 0.1.0, so the documented -rc.N dry-run convention cannot be exercised on 19bb68f without first merging a version-bump PR. A bare v0.1.0 tag passes verify but then publish omits --prerelease and drafts a STABLE release of an unsigned build. That is REL-1: the one true blocker for the dry run, and a one-line fix.

The verify gate also has a correctness hole. evaluateRequiredChecks picks the latest run "by completed_at", but an in-flight re-run has completed_at: null, which collapses to '' and loses the reduce to the older success. I proved it: a payload with a completed success plus an in-progress re-run of the same check reports "all required checks are green", exit 0. The unit tests cover a single pending run and a completed re-run, never the combination. Anyone who re-runs CI on the release SHA and tags while it is in flight ships from an unverified commit (REL-4).

Distribution reality is the public-release wall. forge.config.ts signs only under KB_OSX_SIGN=1 and release.yml sets no such flag and holds no Apple secrets, so the macOS .zip is unsigned and un-notarized — Gatekeeper quarantines a downloaded zip and modern macOS reports "damaged / cannot be opened" without an xattr or right-click-Open workaround. SPEC-0055 RELEASE-4 says an unsigned artifact "must never publish" and SPEC-0034 MACOS-8 makes notarized distribution a must; the shipped workflow violates both by design and says so in its own header. This also keeps #56 (open MUST) unfixed: an unsigned build's TCC grant does not propagate to spawned git/copilot, so a vault in ~/Documents silently stalls. The interim mitigation DID land — appRoute.ts warns on a TCC-protected folder and gates first run behind a permission pre-prompt — but that is a warning, not the MUST.

Windows is weaker than the matrix implies. build/icon.ico is absent (build/ holds only entitlements.mac.plist, icon.icns, icon.png), and @electron/packager's normalizeIconExtension warns-and-skips rather than failing, so the Windows .exe and the Squirrel installer ship the default Electron icon silently. Functionally, shouldQuitOnWindowAllClosed returns true on win32, so closing the window kills the background librarian — the product's core promise — and selection capture and screenshot are darwin-only. Publishing a Windows artifact alongside macOS in v0.1.0 sets a false expectation.

Security posture for a shipped build is mostly good and narrowly bad. Fuses are set correctly (RunAsNode off, cookie encryption on, asar integrity + OnlyLoadAppFromAsar on), crashReporter runs uploadToServer:false, there is no telemetry egress, and gitleaks gates every PR. Of the 46 audit findings only two reach the shipped bundle: electron 42.2.0 (high, patch fix 42.11.2) and dompurify 3.4.5 (moderate, IN_PLACE-mode advisories not reachable given askView's string-mode sanitize). js-yaml 4.1.0 is dev-only — zero imports under app/src, used solely by eval/runner/loader.ts. The genuine gap is renderer hardening: no Content-Security-Policy anywhere (no meta tag, no onHeadersReceived), and no setWindowOpenHandler or will-navigate guard, while preload exposes 79 kb:* channels via contextBridge. Sanitized markdown can still emit an http anchor, and a click navigates the app window to a remote origin that keeps window.kbApi.

On the 18 July issues closed without a linked PR: I traced every one and they all landed (#506 to #542, #507 to #555/#546/#562, #513/#514 to #543, #515 to eec2367/#544, #519/#520 to #547, #521-524 to #550/#557, #526 to #533, #528 to #572/#577, #529 to #560/#569, #530 to #549/#562). No P0 closed without code. That is a bookkeeping habit, not a hole — but it does mean --generate-notes cannot classify per RELEASE-11.

Finally, the nightly has been red every night since 2026-07-13 (~54 consecutive runs) and filed zero tracking issues, because report-red inherits the workflow-level working-directory: app with no checkout step. I confirmed all three failing e2e assertions are stale selectors (.ask-transcript, .agents-hub-title, .activity-empty are all absent from src), not real regressions — but a permanently-red lane that cannot self-report is exactly what hides the next real one.

strengths: The verify gate is genuinely well-built for its size: two pure, CLI-wrapped modules (tagVersion.mjs, verifyRequiredChecks.mjs) with 14 unit tests between them, so the matching rules are testable rather than only exercised in CI. The required check names in REQUIRED_CHECK_NAMES exactly match the live ruleset (17072781) and the real check-runs on main's head — I replayed the workflow's own gh api call and it passes.

ci.yml runs on `push: branches: [main]`, so a squash-merge commit on main really does carry all three required check-runs. The most plausible way a tag-triggered release gate fails (checks only existing on the PR merge ref) does not apply here.

The publish job's authors already spotted the workflow-level `defaults.run.working-directory: app` trap and overrode it with `working-directory: .` on its only run step — the exact bug that silently killed nightly's report-red job. It also refuses to draft an empty release (`if [ ${#FILES[@]} -eq 0 ] ... exit 1`) and never auto-publishes.

Electron hardening at package time is correct and deliberate: FusesPlugin disables RunAsNode, NODE_OPTIONS and CLI inspect, enables cookie encryption, embedded asar integrity validation and OnlyLoadAppFromAsar. BrowserWindow relies on Electron 42 secure defaults (contextIsolation on, nodeIntegration off, sandbox on) rather than weakening them.

Privacy posture is release-clean: crashReporter starts with uploadToServer:false (local minidumps only) and there is no telemetry or analytics egress anywhere in main. The only outbound path is the user's own BYOA copilot CLI.

First-run prerequisite detection is better than the #65/#160 class would suggest: setup surfaces git-installed / is-git-repo / Copilot-detected checks, hard-disables Create Library when git is missing, warns explicitly on a TCC-protected folder, and gates the first run behind a permission pre-prompt whose Continue triggers the real macOS grant dialog with a Blocked recovery loop.
RELEASE-6 is genuinely closed: kb:getAppVersion -> app.getVersion() is wired end-to-end and About renders it defensively ('Version unavailable' on failure, never blank).

The packaging story for native deps is solved and continuously proven: the ubuntu package build-check is required on every PR, and the macOS package build-check has been green every night for 7 weeks, asserting a launchable out/Vellum-darwin-*/Vellum.app. forge.config.ts's hand-written `ignore` carve-out for better-sqlite3 and fsevents is documented with the empirical reasoning behind it.
Traceability held up under audit: all 18 July issues that were closed without a linked PR actually landed in merged commits, and no P0 was closed without code.
Only two of 46 audit findings reach the shipped artifact; js-yaml — the scariest-looking prod-sounding advisory — is correctly a devDependency with zero imports under app/src.
open_questions: Is the intended first tag `v0.1.0-rc.1` (release.yml's own comments and tagVersion.mjs's examples) or `v0.1.0-beta.1` (SPEC-0055 RELEASE-2)? The version-bump PR that unblocks REL-1 has to commit to one, and the answer also decides whether the trigger glob should be tightened to -beta.N only.

Where do the Apple signing/notarization credentials live today? SPEC-0034 section 5 says both Apple Development and Developer ID Application certs are already in the Principal's keychain and only notarization creds (an App Store Connect API key) are missing — if that is still true, REL-2 is closer to an afternoon of secret provisioning than an L, and the estimate should drop.

Is the private rc actually private? release.yml drafts a release on a PUBLIC repo (masra91/Vellum-KB). A draft is maintainer-only until published, but the tag itself is public, so the 'private dry run' framing depends on nobody publishing the draft. Worth confirming the intent before the first tag.

Should the Windows leg ship at all in v0.1.0? SPEC-0055 section 1 says macOS first and puts Windows signing out of v1, yet the build matrix is 50% Windows and the app quits the background pipeline on window close there. This is a product call, not an engineering one.

The nightly has been red for ~54 consecutive runs with nobody notified (REL-5). Was anyone expected to be watching, or was the auto-filed issue the entire monitoring plan? The answer determines whether fixing report-red is sufficient or whether a notification channel is also needed.

No packaged build was produced in this lane, so REL-9 (missing icon.ico), REL-13 (Windows lifecycle) and REL-17 (default menu) are static conclusions. A single `npm run make` on windows-latest via a workflow_dispatch rehearsal would confirm all three cheaply.

domains.label: process
domains.title: Process & repository hygiene (neutral observation of how the work happens)
domains.verdict: A genuinely disciplined-looking process on paper (living specs, requirement IDs, a two-gate design review, a required-checks ruleset) that in practice runs almost entirely on a single human's trust in a single AI identity — self-authored, self-reviewed, self-merged at bursty high velocity — and whose one independent safety net (the nightly lane) has been silently broken and unwatched for the entire 7-week dormancy.
domains.summary:
The repo's process artifacts are unusually rich for a pre-release project: 61 living specs with 868 requirement IDs and 228 Verify: methods, a documented two-gate design-review workflow (SPEC-0033), a required 3-context CI ruleset that is genuinely green, and an INDEX.md that is 100% in sync with the spec files on disk. But the artifacts that record process quality tell a much thinner story than the artifacts that record product intent. Every one of the 505 merged PRs (of 516 total; 0 open) was authored, commented on, and merged by the same single GitHub identity (masra91) — 0 formal GitHub PR reviews exist anywhere in the repo's history, verified both in bulk (GraphQL over all 505) and by direct spot-check. The documented QA/design-gate process (gate-1 AI-patterns detector, gate-2 QA/Driver) is real and is self-reported in prose inside 234/505 (46.3%) of squash-commit bodies ("@KB-Quality-Driver-2 ready for QA," "Fixed the two citation nits KB-QD flagged"), and SPEC-0033 formally specifies it — but every one of its 8 must/should requirements (DESIGN-1..8) is still marked `Verify: none-yet`, and nothing on GitHub's structured layer (reviews, approvals, required-reviewer rules) enforces or records that the gates ran. The trust chain from "closed" to "shipped" holds up well under audit — of 45 issues (70.3% of all 64 closed issues) closed with no GitHub-recognized linked PR, spot-checking ~28 of them found code had landed for all but one (#104, whose shipping commits never mention its issue number by exact digits) — but the traceability is manual archaeology (informal "#521-524" ranges and comma lists that GitHub's auto-linker doesn't parse), not a mechanically verifiable property.

Two verification-of-verification gaps stand out. First, root CLAUDE.md — read by every fresh agent bootstrapping in any worktree — was silently clobbered by an unrelated feature commit (#333, 2026-06-13) with one KB-Developer-2 worktree's local persona instructions, replacing the shared "KB-App" project overview; nothing caught it for a full month, through the project's busiest days, until a dedicated fix commit (#583) on 2026-07-13 restored it and gitignored `.claude/`/`.clubhouse/` to reduce recurrence. Second, and more current: the nightly/weekly lane (`nightly.yml`, added the same day, 07-12/13) is the one channel meant to catch drift the required per-PR gate is too cheap to catch — and its own `report-red` auto-filer job has been broken since day one (workflow-level `defaults.run.working-directory: app` applies to a job with no checkout step, so `bash` can't find `/…/app`). Every fetched nightly run (61/61) has failed, including today's (2026-09-04), the e2e matrix has failed the same 3 deterministic, IA-drifted selectors on both OSes since inception, and the auto-filer that exists specifically to make that visible has itself failed silently every single time — so zero `nightly-red` tracking issues were ever created. The alarm that watches the fire is on fire, and nobody has been alerted to either.

Elsewhere the hygiene picture is mixed-but-mundane: 144 remote branches remain, effectively 100% of them >30 days stale (main has been dormant 7 weeks) and 136 (94%) are simply leftovers from already-merged PRs whose branch-delete step (documented as automatic in CLAUDE.md's `/merge` skill) only actually fires 73.1% of the time. Spec `status` is essentially inert — 57/61 specs (93.4%) sit at `draft` forever, including fully-shipped, iterated features (SPEC-0026 Ask, SPEC-0058 UI State Model), and `deprecated`/`superseded` (both valid per the template) have never been used even once, including for SPEC-0030 (Pipeline Status), whose feature was explicitly dissolved by SPEC-0060 VUX-4. SPECSYS-7 ("spec and code change together") is followed on only 32.3% of code-touching commits despite being a named engineering rule. Acceptance-criteria checkboxes are decorative: 129 checkbox items across 37 issues, zero ever checked, including on issues explicitly closed COMPLETED. And issue #56 — a self-titled "MUST" bug about silent vault-write failures on TCC-protected macOS folders — carries zero labels and a title that still reads as an open, severity-MUST defect 94 days after filing, even though a same-week Principal-ruling comment (06-03, one day after filing) says the functional bug shipped via #201 and only a deferred notarized-distribution tail remains — stale metadata that could mislead exactly the kind of external triage this review performed. None of this looks like negligence so much as a process built for and by a single continuously-present operator, where velocity (89.9% of all merges landed on just 10 of 21 active days; 45.9% of PRs merged within 10 minutes of opening) substitutes for the review layer a multi-party team would need — durable as long as that one operator keeps watching, and untested by 7 weeks of not watching.

Agent-persona structure visibly matured over the project's life (ad hoc KB-Worker-1/2 + KB-Architect in week 1 retired in favor of the current 14-role PM/Lead/7-Developer/2-QD/2-Design-Lead/AI-Detector/Special-Agent structure) rather than staying static.
open_questions: What did the Clubhouse bulletin/board (agent chat) actually contain for the 234 PRs that mention gate/QD/driver sign-off in their commit body — is there a durable transcript anywhere outside GitHub, or does that history disappear once the board channel rolls over?

Is there any intent to promote spec status out of 'draft' as features ship (a lint or manual pass), or is 'draft' now understood project-wide to just mean 'not SPEC-0000/0011/0012/0060' regardless of build state?

Does the human Principal have a documented recovery plan if the single shared GitHub identity's credentials are lost, given 100% of authorship/merge/review history is undifferentiated across all 14 personas?
Was the nightly lane's red status ever actually seen by a human/agent through the Actions UI directly (bypassing the broken auto-filer), or has it truly been unobserved for 7 weeks?

Now that main has been dormant 7 weeks, is there a plan to sweep the 136 orphaned merged-PR branches and the ~4 closed-unmerged-PR branches, or is branch cleanup considered out of scope until active development resumes?

domains.label: deps-security
domains.title: Dependencies, supply chain & security posture
domains.verdict: Genuinely thoughtful security engineering at the code layer (SSRF gate, symlink-safe path containment, prompt-injection fencing, consistent output-escaping, Electron fuses, zero credential storage) sits on top of a supply-chain/process layer that has had zero eyes on it for 7 weeks — no CI vulnerability gate, 44% of deps violate the project's own exact-pin rule, and Actions aren't SHA-pinned; the raw "46 vulnerabilities" number is far scarier than the actual reachable risk once traced against real code paths.
domains.summary:
This domain splits cleanly into two stories that point opposite directions. At the application-code layer, the security engineering is unusually careful for a project this young. The SSRF defense in kb/researchFetch.ts is a genuine two-gate design — a static allowlist (isAllowedUrl) plus a DNS-rebinding-safe connect-time lookup (makeSsrfSafeLookup) that checks the *resolved* address, not just the hostname, and explicitly rejects IPv4-mapped-IPv6 smuggling forms. kb/pathContainment.ts is a single, symlink-safe, shared containment primitive (realpaths the deepest existing ancestor before comparing) used by every fs sink that takes an LLM-derived relative path. kb/untrustedSource.ts fences every source-reading decider against prompt injection from pulled feed content. Every one of the ~130 `innerHTML` assignments I sampled across 15 view files (activityView, agentsView, jobsView, healthView, exploreView, reviewsView, askView, captureView, topbarSearch, appRoute) routes vault/LLM-derived text through the shared `esc()` helper before interpolation — I went looking for a missed-escape XSS hole (the classic failure mode for template-string rendering at this scale) and did not find one; the handful of unescaped interpolations I found were all safe (textContent assignments, or hardcoded showcase-page strings). preload.ts exposes a minimal, fully-typed contextBridge surface with no raw `ipcRenderer`/`require` passthrough. forge.config.ts enables all six recommended Electron Fuses (RunAsNode off, ASAR integrity validation on, OnlyLoadAppFromAsar on, etc.). The app stores zero Copilot/GitHub credentials itself (BYOA — `gh` CLI owns auth entirely), sends zero telemetry anywhere, disables crash-report upload, and never renders PDFs (only `getTextContent()` with `isEvalSupported:false`) or parses archives at all.

The supply-chain and process layer tells a different story. There is no Content-Security-Policy anywhere (no `<meta>` tag in index.html, no `onHeadersReceived` in main.ts) — the sole backstop for that entire manually-escaped rendering surface is developer discipline, with no structural second line of defense. package.json pins 17 of 39 declared dependencies (44%) with `^`/`~` rather than exact versions, in direct violation of SPEC-0011's ENG-4 "must" rule — including three production dependencies (better-sqlite3, electron-squirrel-startup, simple-git). No workflow in .github/workflows/ ever runs `npm audit`, and there is no dependabot.yml or renovate.json, so the 46 vulnerabilities the appendix already caught (3 critical, 36 high) accumulated with zero automated visibility through the entire 7-week main-dormancy — the same blind-spot pattern already seen in the nightly-red story for this repo.

Reachability triage of the actual flagged CVEs, though, undercuts the audit's scary top-line number. Of the 4 direct-dependency CVEs: electron's `ProtocolResponse.url` bug requires the app to register a custom protocol/session, which it never does; js-yaml's merge-key prototype pollution requires the app to feed untrusted YAML through it, but every vault frontmatter parser is explicitly hand-rolled ("no yaml dependency (ENG-5)") — js-yaml is a devDependency used only by the eval harness's scenario loader, over developer-authored files; dompurify's IN_PLACE-mode XSS requires that mode to be enabled, and the app's one DOMPurify call site uses the safe default; vitest's arbitrary-file-read CVE requires the Vitest UI server to be running, which no script in package.json ever starts. None of the four is reachable through this app's actual code paths or CI surface today. That doesn't make them unimportant — all four have cheap, rule-compliant bumps available (all satisfy the project's own ≥7-day-old rule except electron's suggested fix, 42.11.2, which was published on the very day of this review and should be skipped for an older 42.x patch that already contains the fix, e.g. 42.9.x/42.10.1) — but it reframes "46 vulnerabilities, 3 critical" from an emergency into a hygiene backlog. The bulk of the "high" count (34 of 36) traces to the @electron-forge/* build toolchain's transitive tar/extract-zip/tmp dependencies; npm audit's own suggested fix is a downgrade to the old 6.x major line, which is not a real remediation — this repo is already on forge's current stable release (7.11.2 is the `latest` dist-tag), and the vulnerable transitive deps are unresolved upstream with only an 8.0.0-alpha line available. That risk lives entirely on developer/CI machines during `npm run package`, never in the shipped app.

Rounding out the CI supply-chain: all `uses:` references across the three workflows are pinned by mutable tag (`@v4`), not immutable SHA — standard hardening advice that's cheap to apply, notable because the `snapshots` job runs with `contents: write`. The gitleaks binary is downloaded via `curl | tar` with no checksum verification before `sudo install`. And once any version ships, there is currently no delivery path for a security patch to reach an installed user (SPEC-0056 auto-update is still a draft, release.yml has run once and failed) — not urgent with 0 releases to date, but worth planning before that changes.

strengths: researchFetch.ts's SSRF defense is a real two-gate design: a static isAllowedUrl allowlist runs before any socket opens, then makeSsrfSafeLookup enforces on the DNS-*resolved* address at connect time (DNS-rebinding-safe) via a custom http(s).Agent lookup — isPublicHost correctly rejects RFC1918/loopback/link-local/cloud-metadata ranges in both IPv4 and IPv6 form, including the IPv4-mapped-IPv6 smuggling form (::ffff:*).

kb/pathContainment.ts is a single, symlink-safe (realpaths the deepest existing ancestor before comparison) containment primitive that every fs sink taking an LLM-/external-derived relative path routes through — a genuine 'defined once' fix for a path-injection bug class the codebase's own comments say kept recurring (#52/#61/#73/#77).

kb/untrustedSource.ts applies an explicit prompt-injection fence to every source-reading pipeline decider (not just the web researcher), framing pulled content as DATA never instructions, with a belt-and-suspenders delimiter note at the untrusted-content boundary.

Escaping discipline holds up under scrutiny: shell/html.ts's esc() is a correct, null-safe character-class escaper, and every sampled production view (15 files) routes vault/LLM-derived text through it before innerHTML assignment; askView.ts's citation-marker injection is applied BEFORE marked.parse()+DOMPurify.sanitize() so the whole result — including injected markup — gets sanitized together, and citations deliberately carry no href (the obsidian:// scheme is built and opened only in main, never entering the DOM).
preload.ts exposes a minimal, fully-typed contextBridge KbApi with no raw ipcRenderer/require passthrough — every channel is a named, single-purpose invoke.
forge.config.ts enables all 6 recommended Electron Fuses (RunAsNode disabled, ASAR integrity validation on, OnlyLoadAppFromAsar on, NODE_OPTIONS/CLI-inspect disabled, cookie encryption on).

The app stores zero Copilot/GitHub credentials itself — ghRead.ts explicitly delegates all auth to the `gh` CLI's own config (BYOA), matching the durable 'provider is Copilot SDK, never direct' rule; crashReporter is started with uploadToServer:false (dumps stay local); main/telemetry.ts is Electron-free and makes no network calls at all — this is a genuinely no-phone-home app.

PDF text extraction (mediaExtract.ts) explicitly disables pdfjs eval (isEvalSupported:false) and only ever calls getTextContent(), never render() — and the app parses no archive/zip formats at all, eliminating an entire attack-surface class (zip bombs, archive-symlink escapes) by simply not having that code path.
knip found zero unused dependencies and zero unused files — the dependency set, while not fully exact-pinned, is lean and every declared package is actually exercised.

The one dependency SPEC-0011 explicitly worries about as fast-moving/preview (@github/copilot-sdk, ENG-7) is correctly exact-pinned at 1.0.0-beta.7 — the ENG-4 discipline holds exactly where the spec's authors flagged it as most important, even though it slips elsewhere.

CI workflow permissions are scoped per-job with inline rationale (top-level contents:read, escalated to contents:write only in the one job that needs it, checks:read only where a check-runs API call is made) rather than a blanket broad grant.

The eval cassette secret-scrubber (eval/runner/cassette.ts) has a broad pattern set (GH tokens, AWS keys, JWTs, bearer headers, basic-auth URLs, query-string credentials) and a fail-loud re-scan invariant that runs on both record and replay-load, backed by a narrowly-scoped gitleaks allowlist for its own fixture file.
open_questions: Does any pipeline decider or the Ask/recall path ever surface embargoed/private-opinion-labeled (SPEC-0043) source content in an answer, and if so should Save-chat exclude it — the codebase shows no sensitivity gate on the recall/Ask path itself (only on researcher egress).

Has the electron-forge maintainer team acknowledged the transitive tar/extract-zip/tmp CVEs, or is there a tracking issue upstream worth subscribing to instead of re-discovering this each review cycle?
Is there an internal plan/timeline for SPEC-0056 auto-update, given it's the only realistic patch-delivery path once this ships beyond a handful of manually-updated installs?

Should the eval harness's js-yaml usage (developer-authored scenario files) be considered fully trusted, or could a compromised/malicious eval scenario contribution (e.g. via external PR) actually reach it — worth a quick scope check before dismissing SEC-5 entirely.

domains.label: observed-runs
domains.title: Observed runs: instance logs, spans, vault history (the field evidence)
domains.domain: Observed runs: instance logs, spans, vault history (the field evidence)
domains.verdict: The engine's own field trail shows real, working value (99.5% compose success, 71.9% grounded recall, crash-free since the Vellum rename) sitting on top of two live reliability defects — an unbounded ephemeral-worktree leak and multi-minute canonical-lock stalls — that this single 2.5-month test vault already grew to 3.3GB and repeated 18-minute pipeline freezes without anyone noticing, because the one log a user would actually find (app.log) never records any of it.
domains.summary:
This vault (~/kb-test-1, opened under the app's "Vellum", "vellum", "kb-app" and "KB-App" userData identities across a rename) is the only first-party evidence of the product actually running, and it tells a coherent, mostly self-consistent story once the four data sources (app.log, pipeline.log, spans.jsonl, git history) are cross-read against the code that produces them.

The headline finding is a confirmed, code-verified resource leak: `EPHEMERAL_STAGES` in canonicalAdvance.ts (line 74) allowlists `archive, claims, connect, decompose, consolidation` for the boot-time leak-recovery sweep (`reapEphemeralWorktrees`) — but `composeStage.ts` (`STAGE = 'compose'`, line 40) drives every compose item through the exact same `withEphemeralWorktree` machinery, using a worktree name (`compose-<ULID>`) the allowlist's regex never matches. The vault has 185 such directories on disk, 3.3GB, dated 2026-06-09 through 2026-06-28 — and `pipeline.log`'s own `startup.ready` telemetry proves the sweep has run at least 5 times since (06-29, 07-13×3, 08-07) and reaped `reapedWorktrees: 0` every single time despite the pile sitting right there. 8 of the 185 are still git-registered with live `kb/compose-work-*` branches dated exactly to the 2026-06-13 render-process-gone crash captured in last-crash.json (stage "compose", item "Matching Cat Shirts") — direct proof of the leak mechanism (a crash mid-item defeats the try/finally cleanup, and the boot sweep then skips it forever because compose isn't on the list). Vault-root `du` is 3.6GB total; `.kb/cache/worktrees` alone is 3.5GB (97%) against ~25MB of real entities+claims+sources content — a ~140:1 scratch-to-content ratio in a vault with only 767 entities.

The second reliability story is a canonical-writer lock pathology: `stageLock.ts`'s watchdog fired `lock.stuck` 852 times between 2026-06-28 and 07-05, 776 of them held by `connect:link`, with elapsedMs up to 1,087,189ms (18.1 minutes against a 30-second threshold) and up to 6 queued waiters. This directly produced 26 `promote.coalesced-failed: block timeout reached` events over the same week — real, repeated multi-minute pipeline stalls that blocked promotion of finished work. The pattern stops appearing after 07-05, six days before the prior deep-review's #507/#515 (connect-lock/raw-git-hang) were reported closed on 07-13 — worth the code-review lane re-verifying against current `connectStage.ts` rather than assuming this field silence proves the fix, since it may just reflect reduced activity. `claims` stage shows a related tail-latency pathology in the app's own perf-index.json: p50=29.7s but p99=991s and a max of 1,854,368ms (30.9 minutes) for one item ("Urza's Saga"), with a single `copilot.invoke` inside that span alone running 17.3 minutes — the same order of magnitude as the lock stalls, suggesting a shared root cause (an occasionally-hanging Copilot CLI subprocess) rather than two independent bugs.

Product value is real but imperfect: Ask/recall's own audit trail (32 entries, 06-02 to 08-09) shows 71.9% grounded success; three of the nine misses were 60s tool timeouts, two (06-14, since fixed on current main via `overridesBuiltInTool`) were the known grep-builtin collision, and three simply record `ok:false` with no error message at all — the audit schema has no room to say why grounding failed. The starkest example: on 07-13 the user asked "what are good places to eat in santa fe," got zero citations, then immediately retried "theres no food in santa fe?" and failed again — despite the vault holding linked claims about Café Pasqual's and the Belltower Bar at La Fonda. A likely contributor: 27 of 14,633 wikilinks inside KB-generated entities/claims resolve nowhere, several of them exactly these Santa Fe/Albuquerque venue names Connect apparently never turned into entity nodes.

Two structural observability gaps compound all of this: `app.log` (36,094 lines, 2.5 months) contains only `mem.sample`/`mem.leak-suspected` — literally every other operational signal (startup, reaps, stage failures, lock stalls, promote failures) lives in a separate, per-vault `pipeline.log` a user would have no reason to find; and `spans.jsonl`'s 8MB/3-file rotation means only 4 scattered calendar days of tracing survive, so this report's latency numbers are dominated by two anomalous heavy-test days rather than steady-state usage. On the positive side: memory is healthy — RSS median dropped from 436MB to 217MB exactly at the 07-13 freeze point, and all 57 leak-suspected spikes (max +295MB) fully recovered to baseline, never compounding; no crash has been recorded since the app's Vellum rename; and a single 06-28 promote commit that silently deleted 4,969 claims + 982 entities (116,896 lines) in one shot — indistinguishable in git log from routine activity — is flagged for the code-review lane to trace, since causation (intentional consolidation vs. a destructive-write bug) can't be settled from vault evidence alone.
