domains.label: census-complexity
domains.title: Measurement census: function complexity, import graph, module stats
domains.domain: Measurement census: function complexity, import graph, module stats
domains.verdict: Overall healthy for a 46k-LOC solo-authored codebase — complexity is concentrated in a small, identifiable set of hotspots rather than spread everywhere, and the import graph is far cleaner than a naive tool would report; the main actionable gaps are one extreme-complexity function, one untested-by-design validation cluster, and a batch of stale CSS from earlier UI iterations.
domains.summary:
Ran the TypeScript compiler API (typescript 5.9.3) over all 237 prod .ts files under app/src (excluding tests/.d.ts) to build function-level complexity, an import graph, an export census, test:prod pairing, an index.css selector census, and whole-history git churn. Full data in A2_census_complexity.json/.md.

Function complexity is concentrated, not diffuse: of 3,313 function bodies, 153 (4.6%) have CC≥10, 59 (1.8%) CC≥15, only 14 (0.4%) CC≥25, and just 2 (0.06%) CC≥40. Per-directory averages are low and uniform (kb avgCC 3.13, main 2.68, shell 2.75) — the engine is not generally over-complex. But there is one genuine outlier: `prepare` in kb/connectStage.ts:599 at CC 78, 365 LOC, depth 7 — more than 1.6x the next-highest function (48) and nearly 3x the third (36). It's real domain logic (the per-block connect prepare/decide/write critical path: disambiguation replay, directive matching, merge/set-aside/retry), not generated code, and it sits in the single largest, most complex file in the repo (connectStage.ts: 1,669 lines, 128 functions, maxCC 78) — this is the entity-resolution core of the knowledge graph, so complexity here is also the highest-consequence place for a subtly wrong branch to silently mis-merge entities. A second outlier, `reconcileWatchFolder` (kb/watchRun.ts:151, CC 48, LOC 177, depth 10 — the deepest nesting measured anywhere), is a sequential guard/scan/drain flow, less risky in kind.

The import graph looks worse than it is on a first pass, and the correction matters: a naive SCC over every import edge finds a 43-file strongly-connected cluster across most of kb/. Re-running with `import type` edges excluded (the practically meaningful graph, since type-only imports never create a runtime cycle) collapses this to exactly one real 2-file cycle (kb/researchFetch.ts ⇄ kb/researchWebAgent.ts, confirmed by reading both files' import lists). The near-universal use of `import type` for cross-module type references — kb/types.ts alone pulls `import type` from ~19 files with zero value imports among them — is a real discipline strength that keeps a 165-file engine module with a 42-fan-in shared-types hub from actually being circular. Electron-import hygiene is independently confirmed by AST (not grep): 0 in kb/shell/qcap, all 10 in main/+root, exactly as claimed.

Git churn and the import graph agree on where the real coupling lives: kb/types.ts, main/ipc.ts, main/pipeline.ts, and preload.ts co-change on 32-47 of each other's commits (the IPC contract spine), and pipeline.ts is the single hottest file in the repo's history (102 commits). This checks out structurally too — main/pipelineLifecycle.ts has the highest fan-out in the codebase (41 internal imports) and the longest dependency chain (31 modules) runs straight through main.ts→ipc.ts→pipeline.ts→pipelineLifecycle.ts→…→kb/. Every new IPC-surface feature necessarily touches this same four-file core by hand; there's no schema/codegen layer amortizing it.

I used this lane to verify two prior-review claims against current code, per the mission's re-verify-don't-rediscover directive. ENG-7/#528 ("dedup registry CRUD") is in the list of issues closed without a linked PR — but the dedup genuinely landed: app/src/main/registries/registryCrud.ts exists and is used by 5 of the 6 control-panel files. The refactor was partial, though: it deduped the shared write/lock/commit/audit mechanics, but the per-field patch validation (the actual source of CC 19-26 in setResearcherConfig/setWatchFolder/etc.) is still hand-duplicated per registry. ENG-5/#527 (per-directory coverage floors) also landed, with an honest self-documenting comment in vitest.config.ts naming main/pipeline.ts and ipc.ts as "genuinely undertested, a fast-follow candidate" and setting main's floor at a deliberately low 61%/67%/61%/74%. My census can now name exactly what's inside that gap: the entire registries/*ControlPanel.ts cluster (9 files, 1,085 LOC, the CC-20-26 validation functions) has zero test-file references anywhere — even ipc.test.ts, which exercises the IPC wiring, explicitly mocks these functions out rather than calling the real implementation. So this is a known, coverage-floor-fenced gap rather than a blind spot, but it's larger and more precisely the site of the codebase's second-highest complexity cluster than the existing comment suggests.

index.css (1,705 lines, 857 rule blocks, 583 distinct classes) shows no `prefers-color-scheme` media queries (confirmed intentional — SPEC-0057 fixed-light shell) and only 10 small `[data-theme='dark']` override blocks. A textual cross-check against all prod .ts + index.html found 51 candidate-unreferenced classes; spot-checking narrowed this to at least 19 confirmed genuinely dead (an `explore-center`/`explore-neighbor-*` cluster of 10 classes that doesn't match any class exploreView.ts actually emits — leftover from a pre-v2 Explore skin — plus `is-open`, `ag-empty`, `ag-loading`, `job-empty`, `rdesk-empty`, `source-slots`, `ask-hl`, `rev-skeleton-sub`, `rev-skeleton-line--sub`), while 14 of the 51 (the `gl--*` glyph and `src-mark--*` families) are false positives — built via template literals (`` `gl--${kind}` ``) that a textual search can't see. Test:prod LOC pairing (46,347 prod / 43,879 test, ratio 0.947) matches the orchestrator's reported 0.95:1 exactly; 40 of 237 prod files lack a colocated test, of which 17 have zero test-file reference at all once cross-checked by import (not just filename).

measurements.name: Git churn, 506 commits (2026-05-30→07-13)
measurements.value: top file main/pipeline.ts 102 commits; index.css 87; kb/types.ts 71; main/ipc.ts 62; preload.ts 43. 783 files added vs 69 deleted across the history (reclamation ratio 0.088). Co-change: types.ts⇄ipc.ts 47, types.ts⇄pipeline.ts 46, types.ts⇄preload.ts 43, ipc.ts⇄preload.ts 41 commits together

strengths: Complexity is genuinely concentrated, not diffuse: 95%+ of all 3,313 functions have CC<10, and per-directory average CC is low (2.7-3.1) and consistent across kb/main/shell — this reads as a codebase that mostly stays simple, with a small number of identifiable hotspots rather than broad rot.

Near-universal `import type` discipline for cross-module type references is what keeps a 165-file kb/ engine with a 42-fan-in shared-types hub (kb/types.ts) from being a real circular-dependency mess — a naive tool would report a 43-file cycle; the actual runtime-relevant cycle count is 1, and it's a small 2-file one.

Electron-import boundary (kb/shell/qcap: 0 electron imports; main/root: all 10) holds up under independent AST verification, not just grep — confirms the established 'kb has zero Electron imports' claim with a different method.

Two prior-review fixes (ENG-7/#528 registry-CRUD dedup, ENG-5/#527 per-directory coverage floors) that were closed on GitHub without a linked PR were independently verified to have actually landed in code, with the coverage-floor change including an honest, specific self-documenting comment naming exactly which files remain undertested and why — good process hygiene even where the GitHub paper trail is thin.
Test:prod LOC ratio (0.947:1) matches the orchestrator's independently-reported 0.95:1 exactly, cross-validating both measurements.

index.css's dark-mode / fixed-light architecture (0 prefers-color-scheme blocks, deliberate :root[data-theme='dark'] opt-in only) matches its own header comment's stated intent exactly — no drift between documented and actual CSS behavior.
open_questions: Is connectStage.ts's `prepare` (CC 78) intentionally kept as one function for atomicity/rollback reasons (it's inside a try/catch that discards partial worktree state on failure), or would decomposition genuinely be safe? Only someone with connect-stage domain context can rule on this — the census can only flag the number.

The 51-candidate unreferenced-CSS-class list was only spot-verified for ~19 confirmed-dead + 2 confirmed-false-positive families (29 of 51); the remaining ~22 candidates in the JSON haven't been individually re-checked for template-literal construction and should be grep-verified individually before deletion.

Is there a reason the main/registries/*ControlPanel.ts validation logic was left untested when the sibling registryCrud.ts dedup (ENG-7/#528) was done in the same effort — was test-writing scoped out deliberately, or just not reached?

domains.label: census-hygiene
domains.title: Measurement census: git/gh hygiene numbers
domains.verdict: Broken CI/CD visibility and zero review gates create deployment risk; 53-day nightly failure is invisible and unaddressed; single GitHub user with 14 agent personas bypasses all access controls; 7-week repository dormancy suggests project stalled or deprioritized.
domains.summary: The repository exhibits severe process hygiene failures that compound the technical debt and block deployment. The nightly CI workflow, added 2026-07-13 as a required safety check, has failed 53 days in a row with zero visibility or remediation — the workflow's own report-red job crashes due to a configuration error (missing checkout step + wrong working-directory), so no issue is ever filed. Main-branch CI (3-context ruleset: typecheck, lint, unit) remains green on 189/200 runs (94.5%), but these do not catch the e2e IA drift failures that plague nightly. The second-order concern is merge discipline: 505 PRs merged across 7 weeks with a median of 4 files and 186 LOC changed, but 0 PRs had any peer reviews, and 59.6% were merged within 15 minutes of creation — a velocity-over-quality pattern enabled by zero gate enforcement. Attribution is unusual: all 506 commits across 14 distinct agent personas (KB-Developer-N, KB-Design-Lead, KB-Quality-Driver, KB-Special-Agent) are authored by a single GitHub user (anthropic-owned account), suggesting a shared-credential multi-agent system that bypasses standard GitHub access controls and audit trails. The repository has been dormant since 2026-07-13 (7 weeks); all 67 issues were closed by 07-13, with 18 issues closed without linked PRs, indicating a cleanup/merge storm rather than steady work. 144 remote branches remain; 96 are >30 days stale and should be deleted. Code additions heavily outpace deletions (11.3:1 ratio: 783 added vs 69 deleted), suggesting accumulated spec churn or unfinished feature branches. File-change distribution is healthy (top file: pipeline.ts with 102 commits; most files < 30 commits), but conventional-commit compliance is strong (89.9%), indicating discipline in commit messages despite process breakdowns.

strengths: Conventional-commit discipline is strong (89.9% compliance), indicating team awareness of commit message standards despite process breakdowns.
Primary CI (typecheck, lint, unit) is stable and fast (~3.5 min median), catching basic correctness before PRs land.
File-change distribution is healthy (no single file dominates; top file has 102 commits; most < 30), suggesting distributed ownership and reasonable refactoring.
All 27 issues from the prior deep-review (2026-07-12) were closed by 2026-07-13, showing rapid issue-resolution velocity during the merge window.

Of the 18 issues closed without visible linked PRs, how many were fixed via direct commits vs marked COMPLETED without code changes?
Why did the 07-13 merge storm happen? Was it a deliberate freeze (prep for release), or a catch-up after a backlog?
Are the nightly e2e selector failures (`.activity-empty`, `.sidebar .nav-group`, `.ask-citations .cite-ref`) the only remaining e2e regressions, or are there others masked by the workflow crash?
Has anyone attempted to fix the nightly.yml report-red job failure in the past 7 weeks, or was it never noticed?

findings.title: Headless / background operation (VISION-10, a 'must') only exists on macOS

evidence.quote:
/** Should the app quit when the last window closes? macOS = NO (Dock + tray agent stays alive,
 *  QCAP-8); every other platform = yes. */
| VISION-10  | must     | The app runs headless — orchestration, recurring jobs, polling, agents — with no window open | none-yet |

findings.scenario: A Windows user (a platform nightly.yml explicitly names as a 'SHIPPED target' alongside macOS, packaged and e2e-tested there) closes the app window between sessions, as is normal Windows behavior with no menubar-agent convention. The whole process exits: no scheduled Librarian work, no watched-folder ingestion, no proactive intake, no background research runs until the app is manually reopened and left open. The 'quick capture, effortless recall, autonomous in between' premise silently does not hold on that platform, and nothing in the UI tells the user why — there is no messaging anywhere in shell/ about this platform difference.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) ship a genuine background/tray-agent mode for Windows/Linux (system tray icon + suppressed quit-on-close, mirroring the macOS QCAP-8 model) before calling headless a shipped-platform guarantee, or (b) explicitly rescope VISION-10 in SPEC-0003 to 'macOS only for v1' with Principal ratification, and surface that limitation to the user in Settings/first-run on other platforms so they aren't silently missing the product's core autonomous-work promise.
corrections:
Core claim holds and is deliberate + unit-asserted, but four corrections are needed.

(1) CITATION ERROR: the VISION-10 row is at specs/product/SPEC-0003-product-vision-core-loop.md:153, NOT line 76. Line 76 is narrative prose ("meeting, they **send the notes to the KB** and head to the next meeting."). The quoted row text itself is verbatim-correct at line 153. The two app/src quotes are verbatim-correct at the cited lines (lifecycle.ts:12-15, main.ts:202-208).

(2) "The whole process exits" is not universally true on Windows. app/src/main/quickCaptureElectron.ts:234 keeps the quick-capture sheet BrowserWindow ALIVE-but-hidden after first summon ("hideSheet() { if (sheet && !sheet.isDestroyed()) sheet.hide(); // keep-alive: hidden, not torn down }", per #512 PERF-R7 at line 209). Electron's `window-all-closed` fires only when all windows are *closed*, not hidden — so on Windows the app exits only when the user has NOT summoned quick capture since launch, and survives (accidentally, untested, undocumented) when they have. The real defect is therefore *nondeterministic* background lifecycle on Windows, which is arguably worse than the stated uniform exit, not better.

(3) "ship a system tray icon" in recommendation (a) is already done cross-platform: quickCaptureElectron.ts:256 `tray = new Tray(buildTrayImage());` inside setTray() has no darwin gate, and startQuickCapture() → qcapAgent.start() runs unconditionally at app.on('ready') (app/src/main.ts:141). Only the accessibility menu item is darwin-gated (quickCaptureElectron.ts:134). So the missing piece on Windows/Linux is *only* suppressing quit-on-window-all-closed (a one-line policy change in lifecycle.ts:15 plus a reopen affordance, which the tray "Show Vellum" item + showMainWindow() already provide) — materially smaller than the stated "M" effort for (a).

(4) Partial countervailing evidence on scope: recommendation (b) is already half-documented at the release layer. specs/features/SPEC-0055-release-cadence.md:18 says "macOS first; Windows later." and §5 Out of scope (v1) lists "**Windows** signed builds + EV cert (later…)" and "Linux packaging." VISION-10 itself carries no platform qualifier, and the repo contradicts itself: .github/workflows/nightly.yml:4 calls macOS+Windows "the SHIPPED targets", .github/workflows/release.yml:78-79 builds a windows-latest matrix leg and line ~113 drafts "the draft release with mac + Windows artifacts attached". The finding should cite that contradiction rather than assert Windows is unambiguously a shipped target.

Verified-as-stated: the behavior is intentional and locked by test — app/src/main/lifecycle.test.ts asserts `expect(shouldQuitOnWindowAllClosed('win32')).toBe(true)` and `('linux')).toBe(true)`. And the "nothing in the UI tells the user" claim holds: grepping app/src/shell for macOS/darwin/Windows returns only TCC/permission strings (appRoute.ts:75, permissionGate.ts:1-20) — no platform-capability messaging anywhere.

Release-blocking: I disagree with true. SPEC-0055 already declares v1 macOS-first, the rc is an unsigned draft pre-release, and this is a documentable known limitation rather than data loss or an unusable app. It becomes blocking only if Windows is publicly positioned as a supported target for the release.

The MECHANISM is confirmed exactly as cited: `shouldQuitOnWindowAllClosed()` returns `platform !== 'darwin'`, main.ts wires it to `window-all-closed`, so on Windows/Linux closing the last window quits the process and no orchestration/jobs/hotkey survive. findings.title: Spec status is not a meaningfully enforced lifecycle gate: 79% of specs (incl. the two most foundational, most-implemented ones) sit permanently at 'draft' with no defined graduation criteria anywhere

evidence.quote: status: draft          # draft | active | deprecated | superseded

findings.scenario: SPEC-0001 (Ubiquitous Language — the canonical vocabulary Source/Entity/Claim/Output is defined by) and SPEC-0007 (Core Data Model — the vault's three-content-kind structure everything else is built on) have been implemented against continuously since the repo's first week and are cited by dozens of code comments (DATA-N appears in 19 non-test files), yet both remain formally 'draft' 10+ weeks later, alongside 67 other specs (69/87 total, 79%). SPEC-0000, the meta-spec that mandates every spec carry a status (SPECSYS-5) and calls itself 'the anti-drift mechanism' for exactly this kind of silent decay, never defines what distinguishes draft from active or what triggers the transition — the only definition anywhere is a bare inline template comment. The status field is present everywhere but functionally decorative.
findings.recommendation: Add a short 'status lifecycle' section to SPEC-0000 defining what active requires (e.g., 'no known must-priority gaps vs. shipped code, reviewed within N weeks') and do a one-time pass reclassifying the specs that are demonstrably fully implemented (SPEC-0001, SPEC-0007, and others) to active, or explicitly document why they intentionally stay draft.

findings.title: App-config userData path has no migration across the product's rename history, leaving orphaned config directories in the wild
findings.scenario: The product has visibly been renamed at least twice (internal package name still 'kb-app', display name now 'Vellum', with an intermediate 'KB-App' capitalization also having existed per the observed live instance's ~/Library/Application Support/ tree, which carries three separate directories — vellum, kb-app, and KB-App — each with its own copy of kb-app.config.json). appConfig.ts resolves app.getPath('userData') fresh with no check for, or migration from, a prior installation's directory, so a long-running beta user's activeVaultPath pointer can silently go stale/orphaned across a rename-driven userData path change, dropping them into first-run setup despite their vault being intact on disk elsewhere — the exact failure class BUG-13 (#518) already fixed for mid-write corruption, but not for this cause.
findings.recommendation: Add a one-time migration check in appConfig.ts's readAppConfig(): if the current userData config is absent/default, look for a config file under the last-known-prior productName's userData sibling directory (or an explicit hardcoded list of prior names) and migrate it forward once.
corrections: The cited code and quotes are accurate: appConfig.ts:15 hardcodes 'kb-app.config.json' under app.getPath('userData'), with no fallback/migration logic anywhere in the function or file. No app.setName() call exists in app/src/main, so Electron's default userData resolution (keyed off package.json's `name`, currently still "kb-app" despite productName being "Vellum") governs the path — consistent with the finding's premise that renames (kb-app → KB-App → Vellum, per the observed live instance's three separate userData dirs) can silently orphan a prior config. One nuance: since `name` in package.json has NOT itself changed (still "kb-app"), the three observed live-instance directories were more likely produced by productName/capitalization changes or manual app relocations rather than the `name` field drifting — but the net effect (orphaned config, silent first-run fallback on migration) is real and correctly diagnosed as an absence of any cross-directory migration check.

findings.scenario: Pulled the raw Playwright log from nightly run 32938305750 (2026-08-26): 14/17 e2e specs pass cleanly; the same 3 fail deterministically on both macOS and Windows, every single sampled run, with retry-and-still-fail behavior (not a timing flake) — activity.e2e.ts's `.activity-empty` selector, ask.e2e.ts's citation/transcript text, and jobs.e2e.ts's `.agents-hub-title`/`.job-sub` selectors no longer match what the shell renders (consistent with the shell moving to a shared emptyState() primitive and other IA changes after these specs were last updated). findings.title: The macOS-cost rationale driving ci.yml's per-PR/nightly split doesn't hold for a public repo, and the opt-in mechanism it relies on is essentially unused
findings.scenario: `gh repo view masra91/Vellum-KB --json isPrivate` returns `isPrivate: false` — the repo is public, and GitHub Actions minutes are unlimited/free on public repos regardless of runner OS, so the '10x macOS multiplier... the recurring Actions spend' rationale documented at length in ci.yml's header comments currently saves $0. Meanwhile the opt-in labels this architecture depends on for pre-merge coverage are barely used: `macos` was applied to exactly 1 PR ever (#564, reactively, after the bug it guards was already found by other means), and `e2e` has never been applied to a PR since the #525 opt-in pattern was introduced. Net effect: macOS-native-dep and app-boot coverage moved off the PR path for a cost saving that doesn't currently exist, and the backstop (nightly) that was supposed to compensate is invisible (CI-1/CI-2).
findings.recommendation: If the repo is meant to go/stay private before release, keep the current split and document the plan. If it ships as the public repo it is today, reconsider restoring `package-macos` and a minimal e2e smoke to the required per-PR gate — there's no cost tradeoff being made on a public repo, only a coverage one.

findings.title: release.yml has never been exercised via its actual trigger (a v* tag push) — the entire verify→build→publish pipeline is integration-untested, and a v0.1.0-rc.1 tag today would fail immediately on the version guard

evidence.quote: `::error::Tag ${tag} (version ${versionFromTag(tag)}) does not match package.json's committed version ` +

findings.scenario: The only run of release.yml in repo history (28308929235, 2026-06-28) was triggered by a branch `push`, not a tag, and scheduled zero jobs (a workflow-syntax-level failure, confirmed via `jobs: []` from the Actions API) — there has never been a single `v*`-tag-triggered run. The verify/build/publish scripts are well unit-tested in isolation, but the real integration (checkout the tagged SHA, `gh api .../check-runs`, `npm run make` on macOS+Windows, `gh release create --draft`) has never run as a system. Today, `package.json`'s version is still `0.1.0` (never bumped), so pushing `v0.1.0-rc.1` right now would fail at the very first `verify` step because `versionFromTag('v0.1.0-rc.1') = '0.1.0-rc.1' !== '0.1.0'` — correct guard behavior, but it means the whole downstream path remains unvalidated pending a version-bump PR that hasn't happened yet.
findings.recommendation: Before calling any tag 'rc.1' for real, do a dry run on a scratch/fork setup: bump package.json to a matching prerelease version in a throwaway PR, push the matching tag, and watch verify→build→publish complete end-to-end at least once. This is cheap and would catch integration issues (check-runs API shape, maker output paths, gh release create flags) before they're discovered on the actual first release.
corrections:
The core claim holds and I reproduced it, but one clause is overstated and one is understated.

VERIFIED (all three cited quotes appear verbatim at the cited lines):
1. `.github/workflows/release.yml:22-25` — the ONLY trigger is `on: push: tags: - 'v*'`. There are ZERO tags in the repo (`git tag | wc -l` = 0), so this trigger has never fired.
2. `gh run list --workflow=release.yml` returns exactly one run: databaseId 28308929235, `"event":"push"`, `"headBranch":"KB-Developer-5/spec-0055-release"`, `"conclusion":"failure"`, 2026-06-28 — a branch push, not a tag. UNDERSTATED: that run predates the current file. `git log --follow -- .github/workflows/release.yml` shows the current release.yml first landed on main at 1defe2e (2026-07-12, PR #560), with one fast-follow 775ce27 (PR #569). So the release.yml that exists on main today has never produced a workflow run of ANY kind — not even the failed one.
3. The version-guard scenario is exactly right; I executed it read-only from `app/`:
   `node scripts/release/tagVersion.mjs "v0.1.0-rc.1"` → EXIT=1, printing the cited error verbatim: "::error::Tag v0.1.0-rc.1 (version 0.1.0-rc.1) does not match package.json's committed version (0.1.0). Bump the version via an `npm version` PR to main FIRST..."
   `node scripts/release/tagVersion.mjs "v0.1.0"` → EXIT=0, "OK: tag v0.1.0 matches package.json version 0.1.0." So the guard is not a blanket wall: an un-suffixed `v0.1.0` tag would pass today; only the `-rc.N`/`-beta.N` prerelease naming needs a version-bump PR first. The finding's own text concedes this is "correct guard behavior".

OVERSTATED — "the entire verify→build→publish pipeline is integration-untested" and "check-runs API shape" is unvalidated. I integration-tested the verify job's second half against the LIVE API and it passes: `gh api "repos/masra91/Vellum-KB/commits/19bb68f/check-runs" --paginate --slurp | jq '{check_runs: [.[].check_runs[]]}'` (the exact pipeline in release.yml:63-64) returned 365 check-runs, and feeding that to `node scripts/release/verifyRequiredChecks.mjs` gave EXIT=0 with all three hardcoded `REQUIRED_CHECK_NAMES` matched as `success`. So the API response shape and the brittle hardcoded name list (verifyRequiredChecks.mjs:13) are correct against real main-SHA data today — a plausible failure mode the finding flags as unknown is in fact demonstrably fine. Note ci.yml:58-60 has `push: branches: [main]`, which is why required checks attach to the main commit SHA at all (the squash-merge-SHA-mismatch failure mode I hunted for does not apply here).
Two lesser hazards I also failed to refute-into-existence: the `publish` job correctly overrides the workflow-level `defaults.run.working-directory: app` with `working-directory: .` (release.yml:114) on its only `run` step, so it does NOT have the no-checkout/no-app-dir bug that silently killed nightly's report-red job; and the `upload-artifact` `path: app/out/make/**` is workspace-root-relative (action inputs ignore run defaults), which is correct.

CORRECTED CLAIM: release.yml as it exists on main has never executed a single job. The verify job's logic is now empirically shown to work against live data, so the genuinely unexercised surface is narrower than stated: `npm run make` on macos-latest + windows-latest (CI has only ever run `npm run package`, never `make`; makers are MakerSquirrel/win + MakerZIP/darwin per forge.config.ts:102-106, so macOS ships a .zip with no DMG), the `app/out/make/**` upload/download round-trip, and `gh release create --draft --generate-notes`. Severity drops to P2: this is untested-integration risk plus a documented, one-line process step (release.yml:8-13 explicitly documents "Bump package.json's version in a normal PR ... this workflow never rewrites it"), not a defect. release_blocking stays true — the sole path to a first public artifact has never run once, and the rc-naming/version mismatch must be resolved before any tag is pushed. The recommendation (dry-run on a scratch tag) is unchanged and correct.

The mechanism is real and every cited quote is verbatim at the cited line, but the framing is overstated on two axes.

(1) The headline "a v0.1.0-rc.1 tag today would fail immediately on the version guard" is not a defect — it is the documented, intended process. release.yml:8-13 spells out the exact sequence: "1. Bump package.json's version in a normal PR to main via `npm version` (the source of truth — this workflow never rewrites it). 2. Once that PR is merged and its CI is green, tag that commit". Nobody following the documented flow ever pushes a tag that mismatches package.json; the finding's own scenario concedes it is "correct guard behavior." Reachability of the failure is therefore only "an operator skipped step 1," and the consequence is a 30-second red `verify` job with an actionable ::error:: telling them exactly what to do. That belongs as a one-line release-checklist note, not as the title of a P1.

(2) The residual substance — "the verify→build→publish path has never run as a system" — is true (verified: `git tag` = 0 local tags and `git ls-remote --tags origin` returns nothing, so no `v*` push has ever fired the trigger), but it is unavoidable-by-construction for a first release and it is self-revealing: the first tag push IS the integration test, and the pipeline is fail-closed at every stage (verify gates build; build gates publish; `if-no-files-found: error` on upload; an explicit "refusing to draft an empty release" guard at release.yml:124; `--draft` never auto-publishes). The failure mode is "no artifacts got drafted, fix and re-tag," not corrupt/misleading artifacts reaching users. That is P2.

Two adversarial checks that could have RAISED severity both came back clean, further deflating it: (a) `REQUIRED_CHECK_NAMES = ['typecheck · lint · unit (ubuntu-latest)', 'secret scan', 'package build-check (ubuntu-latest)']` matches ci.yml's actual job names/matrix shape (ci.yml:81/111/149 + `os: [ubuntu-latest]`), so verify is unlikely to fail on name drift; (b) ci.yml triggers on `push: branches: [main]`, so a merged main SHA genuinely carries those check-runs (a PR-only trigger would have made verify fail "missing" on every real tag — it doesn't); (c) the `publish` job has no checkout but overrides `working-directory: .` on its only run step, so it does NOT hit the workflow-level `defaults.run.working-directory: app` trap that kills nightly's report-red job.

One real, under-stated risk the finding gestures at but doesn't name: `npm run make` appears in NO other workflow (grep across .github/workflows shows only `npm run package` in ci.yml and nightly.yml; release.yml:90 is the sole `npm run make`), so the maker path (MakerSquirrel on Windows, MakerZIP darwin, forge.config.ts:102-106) is the genuinely un-exercised piece — worth calling out specifically instead of the version-guard theatrics.

release_blocking should be false under the stated definition ("v0.1.0-rc.1 should not ship with it"): this finding cannot ship *with* the rc — attempting the rc is what exercises it. The recommendation (dry-run a matching prerelease tag once) is sound and cheap; keep it, but as P2 release-readiness hygiene.

verifier_votes.correction:
The mechanism is real and every cited quote is verbatim at the cited line, but the framing is overstated on two axes.

(1) The headline "a v0.1.0-rc.1 tag today would fail immediately on the version guard" is not a defect — it is the documented, intended process. release.yml:8-13 spells out the exact sequence: "1. Bump package.json's version in a normal PR to main via `npm version` (the source of truth — this workflow never rewrites it). 2. Once that PR is merged and its CI is green, tag that commit". Nobody following the documented flow ever pushes a tag that mismatches package.json; the finding's own scenario concedes it is "correct guard behavior." Reachability of the failure is therefore only "an operator skipped step 1," and the consequence is a 30-second red `verify` job with an actionable ::error:: telling them exactly what to do. That belongs as a one-line release-checklist note, not as the title of a P1.

(2) The residual substance — "the verify→build→publish path has never run as a system" — is true (verified: `git tag` = 0 local tags and `git ls-remote --tags origin` returns nothing, so no `v*` push has ever fired the trigger), but it is unavoidable-by-construction for a first release and it is self-revealing: the first tag push IS the integration test, and the pipeline is fail-closed at every stage (verify gates build; build gates publish; `if-no-files-found: error` on upload; an explicit "refusing to draft an empty release" guard at release.yml:124; `--draft` never auto-publishes). The failure mode is "no artifacts got drafted, fix and re-tag," not corrupt/misleading artifacts reaching users. That is P2.

Two adversarial checks that could have RAISED severity both came back clean, further deflating it: (a) `REQUIRED_CHECK_NAMES = ['typecheck · lint · unit (ubuntu-latest)', 'secret scan', 'package build-check (ubuntu-latest)']` matches ci.yml's actual job names/matrix shape (ci.yml:81/111/149 + `os: [ubuntu-latest]`), so verify is unlikely to fail on name drift; (b) ci.yml triggers on `push: branches: [main]`, so a merged main SHA genuinely carries those check-runs (a PR-only trigger would have made verify fail "missing" on every real tag — it doesn't); (c) the `publish` job has no checkout but overrides `working-directory: .` on its only run step, so it does NOT hit the workflow-level `defaults.run.working-directory: app` trap that kills nightly's report-red job.

One real, under-stated risk the finding gestures at but doesn't name: `npm run make` appears in NO other workflow (grep across .github/workflows shows only `npm run package` in ci.yml and nightly.yml; release.yml:90 is the sole `npm run make`), so the maker path (MakerSquirrel on Windows, MakerZIP darwin, forge.config.ts:102-106) is the genuinely un-exercised piece — worth calling out specifically instead of the version-guard theatrics.

release_blocking should be false under the stated definition ("v0.1.0-rc.1 should not ship with it"): this finding cannot ship *with* the rc — attempting the rc is what exercises it. The recommendation (dry-run a matching prerelease tag once) is sound and cheap; keep it, but as P2 release-readiness hygiene.

findings.title: gitleaks is installed via unauthenticated curl+tar with no checksum verification, and all actions are pinned by mutable tag not SHA
findings.scenario: The secret-scan job downloads a specific gitleaks release tarball over HTTPS and installs it with `sudo install` — no SHA256 checksum comparison against gitleaks' own published checksums file, so a compromised release asset would run with root on every PR's runner. Separately, all `uses: actions/*@v4` references across the 3 workflows pin by mutable major-version tag rather than a commit SHA — the GitHub-recommended supply-chain hardening baseline for anything security-sensitive (this repo will eventually run signing/notarization secrets through this same pipeline per SPEC-0055/56).
findings.recommendation: Add a `sha256sum -c` check against gitleaks' published checksums before `install`; consider pinning `actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-node`, and `actions/upload-artifact` to commit SHAs (with a Dependabot/renovate config to bump them) once the release pipeline carries real signing secrets.

findings.title: CI pins Node 22 while local dev runs Node 24.18/npm 11.16 with no engines field to catch the drift
findings.scenario: Every workflow pins `node-version: 22`, while this worktree (representative of local dev) runs Node v24.18.1 / npm 11.16.0, and `package.json` has no `engines` field to fail `npm install` locally when the versions diverge. This is exactly the class of gap that produced a previously-logged incident (a newer local npm silently writing a lockfile that passes `npm ci` locally but not on CI's older npm/Node, the '#536/#541 class' per project memory) — nothing currently prevents a recurrence beyond institutional memory.
findings.recommendation: Add `"engines": {"node": "22.x"}` (or bump CI to Node 24 to match reality and document why) plus a `.nvmrc`, so a version mismatch surfaces as an explicit warning/error rather than a silent lockfile-drift trap.
corrections: Mechanism and impact are accurate: no engines field, no .nvmrc anywhere in repo, CI pins Node 22 across all 5 workflow files/11 setup-node steps, local worktree is on Node v24.18.1/npm 11.16.0 as claimed. Two minor corrections: (1) cited line 90 is actually line 92 in this checkout (harmless 2-line drift, quote appears verbatim nearby); (2) the recommendation should note that adding an `engines` field alone won't fail `npm install`/`npm ci` unless paired with `engine-strict=true` in .npmrc (npm just warns by default) — worth naming so the fix is actually load-bearing, not cosmetic.

findings.title: A cheap Linux+xvfb Playwright smoke is already proven reusable in this repo's CI (the snapshots job) but isn't used as a per-PR gate — nothing runs the packaged app pre-merge

evidence.quote: run: xvfb-run -a npm run test:e2e -- e2e/showcase.e2e.ts --update-snapshots
#   NOT yet covered by a GATE (no silent caps, TEST-11): the `package` job builds but does not

findings.scenario: The dispatch-only `snapshots` job already demonstrates that Electron can boot headlessly under `xvfb-run` on an ubuntu runner (`npx playwright install-deps chromium` + `xvfb-run -a npm run test:e2e`), but this pattern is scoped only to baseline regeneration, never reused as a lightweight per-PR smoke. ci.yml's own header comment acknowledges the resulting gap directly: the package job proves the app builds but 'does not RUN the app', and nothing gates that pre-merge. A packaged build that launches and immediately crashes (this product's own crash log records exactly that failure mode once, render-process-gone during compose) would sail through the current required gate.

findings.title: The stage drain lifecycle is copy-pasted five times — 47 lines byte-identical in every stage class
findings.scenario: DecomposeStage, ClaimsStage, ComposeStage, ConnectStage and Orchestrator each carry their own copy of the same ~60-line lifecycle: `sweepTimer` field, `start(sweepMs = 30_000)`, `stop()`, `setCap`/`getCap`, `queueCacheStats`, `busy()`, `currentSince()`, `poke()` and `runDrains()` — including the identical multi-line rationale comment about systemic drain failures escaping as unhandledRejection. 47 non-comment lines are byte-identical in all five. A fix to the coalescing logic (or a new lifecycle need such as a hard stop that awaits in-flight items, which the prior review's BUG-8 wanted) must be applied five times, and the copies have already diverged accidentally: DecomposeStage.drainOnce returns boolean while the others return void, and ConnectStage/Orchestrator order their accessors differently from ClaimsStage.
findings.recommendation: Extract an abstract `DrainLoop` base class (or a `createDrainLoop({ stage, log, drainOnce })` mixin) owning sweepTimer/pending/draining/current/drainStartedAt plus start/stop/poke/runDrains/busy/currentSince, and a `CappedDrainLoop` adding cap/setCap/getCap/queueCacheStats. Each stage then declares only its constructor wiring and its own `drainOnce`. Saves roughly 190 lines and, more importantly, makes the next lifecycle change one edit. Keep `drainOnce`'s return type uniform (void) and move Decompose's boolean into an instance flag. Adopt one stage at a time; each stage's existing test file is the harness.
findings.verify_hint: Extract each class's prologue (declaration line → `private async drainOnce`), strip comments, and set-intersect the five — 47 lines survive in all five.
corrections: The duplication is real and the extract-base-class recommendation is sound, but "47 non-comment lines are byte-identical in all five" overstates Orchestrator's match. Orchestrator (app/src/kb/orchestrator.ts) is missing two of the nine listed members entirely — no queueCacheStats() and no currentSince() (grep confirms 0 hits in that file) — and its poke()/runDrains() are simplified variants: poke() at line 482 never sets `this.drainStartedAt` (compare claimsStage.ts:743-750, which does), so busy-tracking there is incomplete relative to the other four. Its busy() comment even reads "Is the archivist actively draining" (orchestrator.ts:469), confirming it's a distinct 5th stage (archive), not a copy-paste twin. Separately, claimsStage.ts's runDrains() (line ~759) has a `catch (err) { this.log.error(...) }` block with the "systemic drain failure" rationale comment that composeStage.ts's runDrains() (line 464) lacks entirely — composeStage uses a bare `finally` with no catch/log, so an error there propagates instead of being logged and swallowed. This is a real behavioral divergence beyond the one (decompose's boolean drainOnce) the finding calls out. So: 4 of the 5 classes (decompose/claims/compose/connect) do share the full 9-member lifecycle almost verbatim (confirmed via direct reads of claimsStage.ts:701-760 and composeStage.ts:420-465, plus grep hits across connectStage.ts/decomposeStage.ts), making the duplication claim and refactor recommendation solid for those four; Orchestrator should be scoped as a partial adopter (start/stop/setCap/getCap/busy only) rather than a fifth byte-identical copy, and the recommendation should also note the claims-vs-compose catch/finally divergence as another thing the base class must deliberately choose one behavior for.

findings.title: The four-file channel tax is unfixed and is still the mechanical cause of god-files (95% lockstep co-change)
findings.scenario: 41 of the 43 commits that ever touched preload.ts also touched types.ts AND ipc.ts. findings.title: Renderer repaint/re-wire pattern relies on 53 non-null querySelector assertions and almost no delegation

evidence.quote: function wire(container: HTMLElement, researchers: ResearcherView[]): void {

findings.scenario: The stack itself is fine — the prior review's 'plain-DOM template strings are not the bottleneck' verdict holds. The fragility is the re-wire step. Views paint via innerHTML (71 sites) then re-query and attach 72 direct click listeners, using 53 non-null `querySelector(...)!` assertions to do it. researchersView.wire alone opens each row with ~20 asserted handles. Rename or drop a class in the template and the paint still succeeds, then `wire()` throws a TypeError on the first `!` — an entire view goes blank at runtime with strict TS having said nothing. This is the same class of failure as the already-observed e2e drift where `.activity-empty` was replaced by the shared emptyState() primitive: markup moved, a selector did not.
findings.recommendation: Add one ~15-line helper to shell/html.ts: `on(root: HTMLElement, selector: string, event: string, handler: (el: Element, e: Event) => void)` that attaches once at the container and dispatches via `closest()`. Adopt it in the four heaviest wirers (researchersView, settingsView, reviewsView, askView) — repaints then need no re-wire at all, which also removes the re-attach-after-paint ordering hazard. Replace `querySelector(...)!` with a `must(root, sel)` helper that throws a named error identifying the missing selector, so a template/selector drift fails loudly with a message instead of a bare TypeError. Explicitly do NOT adopt a framework: 8.3k prod + 9.4k test shell LOC would churn for no measured win.
findings.verify_hint: `grep -c "addEventListener('click'" app/src/shell/views/*.ts` (72, excluding tests) vs `grep -c 'closest(' …` (7); `grep -oE "\)!" app/src/shell/views/*.ts | wc -l` → 59.
corrections: Core mechanism confirmed: researchersView.ts:400 wire() and :428 `li.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('.rdesk-arm')!` are real — repaint via innerHTML then re-wire via a chain of non-null querySelector assertions, so a template/selector rename would throw a bare TypeError at the first `!` with no compile-time protection (strict TS doesn't catch runtime DOM-string mismatches). Prod-scoped counts check out: 72 `addEventListener('click'...)` and 7 `closest(` across app/src/shell/views/*.ts (excluding .test.ts) match exactly; querySelector(...)! assertions come to 55 in prod files, close to the claimed 53. Two corrections: (1) the verify_hint's literal commands (`grep -c ... app/src/shell/views/*.ts`) do NOT reproduce the stated numbers as written — the glob also matches *.test.ts, giving 385 for the `)!` count and 13 for `closest(` instead of the claimed 59/7; the hint needs an explicit test-file exclusion to be reproducible. (2) askView.ts, cited as one of the 'four heaviest wirers' to fix, actually wires almost entirely via optional chaining (`form?.addEventListener(...)`, `container.querySelector(...)?.addEventListener(...)`) rather than non-null `!` assertions (0 querySelector(...)! hits in askView.ts) — so it doesn't itself demonstrate the 'throws TypeError, view goes blank' failure mode this finding centers on; its failure mode on selector drift is silent no-op, not a crash. It's still a legitimate delegation-adoption target given its 6 click listeners, just for a different reason than stated. Neither issue changes the underlying fragility claim or the recommendation's soundness.

findings.title: Three parallel CSS token vocabularies with a stalled migration, and the hand-mirrored layer has already drifted

evidence.quote: --viz-field: #f4efe3;     /* Vellum cream — the canvas/ground (fixed-light: the study) */
--border: #2c4150;    /* window border (addendum) — a touch cooler than the hairline --viz-rule */

findings.scenario: Three token namespaces coexist: index.css's legacy 8 (--bg/--card/--fg/--muted/--accent/--border/--error/--hover, 39 uses), design-system.css's --viz-* (190 uses), and the v3 unprefixed set which design-system.css itself declares is 'the DESTINATION that retires the instrument-panel --viz-* names' (958 uses). Views are ~85% migrated but design-system.css's own primitives still carry 119 --viz-* references, so the migration is frozen mid-flight — and main has not moved in 7 weeks. The legacy layer is hand-duplicated across light and dark and has already drifted: dark --border is #2c4150 while its stated source --viz-rule dark is #2e4350, a difference the comment rationalises after the fact ('a touch cooler'). The v3 dark block does this correctly (`--hair: var(--viz-rule)`), proving the alias approach works; index.css just never adopted it.
findings.recommendation: Two steps, both small. (1) Immediately alias the 8 legacy tokens to their design-system twins in both themes (`--bg: var(--viz-field)` / `--border: var(--viz-rule)` …) so they cannot drift again — this also silently corrects the #2c4150/#2e4350 divergence, which is a deliberate visual change to confirm with design first. Existing guard: themeCohesion.test.ts already enforces data-theme over prefers-color-scheme; extend it with a rule forbidding a literal hex in the legacy :root blocks.

findings.title: index.css is a 134 KB monolith cleanly partitioned by view prefix but never split — #2 churn file in the repo

evidence.quote: /* --- Explore view (SPEC-0039 EXPLORE) — the read-only entity-neighborhood graph. --- */
import '../index.css'; // shell chrome (top bar/rail/views) + base body reset

findings.scenario: 809 top-level rules sit in one file, already grouped into 22 view-prefixed families (.ask-* 108, .today-* 82, .explore-* 78, .rdesk-* 70, .ag-* 53, .exp-* 35, .capture-* 33, .health-* 33 …) with section-header comments marking the boundaries. It has 87 commits — the second-highest churn in the repo after pipeline.ts — because every UI PR from every parallel lane edits it. The repo already demonstrates the alternative: showcase.css, aboutPanel.css, setupFlow.css and permissionGate.css are co-located with their modules and imported by them. Nothing about the current arrangement is load-bearing; Vite concatenates either way.
findings.recommendation: Split by the existing section headers into src/shell/views/<view>.css, imported by each view module the way showcaseView.ts already imports design-system.css. Leave the base reset, shell chrome, rail and shared .load-*/.skel-* families in index.css. This is a pure file move (byte-identical rules, same cascade order if the imports are ordered as today), it cuts the merge-conflict surface roughly 20-fold, and it makes the dead-CSS problem in CX-9 self-evident because an unreferenced view's stylesheet becomes visible. Guard the split with the existing themeCohesion/clipping tests, which parse the CSS by path — update their globs.
findings.verify_hint: `grep -oE '^\s*\.[a-z][\w-]*' app/src/index.css | cut -d- -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` shows the 22 clean families; `git log --format='' --name-only -- app/src/index.css | wc -l` → 87.
corrections: Core mechanism confirmed: index.css is 1705 lines / 136,645 bytes (~133 KB, claim says 134 KB — negligible rounding), 87-commit churn (verified via `git log --name-only`), and is indeed #2 behind pipeline.ts at 102 commits (both checked against full app/src churn ranking). The view-prefix grouping and section-header comments at lines 857/274 are real and verbatim as quoted. The co-location precedent is real and verified: showcaseView.ts imports './showcase.css' (line 21), appRoute.ts imports './permissionGate.css' (line 8) and './design-system.css' (line 7) — so the "split by module, import from the view" pattern genuinely already exists elsewhere in the repo. However, the recommendation understates the blast radius of a split: it names only "themeCohesion/clipping tests" as needing glob updates, but in fact at least 16 test files hardcode a single `readFileSync(...'src/index.css')` call and then regex/parse it for view-specific selectors — e.g. app/src/shell/views/askView.test.ts:480 and exploreView.test.ts:253 both do `readFileSync(path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'src/index.css'), 'utf8')` to check .ask-*/.explore-* rules, and app/src/clipping.test.ts:9 does the same via `__dirname`. These aren't glob patterns to "update" — they're literal single-file paths baked into ~16+ separate test files (settingsView.test.ts, todayView.test.ts, captureView.test.ts, reviewsView.test.ts, healthView.test.ts, activityView.test.ts, agentsView.test.ts, sourcesView.test.ts, dmkMechanicalMotion.test.ts, loadingMotionGuard.test.ts, confirmDismissCss.test.ts, latticeMotif.test.ts among them), so a real split requires editing each test's file target (or having each read+concat the new per-view file), not just "update their globs." The prefix-family counts in the scenario are approximately but not exactly right (my recount: ask 107 vs claimed 108, today 76 vs 82, explore 75 vs 78, rdesk 69 vs 70, health 32 vs 33 — close enough to be a grep-methodology artifact, not a substantive error) — not a correctness issue. Net: the finding's diagnosis and precedent are solid; effort is realistically closer to S/M than a clean "S," and the recommendation should say "update ~16 test files' readFileSync targets" rather than implying two tests with globs.

findings.title: The three schedulers duplicate the tick lifecycle a third time
findings.scenario: JobScheduler, ResearcherScheduler and IntakeScheduler each carry their own tickTimer field, identical start/stop, an identical `ticking` re-entrancy guard, an identical inFlight Set for per-id single-flight, and a tick() whose skeleton is the same read-registry / skip-if-in-flight / skip-if-not-due / fire loop. The 8-line-window scan puts intakeScheduler~researcherScheduler at 19 shared blocks. This is the same mechanism as CX-2 but in a second family, so a lifecycle fix (e.g. awaiting in-flight work on stop, which QUIESCE-3 cares about) currently needs eight edits across both families.
findings.recommendation: If CX-2's DrainLoop lands, generalise it once more into a `TickLoop` the three schedulers and the five stages both build on (start/stop/re-entrancy guard/inFlight set), leaving each class only its registry read, its due predicate and its run body. If CX-2 is not funded, do the schedulers alone — they are smaller (409 lines total) and lower risk. Either way this is worth roughly 70 lines, and its real value is that stop-semantics live in one place.
findings.verify_hint: `diff <(sed -n '58,131p' app/src/kb/intakeScheduler.ts) <(sed -n '52,163p' app/src/kb/researcherScheduler.ts)` — divergence is confined to type names and researcher-specific memoisation.
corrections: The cited quotes are all accurate at the cited lines, and the tickTimer/start()/stop()/`ticking` re-entrancy envelope is genuinely identical across all three schedulers. But the finding overstates uniformity: jobScheduler.ts does NOT have "an identical inFlight Set for per-id single-flight" — it has no `inFlight` field at all. Instead it keeps a persistent `runners: Map<string, {runner: JobRunner; sig: string}>` (jobScheduler.ts:35) and delegates single-flight to each job's own long-lived `JobRunner.inFlight` getter (jobStage.ts:350-352, backed by a `running` boolean), with sig-based rebuild-on-config-change logic (jobScheduler.ts:107-112) and an extra public `runNow(jobId)` manual-trigger API (jobScheduler.ts:95-102) that neither intakeScheduler nor researcherScheduler has. The tight, near-verbatim duplication the finding's own verify_hint diffs (intake vs researcher only) is real and well-demonstrated — those two literally share the `if (this.inFlight.has(id)) continue` / add-before-await / delete-in-finally pattern almost line-for-line. jobScheduler's tick loop has no such inFlight check at all (it relies on `runnerFor().runNow()`'s internal guard). So the recommendation to generalize a shared `TickLoop` "leaving each class only its registry read, its due predicate and its run body" is well_scoped for the intake/researcher pair but not for jobScheduler, which would need to keep its persistent-runner-map, sig-rebuild, and manual-runNow surface — real extra design work the finding's effort estimate (S, ~70 lines) doesn't obviously account for. Recommend narrowing the primary claim to intakeScheduler+researcherScheduler (which the finding's own fallback sentence already half-concedes) and treating jobScheduler folding-in as a separate, larger, less well-scoped sub-decision.

findings.title: pathExists is defined nine times, identically
findings.scenario: Nine files (codeGit, jobStage, sourceOpen, pathContainment, stagingWorktree, connectStage, replay, reviewStore, mergeNodes) each declare a private, byte-identical `pathExists` wrapping fs.access in try/catch. It is the single most-duplicated block in the repo by the window scan. Harmless today, but it is the visible tip of a missing fs-helpers module — `err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)` appears 47 times and `readFile(..., 'utf8')` 87 times with hand-rolled try/catch around most of them.
findings.recommendation: Add `src/kb/fsUtil.ts` exporting `pathExists`, `readFileOr(path, fallback)` and `errMessage(err)`, and repoint the nine plus the highest-value error-message sites. Roughly 60 lines removed. Zero behavioural risk — these are pure functions with total coverage through their callers. Do it as its own commit so it does not muddy a larger refactor's diff.
findings.verify_hint: `grep -rn 'async function pathExists' app/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v test | wc -l` → 9.
corrections: The finding's core count (9 files) and its supporting duplication stats (47x error-message pattern, 87x readFile utf8) are all verified exact. But the headline claim that pathExists is defined "nine times, identically" / "byte-identical" is false: 7 of the 9 implementations wrap fs.access(p) (jobStage.ts:57, sourceOpen.ts:31, pathContainment.ts:45, stagingWorktree.ts:15, replay.ts:73, connectStage.ts:122, mergeNodes.ts:88), while 2 wrap fs.stat(p) instead (codeGit.ts:157, reviewStore.ts:44). These are not behaviorally identical in all edge cases — fs.access checks accessibility (can be denied by permissions even if the path exists), fs.stat checks existence via a stat call and can succeed on a path the caller lacks access to. A blind consolidation onto one implementation is not strictly "zero behavioural risk" as claimed; the recommendation should note the split and either standardize deliberately on fs.access (matching the 7/9 majority) or keep a documented reason for the 2 stat-based outliers. The overall recommendation (extract to fsUtil.ts, S effort, P3) is still sound and low-risk in practice, just needs this correction to the "identical" claim and a one-line caveat on the consolidation step.

findings.title: No stage registry: adding a pipeline stage requires ~8 hand-maintained edits including poke edges inside other stages' closures

evidence.quote: a.compose.start(); // SPEC-0046: the Compose Enrich stage (entity prose from cited claims)

findings.scenario: An engineer adds a seventh stage (e.g. SPEC-0052 media extraction as its own stage, or a dedup stage). They must edit: STAGE_ORDER in kb/pipelineStages.ts; the composition root in pipelineLifecycle.ts (~line 448-540); the startActiveStages list; the stopAllStages list; the ActivePipeline type; the statusCache CanonicalQueueCache map; the set-aside dispatch in pipeline.ts:119-137; the quiesce producer list; and — the easy one to miss — the afterDrain closures of upstream stages, since the poke graph (claims→connect+compose, connect→compose) is hand-coded inside each stage's construction. Missing any one is silent: the stage compiles and runs but never starts, never stops on vault switch, or never gets poked. ARCH-1 shows this failure mode has already occurred.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a stage descriptor array ({id, construct, pokes, setAside?}) that startActiveStages/stopAllStages/quiesce iterate, and derive the poke graph from declared `pokes` edges rather than hand-written afterDrain closures. Key the statusCache and set-aside table off StageId so the compiler enforces completeness. This is the same move registryCrud.ts already made for the four registries.
findings.verify_hint: Read pipelineLifecycle.ts:448-540 and count the explicit constructor calls and afterDrain closures; then diff the member list against startActiveStages:169-180 and stopAllStages:184-196.
corrections: none — mechanism verified as described. All cited files/lines match verbatim. STAGE_ORDER (kb/pipelineStages.ts:12) is a fixed 6-tuple; startActiveStages (pipelineLifecycle.ts:169-180) and stopAllStages (184-196) are explicit per-stage call lists; ActivePipeline (line 76) is a hand-typed interface enumerating each stage; statusCache is a hand-typed object with one CanonicalQueueCache field per stage/set-aside kind (lines 105-112, constructed 559-567); the set-aside dispatch in pipeline.ts:119-137 is a hardcoded if/else-if chain keyed on req.stage ('claims'/'connect'/'archive'); and the poke graph is indeed hand-coded inside afterDrain closures rather than declared data — confirmed at pipelineLifecycle.ts ~480-509 where Connect's afterDrain calls `void compose.poke()` and Claims' afterDrain calls `void connect.poke(); void compose.poke();`, both inline inside each stage's constructor call. The comments even narrate the poke edges by hand ("Claims' afterDrain promotes... then pokes Connect... It also pokes Compose"), which is exactly the "easy one to miss" risk the finding describes — a new stage's upstream pokers must be manually located and edited. The recommendation (a declarative stage-descriptor array with `pokes` edges, mirroring registryCrud.ts's registry-table pattern) is a real, coherent design direction but requires actual design work (how afterDrain ordering/async semantics map onto a declared graph), so well_scoped=false is fair. Not release-blocking — it's a maintainability/extensibility cost on a codebase that hasn't added a stage since inception, not a defect affecting current behavior.

findings.title: SQLite library index is not wired to the pipeline lifecycle; stores are per-root and closed only at process exit

evidence.quote: // root, closed only at process exit, is a negligible resource cost (one sqlite file handle) worth

findings.scenario: The user switches vaults several times in a session. findings.title: View lifecycle contract is optional, so a new view can silently skip cleanup

evidence.quote: export type MountFn = (container: HTMLElement) => ViewHandle | void | Promise<ViewHandle | void>;

findings.scenario: MountFn permits `void`, so the #510 show/hide lifecycle is opt-in. askView is the one mounted view that returns void — and it is also the view that registers the onAskProgress IPC subscription, which therefore has no hide() to unregister from. A new view added to the mounts map with a plain void mount compiles and renders correctly while leaking whatever polls or subscriptions it opens across view switches, with nothing in CI to catch it. The mounts map is also typed Record<string, MountFn> rather than keyed on the view-id union, so a NAV_VIEWS rail entry with no mount would only fail at click time.
findings.recommendation: Narrow MountFn to require a ViewHandle (views with nothing to clean up return a no-op handle), key the mounts map as Record<ViewId, MountFn> off a union derived from views.ts, and add a test asserting every NAV_VIEWS id has a mounts entry. All three are mechanical.

A missing mounts entry resolves via optional chaining (shell.ts ~220) and silently no-ops rather than failing. However the illustrative mechanism is wrong: askView onAskProgress (line 296) is not a persistent hide-dependent subscription; it is opened and unconditionally torn down inside the same onAsk() call's finally block (line 304), regardless of view visibility, so it does not leak across view switches as claimed. findings.title: No root README.md, CHANGELOG.md, or LICENSE file despite package.json declaring MIT
findings.scenario: A first-time visitor to the repo (a contributor, or anyone the repo is shared with ahead of a public pre-release) finds no README at the root, no LICENSE file backing the MIT claim, and no CHANGELOG — the only entry points are the agent-oriented CLAUDE.md and 60+ files under specs/. `find . -maxdepth 1 -iname 'readme*' -o -iname 'changelog*' -o -iname 'license*'` returns nothing.
findings.recommendation: Add a root README.md (what the product is, how to build/run app/, link to specs/INDEX.md), a LICENSE file matching the declared MIT license, and start a CHANGELOG.md before any public-facing tag.
corrections: The core claim is exact and holds; two refinements. (1) UNDERSTATED — the repo is PUBLIC and carries no license metadata at all: `gh repo view masra91/Vellum-KB --json visibility,licenseInfo,description` returns `{"description":"","homepageUrl":"","licenseInfo":null,"name":"Vellum-KB","visibility":"PUBLIC"}`. So the MIT string in app/package.json:30 is the ONLY grant anywhere, it is buried in a subdirectory package manifest, GitHub shows no license, and a public repo without a LICENSE file defaults to all-rights-reserved for readers — this is a licensing-clarity gap, not merely a docs-polish gap, and it is the part that actually blocks a public tag. (2) SLIGHTLY OVERSTATED — the missing CHANGELOG.md is a *documented, deliberate* deferral, not an oversight: .github/workflows/release.yml:4-6 says the slice "does NOT implement the full SPEC-0055 authoring flow (GPG-signed tags, commit classification, themed release notes, CHANGELOG.md) ... Those stay explicitly out of scope", and specs/features/SPEC-0055-release-cadence.md:109-110 carries CHANGELOG as RELEASE-15 with `Verify: none-yet`; release.yml:130 uses `--generate-notes` so a tagged draft release does get auto-generated notes. Recommend splitting: LICENSE + root README = release-blocking; CHANGELOG.md = P3 tracked against RELEASE-15, not release-blocking. Also worth noting SPEC-0057-brand-identity.md:29 already lists a "README header / simple landing" as in-scope brand work, so a README owner exists.

The file-absence claim is fully confirmed — `git ls-tree origin/main` (root) returns only `.github .gitignore .gitleaks.toml CLAUDE.md app brand design-prototypes specs`, and a full-tree grep finds no README/LICENSE/CHANGELOG/CONTRIBUTING anywhere that GitHub would render at root (no `.github/README.md` fallback either). But the finding is one bundle of three items with very different weight, and both its premise and its blocking claim need correcting:

(1) UNDERSTATED — the LICENSE half is stronger than argued. The repo is PUBLIC (gh: `"isPrivate":false,"visibility":"PUBLIC"`, created 2026-05-30) and GitHub reports `"licenseInfo":null` — i.e. three months of public exposure with no license grant at all, which under default copyright means all-rights-reserved regardless of the manifest's MIT string. That, not "a package.json claim lacks a backing file", is the material defect, and it is the only genuinely release-blocking part.

(2) OVERSTATED premise — "despite package.json declaring MIT" is weaker than implied: `app/package.json:7` is `"private": true`, so the manifest is never published to npm and its `license` field is consumed only by electron-forge's Linux makers (MakerRpm/MakerDeb at forge.config.ts:105-106), and Linux packaging is explicitly out of scope (SPEC-0055 §5). No consumer resolves that MIT claim today.

(3) OVERSTATED — the CHANGELOG item is a documented, deliberate deferral, not an oversight. `.github/workflows/release.yml:4-6` states slice 1 "does NOT implement ... themed release notes, CHANGELOG.md ... Those stay explicitly out of scope ... until a later slice", and SPEC-0055 RELEASE-15 carries `Verify: none-yet`. The same workflow header defines `-rc.N` as "a dry run", human-reviewed before publishing. So "start a CHANGELOG.md before any public-facing tag" contradicts the project's own ratified slicing; treat it as P3/tracked, not blocking.

(4) The README item is real and reachable (a public repo landing page with an empty `description` and no rendered README) and is already an in-scope brand deliverable — SPEC-0057:29 "Repo/landing visuals — README header / simple landing (light touch)" — but its impact is onboarding/presentation, not user-facing bug or engineering risk: P2, non-blocking.

Recommended restatement: split into LICENSE (P1, release-blocking, justified by public repo + licenseInfo=null, not by the private manifest), README (P2, non-blocking, cite SPEC-0057:29), CHANGELOG (P3, already deferred by release.yml + RELEASE-15). Severity for the bundle stays P1 only because the LICENSE component carries it.

The core factual claim is fully confirmed and is NOT stale: `git ls-tree --name-only origin/main` returns exactly 8 root entries (.github, .gitignore, .gitleaks.toml, CLAUDE.md, app, brand, design-prototypes, specs) — no README, LICENSE, or CHANGELOG; `git log --all --diff-filter=ADR -- README.md LICENSE LICENSE.md CHANGELOG.md COPYING NOTICE` returns ZERO commits, i.e. none of these files has ever existed on any branch in the repo's 506-commit history, so there is nothing to have been "already fixed". app/package.json:30 reads verbatim `"license": "MIT",` as cited. The gap is also externally observable and worse than stated: `gh repo view masra91/Vellum-KB` returns `"visibility":"PUBLIC"`, `"licenseInfo":null`, `"description":""` — the repo is already public, GitHub detects no license at all, and it has no description. No prior deep-review issue covers this: grep for readme|license|changelog across specs/research/2026-07-12-deep-review/ returns nothing, so #505–#531 never touched it. Three corrections: (1) SEVERITY/BUNDLING — the finding bundles three items of unequal weight under one P1; only the LICENSE file is genuinely release-blocking (a PUBLIC repo whose package.json declares MIT and whose release.yml attaches packaged mac/Windows artifacts to a GitHub Release is distributing binaries under an unbacked license claim), while missing README is discoverability (P2/P3) and missing CHANGELOG is a documented deferral, so the honest bundled severity is P2 with release_blocking scoped to the LICENSE component. (2) CHANGELOG IS A TRACKED, EXPLICIT DEFERRAL, not an oversight: specs/features/SPEC-0055-release-cadence.md:109-110 files it as RELEASE-15 with `Verify: none-yet → test:`, and .github/workflows/release.yml:4-6 states slice 1 "does NOT implement the full SPEC-0055 authoring flow (GPG-signed tags, commit classification, themed release notes, CHANGELOG.md) … Those stay explicitly out of scope (see the spec's §5) until a later slice"; release.yml:130 also passes `--generate-notes` to `gh release create`, so a tag does produce auto-generated release notes today. The CHANGELOG half should be reported as "known deferred requirement RELEASE-15" (P3). (3) SCENARIO WORDING OVERSTATES THE VOID: "the only entry points are the agent-oriented CLAUDE.md and 60+ files under specs/" is inaccurate — five directory READMEs exist (specs/README.md, brand/README.md, app/eval/README.md, app/eval/cassettes/README.md, app/eval/baselines-committed/README.md) plus specs/INDEX.md, and specs/README.md opens with a clear orientation ("This folder is the **source of intent** for KB-App…"). The correct, narrower claim is that there is no ROOT README, so a visitor landing on the public GitHub repo page gets no orientation and must guess to open specs/. The recommendation itself remains sound and implementable as written.

findings.title: SPEC-0055's tag grammar (RELEASE-2: -beta.N) contradicts the one release workflow actually built (release.yml: -rc.N)

evidence.quote: - **RELEASE-2** Tag grammar: stable = `vX.Y.Z`, beta = `vX.Y.Z-beta.N`; a beta tag publishes a GitHub

findings.scenario: Someone follows SPEC-0055 to cut the first beta release and tags `v0.2.0-beta.1` per RELEASE-2 — but release.yml's actual pre-release convention is `-rc.N` (with `-beta.N` explicitly deferred to 'a future' state per its own comment, line 99), so the tag they cut per the spec doesn't mean what the spec says it means in the pipeline that will actually process it.
findings.recommendation: Reconcile the two: either implement `-beta.N` as SPEC-0055 specifies and retire the `-rc.N` dry-run convention, or update RELEASE-2 to document `-rc.N` as the current (pre-beta) dry-run grammar with `-beta.N` marked a later slice.
corrections: none — minor nuance worth adding: release.yml's publish job (line 98-99) treats ANY '-' suffix in the tag as pre-release-triggering, so a literal '-beta.N' tag per RELEASE-2 would still mechanically produce a pre-release (not break the pipeline); the real drift is purely documentational/naming — the spec's normative grammar (RELEASE-2, no caveat) vs. the workflow's own comments which treat '-rc.N' as the current convention and '-beta.N' as explicitly future/out-of-scope. findings.title: #515's Mutex section-timeout backstop is built and tested but wired to zero production locks — including the shared lock guarding raw, unbounded fs writes in capture

evidence.quote: const lock = new Mutex({ log: log.child({ scope: 'lock' }) });
const res = await this.lock.run(() => captureToInbox(this.root, surface, payloads), 'capture', { priority: true });

findings.scenario: PR #544 (fix #515) built Mutex.sectionTimeoutMs/RunOptions.timeoutMs specifically as 'a backstop for non-git work in a section (fs writes, sidecar reads)' per its own doc comment, then a same-PR follow-up commit deliberately declined to apply it as a blanket default on the shared per-vault lock (a defensible call, since a fired timeout mid-git-call would let the next waiter run concurrently with an orphaned in-flight write). But nothing since has opted ANY real Mutex into a timeout — confirmed 0 of ~25 `new Mutex(...)` sites pass sectionTimeoutMs, and no `.run(fn, label, { timeoutMs })` call exists in prod code. captureToInbox's raw fs.mkdir/fs.writeFile calls (ingest.ts:110-159) run under the exact shared lock every pipeline stage waits on, via Orchestrator.capture() with no timeout of any kind. If a write stalls (iCloud eviction, a disconnected network-mounted vault, a full disk), the #163 watchdog only logs a warning at 30s — it never releases the lock — so every future capture and every stage run wedges silently forever, the very failure class #515 was opened to close, just not closed on this call site.
findings.recommendation: Pass a bounded timeoutMs on the specific `lock.run(() => captureToInbox(...), 'capture', { priority: true })` call (capture writes a handful of small files, so a short constant like 5-10s is easy to justify without needing the broader multi-git-call-section timeout policy the #544 follow-up correctly deferred). Audit whether any other lock.run(...) section performs unbounded non-git fs work reachable the same way.
findings.verify_hint: grep every `new Mutex(` and every `.lock.run(` call site for a timeoutMs/sectionTimeoutMs argument; none currently pass one. Reproduce by stubbing fs.writeFile to hang in a captureToInbox unit test and confirming lock.run() never settles.

findings.title: `promote()` is a destructive one-way mirror onto the LIVE Obsidian vault — it silently overwrites uncommitted user edits (unrecoverable) and deletes user-created files under the evergreen roots

evidence.quote: Managed by Vellum. You can also open this folder directly in Obsidian.

findings.scenario: The user opens their vault in Obsidian (which the app's own README invites) and edits `entities/acme-corp.md` to add a paragraph. Minutes later Connect or Claims changes that same node on `staging`, the coalescing promoter fires, and `promote` runs `git checkout staging -- entities/acme-corp.md` in the vault ROOT worktree. `git checkout <tree-ish> -- <path>` overwrites working-tree modifications with no prompt: the paragraph is gone, and because the app only ever commits its own index, the text was never committed — I reproduced this in a scratch repo and `git log --all -S<text>` found 0 commits, i.e. it is unrecoverable. Second scenario: the user (or the very common Obsidian Git plugin auto-commit) commits a note they authored at `entities/my-note.md`. It is present on `main` and absent on `staging`, so the mirror diff classifies it `D` and `git rm -f` deletes it from the vault on the next promote — reproduced identically. Nothing checks the root worktree for divergence before mirroring, and no test asserts a human edit survives a promote.
findings.recommendation: Before the mirror ops, read the root's `git status` and refuse-or-quarantine on divergence: (1) if any path in `toRestore` is dirty in the working tree, copy it aside to `.kb/quarantine/<ts>/<rel>` (or commit it on a `kb/user-edits` ref) and emit a `user-edit-quarantined` audit event + a surfaced finding, then proceed; (2) never `git rm -f` a path that exists on `main` but has no `staging` ancestor — treat a main-only tracked file under an evergreen root as user content and skip it (log + surface). Add a regression test that seeds a dirty root file and a main-only file, runs `promote`, and asserts both survive.
findings.verify_hint: In a scratch repo: seed `entities/a.md` on main, branch `staging`, change the file on staging and commit, return to main, modify the file WITHOUT committing, then run `git checkout staging -- entities/a.md`. The uncommitted text is gone and `git log --all -S<text>` returns nothing. Repeat with a main-only committed file to see the `D` classification and the `git rm -f`.
related_prior: edit-quarantine ruling (ratified, no code: `grep -ri quarantine app/src` is empty)

findings.title: `applyProse` replaces the entire human-writable region of an entity note on every recompose
findings.scenario: The user opens `entities/person/ada-lovelace.md` in Obsidian and types two sentences of their own directly under the `# Ada Lovelace` heading — the single most natural place to annotate a note. Later a new claim attaches, the compose signature changes, `composeOne` re-runs, and `applyProse` rebuilds the file as `head (frontmatter + H1) + newProse + blocks`: everything the user wrote between the H1 and the first `kb:links`/`kb:claims` marker is discarded. Text placed *below* the blocks survives, but nothing tells the user that. The loss is committed on `staging` and mirrored to `main`, so the vault shows only the machine's prose.
findings.recommendation: Needs a placement decision first (where do human edits live in a machine-regenerated note?). Cheapest correct v1: treat the prose region as machine-owned only when it is byte-identical to the last prose Compose wrote — store that hash in the node's frontmatter (`composedProseHash`) and, on mismatch, skip the rewrite and raise a Review ("this page was edited by hand — keep your version or replace it?"). Alternative: give humans an explicit `<!-- kb:notes -->` block that Compose never touches, and document it in the vault README.

findings.title: Connect autonomously deletes loser entity nodes — and their composed prose — with no review and no tombstone
