findings.title: BUG-1's invariant is not held: Connect's three lock-held sweeps spawn unbounded git via `ensureWorktree`, and the shared mutex has no section deadline

evidence.quote: const res = await this.lock.run(() => linkOne(this.root, nodeRel, this.log), 'connect:link');
const lock = new Mutex({ log: log.child({ scope: 'lock' }) });

findings.scenario: BUG-1's stated AC was a greppable invariant — "no `simpleGit(` without a timeout inside any `lock.run` closure". `linkOne` (1599), `linkOrphansOnce` (1620) and `dedupClaimsOnce` (1635) all run inside `this.lock.run(...)`, and each begins with `ensureWorktree(root)`, which builds a RAW `simpleGit(root)` (437) and then runs `ensureGitIdentity` (`git config user.email`), `resolve BaseBranch` (`rev-parse`), `worktree prune`, a `simpleGit(wt).revparse`, and on an unhealthy worktree `worktree add`. That is 3-5 unbounded git children per lock hold, and the shared per-vault mutex deliberately sets no `sectionTimeoutMs` (the comment at pipelineLifecycle.ts:390-401 explains why). On an iCloud Drive vault — a configuration the app explicitly detects and merely warns about (permissions.ts:12) — a not-yet-materialized `.git` object can stall a git child indefinitely. From that moment every capture, every Settings write, every stage advance and every promote queues behind the holder forever; the watchdog only emits `lock.stuck` to a dev log no UI reads (see REL-6). Symptom: "the app hangs, needs a restart."
findings.recommendation: Route `ensureWorktree`'s client through `boundedGit(root)` (and the health probe through `boundedGit(wt)`) — a one-line-per-site change matching every other converted site. Then either extend `boundedGitUnderLock.test.ts` with a `connect:link` case using the existing blocking-pre-commit-hook harness, or add a lint/test that greps every `lock.run` closure's transitive call graph for a bare `simpleGit(`. Separately, reconsider a generous per-section deadline on the shared mutex now that every git call inside is bounded.
findings.verify_hint: `grep -n "ensureWorktree(" app/src/kb/connectStage.ts` → 436 (def), 1168, 1233, 1302; then `grep -n "lock.run(() => linkOne\|linkOrphansOnce\|dedupClaimsOnce" app/src/kb/connectStage.ts` → 1599, 1620, 1635. `ensureWorktree` line 437 constructs a bare `simpleGit`, not `boundedGit`.

findings.title: The watch dedup ledger is non-atomic, untracked, self-heals to empty, and is deleted wholesale by the staging-worktree repair — losing it re-mints every watched file as a duplicate immutable source

evidence.quote: for (const e of Object.values(ledger)) hashIndex.set(e.hash, e.sourceId);
if (await pathExists(wt)) await fs.rm(wt, { recursive: true, force: true });

findings.scenario: `.kb/watch/<id>/seen.json` is the only record of which watched files have already been ingested, and the content-hash dedup index is rebuilt FROM it each pass (watchRun.ts:196-197). It is written with a plain truncate-then-write, read with a catch that returns `{}` on any parse failure, is never git-committed, and lives inside the staging worktree — which `ensureStagingWorktree` deletes with `fs.rm -rf` whenever a one-line `rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` probe fails (a broken worktree admin entry, a cloud-synced volume hiccup, an interrupted `worktree add`). Any of those three events empties the ledger. The next watch pass then re-reads every file in every watched folder, finds no ledger entry and no hash match, and mints a brand-new immutable primary source for each — hundreds of duplicates that Decompose/Claims/Connect then all re-process (duplicate Copilot spend), with no delete path in the product (SPEC-0059 is still a draft PR). Nothing is logged as a duplicate; it looks like a successful ingest.
findings.recommendation: Three independent hardenings, any of which alone shrinks the blast radius: (1) write the ledger via the existing `writeJsonAtomic` (tmp+rename); (2) make the content-hash index authoritative by deriving it from `sources/` provenance rather than solely from the ledger, so a lost ledger degrades to a rescan-and-dedup instead of a re-mint; (3) have `ensureStagingWorktree` copy `.kb/watch`, `.kb/intake` and `.kb/research` aside (or `git stash`-equivalent) before the `fs.rm`, and emit a `maintenance` audit event naming what it discarded.

The git-tracked ones (registries, instance.json) are recoverable by hand from history; the ledgers are not.

Add a small test that writes a truncated file and asserts the reader still returns the LAST GOOD value where a `.bak` exists, or at minimum logs a loud `state.corrupt` event instead of silently returning empty.

findings.title: No `requestSingleInstanceLock()` — the canonical writer is an in-process mutex, so two app instances on one vault are two uncoordinated writers

findings.title: Worktree health is probed with a single `rev-parse`, and the "unhealthy" repair is an unaudited `rm -rf` of everything untracked in it

findings.title: Hand-rolled YAML quoting misses YAML indicator characters — common filenames produce malformed frontmatter in the user's Obsidian vault
findings.scenario: `scalar()` quotes only on `:`, `#`, `'`, `"`, newline, or leading/trailing whitespace. YAML's other indicator characters are unhandled, and `title`/`originalName` come straight from user filenames. Dropping `[2024] Q3 Report.pdf` writes `title: [2024] Q3 Report.pdf` — a YAML flow sequence that fails to parse, so Obsidian's Properties panel shows a frontmatter error on that source and any YAML consumer chokes. Same for names starting with `{`, `- `, `? `, `@`, `` ` ``, `*`, `&`, `!`, `|`, `>`, or `%`. The app's own readers use regex so they round-trip fine, which is exactly why this would go unnoticed — the breakage is only visible in the product's headline surface, the Obsidian vault.

Add a table-driven test over those inputs asserting the emitted frontmatter round-trips through a real YAML parser (dev-dependency only).

findings.title: Vault boot provisioning uses unbounded git and its failure is fire-and-forget — a stalled git at startup leaves the app running with no pipeline and no message

Because it is launched fire-and-forget (`void initPipeline().then(...).catch(...)`), `createWindow()` proceeds and the user gets a normal-looking window whose views all report no data, forever, with no error — the `catch` only writes `boot.init-pipeline-failed` to the app log, and a hang never reaches the catch at all. findings.recommendation: Use `boundedGit(vaultRoot)` inside `ensureStagingWorktree` (and for the `simpleGit(wt)` probe), then wrap the `ensureStagingWorktree` await in `startPipeline` with an explicit deadline that throws a typed `VaultProvisionTimeout`. findings.title: No signed/notarized build and zero in-app or in-repo install guidance — first launch is a Gatekeeper dead end

evidence.quote: OPT-IN (`KB_OSX_SIGN=1`) so the default `npm run package` stays UNSIGNED — CI's package build-check
import/manage signing credentials in CI (no such secrets exist in this repo yet).
const CREDITS = 'Built on an Obsidian-compatible markdown vault · GitHub Copilot · Electron · OFL faces (Inter · Spectral · IBM Plex Mono).';

findings.scenario: A tester on a clean Mac downloads the release artifact release.yml would attach, double-clicks it, and macOS Gatekeeper reports the app is 'damaged and can't be opened' (unsigned/unnotarized). There is no README at the repo root, no link in About or Settings, and no in-app message explaining the right-click-Open or `xattr -cr` workaround — the app is simply unusable for anyone without prior Electron/macOS packaging knowledge. A Windows user gets an unsigned Squirrel installer and a SmartScreen warning with the same lack of guidance.
findings.recommendation: At minimum, ship a root README with the Gatekeeper/SmartScreen workaround for unsigned builds and link it from the About panel/Settings footer; longer-term, obtain an Apple Developer ID + notarization and a Windows code-signing cert per the SPEC-0034 MACOS-3/8 groundwork that already exists (osxSign scaffolding is present, just opt-in and unused in the release pipeline).
corrections:
The substance holds and all four cited quotes are verbatim at the cited lines. Two corrections, both to mechanism/wording, plus one weak evidence item.

(1) MECHANISM — the mac artifact is not strictly "unsigned". `@electron-forge/plugin-fuses@7.11.2` (app/node_modules/@electron-forge/plugin-fuses/dist/FusesPlugin.js) passes `resetAdHocDarwinSignature: !hasOSXSignConfig && applePlatforms.includes(platform) && arch === 'arm64'`. Since `KB_OSX_SIGN` is unset in release.yml's build job (it runs a bare `npm run make` with no env), `osxSign` is absent from packagerConfig, so on macos-latest (arm64) the packaged Vellum.app gets a re-applied AD-HOC signature. Consequence: it launches fine when built/copied locally; what actually blocks the tester is the quarantine xattr on the downloaded MakerZIP `.zip`, evaluated against an ad-hoc (non-Developer-ID, un-notarized) signature. The corrected claim is "ad-hoc-signed, not Developer-ID-signed and not notarized → Gatekeeper rejects the downloaded copy", not "unsigned binary". On Intel/x64 there is no signature at all.

(2) WORKAROUND IN THE RECOMMENDATION IS DATED — for the ad-hoc/quarantine case macOS commonly reports "damaged and can't be opened", and on macOS 15+ right-click→Open no longer bypasses that dialog; the reliable instruction is `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Vellum.app`. A README that tells testers to right-click→Open will not work.

(3) WEAK EVIDENCE ITEM — evidence items 3 and 4 (aboutPanel.ts:18 CREDITS, settingsView.ts:241 About footer) are true (About renders wordmark/tagline/credits/version/Close with zero links; grep for `http|href|Help|Docs` in aboutPanel.ts hits only the focus-trap selector) but are near-irrelevant to a Gatekeeper dead end: an app Gatekeeper refuses to launch never renders About or Settings. The load-bearing evidence is repo-level and is even stronger than stated: `git ls-files | awk -F/ 'NF==1'` returns ONLY `.gitignore`, `.gitleaks.toml`, `CLAUDE.md` — no README, no LICENSE, no INSTALL, no docs/ dir; `package.json` has no `homepage`, `repository`, or `bugs`; release.yml drafts with `--generate-notes` only (auto commit list, no install section); and a repo-wide grep for `gatekeeper|xattr|quarantine|smartscreen|unidentified developer|damaged and` finds ZERO user-facing hits (only the unrelated `orchestrator.ts` archive-poison "quarantine" and SPEC-0034's internal MACOS-8 row). Windows: `new MakerSquirrel({})` with no `certificateFile`/`certificatePassword` anywhere → unsigned installer, SmartScreen warning, same absence of guidance. So the recommendation's "link it from the About panel/Settings footer" half should be demoted to nice-to-have; the blocking fix is a root README + an install section in the drafted release body.

evidence.quote: `<g class="exp-node${spec ? ' exp-node--spec' : ''}" data-rel="${esc(n.rel)}" data-name="${esc(n.name)}" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-label="${esc(n.name)} — ${esc(kind)}, explore">

findings.title: `compose` is missing from the ephemeral-worktree reap allowlist — 185 orphaned worktrees / 3.3 GB already leaked into the live vault

evidence.quote: await withEphemeralWorktree(root, STAGE, base, async ({ wt, workBranch }) => {

findings.scenario: Compose creates a per-item worktree named `compose-<ULID>` via withEphemeralWorktree. If the teardown in the `finally` block fails or the process is killed mid-item, the directory survives. `reapEphemeralWorktrees` — the recovery path that runs at boot/staging-provision — only reaps names matching EPHEMERAL_WT_NAME, which does not include `compose`, so those directories are never collected; and `pruneStaleWorktreeBranches`' `branch -D` is refused for any branch still checked out in a registered worktree. Measured on the live vault at ~/kb-test-1: 185 `compose-*` directories totalling 3.3 GB (individual dirs 2.8–26 MB) inside a 3.6 GB vault, with only 14 entries in .git/worktrees. The module's own comment predicts the endgame: 'each new item gets slower as the leak grows — eventually starving the pipeline / the IPC event loop so the Jobs UI reads as hung.'
findings.recommendation: Add 'compose' to EPHEMERAL_STAGES (and add a unit test asserting that every stage that calls withEphemeralWorktree appears in the allowlist — derive the list from the call sites or assert the set equality, so a future stage cannot be added without it). Ship a one-time migration that reaps existing `compose-*` worktrees on next boot. Separately, make the guard self-checking: `withEphemeralWorktree` should reject at call time if `stage` is not in EPHEMERAL_STAGES, so an unreapable worktree can never be created in the first place.
findings.verify_hint: grep -n EPHEMERAL_STAGES app/src/kb/canonicalAdvance.ts and grep -n "const STAGE" app/src/kb/composeStage.ts — 'compose' is absent from the first. Then: ls -d ~/kb-test-1/.kb/cache/worktrees/staging/.kb/cache/worktrees/compose-* | wc -l (185) and du -ch on the same glob (3.3G).
corrections:
The core mechanism is fully confirmed and, if anything, understated in one place and overstated in another.

findings.scenario: index.html declares only a charset meta and there is no `session.defaultSession.webRequest.onHeadersReceived` CSP anywhere in src — grep for 'Content-Security-Policy' returns zero matches. The renderer composes 71 innerHTML sites across 24 modules from vault- and LLM-derived strings, protected only by a hand-rolled `esc()` and (in exactly one place) DOMPurify. Ask renders web-research findings that were fetched from arbitrary public pages, so the content is genuinely attacker-influenced. One missed `esc()` — or one DOMPurify bypass — yields script execution in a renderer that holds the full 74-channel `kb:*` bridge (capture, pipelineControl, fullReplay, setInstanceSettings, saveRecallOutput), turning defacement into vault mutation. A CSP of `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'` would make that step inert.
findings.recommendation: Add a restrictive CSP — either a `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` in index.html or an `onHeadersReceived` header in main — with `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-src 'none'`. Add an e2e or unit assertion that the policy is present so it can't silently regress. Separately add an eslint rule (or a shell-tier test) that flags an `innerHTML` assignment whose template interpolates anything other than `esc(...)`, `emptyState(...)` or a known-trusted constant.
findings.verify_hint: grep -rn 'Content-Security-Policy' app/src app/index.html → no matches; grep -rn 'DOMPurify.sanitize' app/src → one hit (askView.ts:26); grep -rn innerHTML app/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v test | wc -l → 71.

The factual core is CONFIRMED, but the framing overstates the exposure on three points, and release_blocking should be false.

CONFIRMED as stated:
1. There is no CSP anywhere. `grep -rniI 'content-security-policy' app/src app/index.html app/forge.config.ts app/vite.*.ts` returns exit 1 (zero matches). app/index.html is 10 lines and carries only charset + title. There is no `onHeadersReceived`, no `contentSecurityPolicy` key.
2. 71 non-test `innerHTML` sites across 24 modules (`grep -rn innerHTML app/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v '\.test\.' | wc -l` → 71; by-file breakdown: askView 11, exploreView 6, healthView 5, activityView 5, captureView 4, topbarSearch 4, shell 4, loadGuard 4, …).
3. Exactly one `DOMPurify.sanitize` call in prod code (askView.ts:26).
4. The escalation path is real: `app/src/preload.ts:102` does `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('kbApi', kbApi)` exposing 72 `ipcRenderer.invoke` wrappers (72 `ipcMain.handle` sites) into the main world, including `capture`, `pipelineControl`, `fullReplay`, `setInstanceSettings`, `saveRecallOutput`. contextIsolation does NOT stop injected main-world script from calling `window.kbApi.*`, so CSP genuinely is the missing layer here. Attacker-influenced content does reach the renderer (web-researcher findings land in the vault — app/src/kb/researchInline.ts:51).

CORRECTIONS:
(a) The title's implication — "a single DOMPurify call guarding 71 innerHTML sites" — is wrong. DOMPurify guards exactly ONE site: the Ask markdown answer. The other 70 are template-literal composition guarded by `esc()` (app/src/shell/html.ts:11-17, which escapes & < > " ' — correct for both text and quoted-attribute contexts), and the majority interpolate trusted constants/nested fragments (icons, skeletons, class flags), not untrusted data. The one path that renders genuinely untrusted markdown IS sanitized. Reword to "no CSP backstop behind a hand-rolled `esc()` discipline across 71 innerHTML sites, with DOMPurify covering only the Ask answer".
(b) The "one DOMPurify bypass" leg has no live CVE behind it. The two advisories against the pinned dompurify 3.4.5 (A4_npm_audit_summary.txt:37-39) are both IN_PLACE-mode issues ("Cross-realm IN_PLACE sanitization…", "IN_PLACE mode preserves attributes of a clobbered root element"). askView.ts:26 calls the string form `DOMPurify.sanitize(<string>)`, not `{IN_PLACE: true}` on a DOM node, so neither applies. The upgrade to 3.4.14 is still hygiene, but it is not an open hole today.
(c) Unstated implementation wrinkles that the recommendation's literal policy would break, and that an implementer must resolve: `default-src 'self'` with no `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` blocks the 3 inline style attributes at app/src/shell/views/todayView.ts:156-158, and blocks Vite's dev-mode JS-injected `<style>` tags and its ws:// HMR channel (renderer.ts imports @fontsource CSS through the bundler; prod emits a linked stylesheet, dev injects inline). A meta CSP in index.html therefore needs a dev/prod split or `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` + `connect-src 'self' ws:`. Also note `onHeadersReceived` is unreliable for the production `loadFile` file:// load path (main.ts:65-69 and quickCaptureElectron.ts:112 both load from file:// when packaged), so the meta-tag variant is the one that actually applies in production.

UNSTATED SUPPORTING GAPS (strengthen the finding, worth folding in): there are ZERO `setWindowOpenHandler` / `will-navigate` / `web-contents-created` guards in app/src, and both BrowserWindows set `webPreferences: { preload }` only, relying entirely on Electron 42 defaults for contextIsolation/sandbox rather than asserting them explicitly.

STRENGTH to record: the shell has ZERO `href=` attributes in any prod module (`grep -rn 'href=' app/src/shell app/src/qcap --include='*.ts' | grep -v test` → no output) — a deliberate ASK-15/#93 decision documented at app/src/main/ipc.ts:558-561 ("we never build the URI in the renderer, so the `obsidian:` scheme never touches the DOM"). That removes the `javascript:`-URL sink class outright.

RELEASE_BLOCKING: downgrade to false. This is defense-in-depth with no demonstrated injection: the app loads only file:// (no remote origins), the one untrusted-markdown path is sanitized with a version whose known CVEs do not apply to its call mode, and there is no href sink. P1 / fix-before-1.0 is right; it should not gate v0.1.0-rc.1.

findings.title: Shipped Electron is 42.2.0 with a published advisory fixed in 42.11.2 — nine patch releases of Chromium fixes behind, on a tree dormant seven weeks
findings.scenario: npm audit reports electron 42.2.0 as high with fix 42.11.2 (a non-major patch): 'ProtocolResponse.url reuses the default session cache instead of the registering session'. Electron patch releases also roll up Chromium security fixes, and main has not moved since 2026-07-13. Any v0.1.0-rc.1 cut today ships a runtime with a known advisory and ~7 weeks of unapplied Chromium patches to every user, in an app that renders fetched web content. The dompurify bump to 3.4.14 is likewise a patch. Note the honest scope: of 46 advisories only these two reach the shipped bundle, and both dompurify advisories are IN_PLACE-mode-specific while askView uses string-mode sanitize — so dompurify is hygiene, electron is the one that matters.
findings.recommendation: Bump electron to >= 42.11.2 and dompurify to >= 3.4.14 (both patch-level, no API change expected) and re-run the package build-check. Add a scheduled dependency-audit job that fails only on advisories whose package appears in the SHIPPED dependency closure (`dependencies` + electron), so the 43 dev/build-chain advisories don't drown the two that matter. Do NOT run `npm audit fix` — its suggested remediation for the electron-forge chain is a downgrade to 6.4.2 (major=True), which would break the build.
findings.verify_hint: grep -n '"electron"' app/package.json → 42.2.0; A4_npm_audit_summary.txt line for electron shows fix=electron@42.11.2 major=False. Confirm nothing else in `dependencies` is flagged: js-yaml/vitest/vite/tar/extract-zip are all dev.
corrections:
The factual core is exactly right and both quotes are verbatim at the cited lines: app/package.json:50 `"electron": "42.2.0",` (note: it sits in the devDependencies block, lines 31-58 — correct for Electron, and node_modules/electron resolves to 42.2.0, so 42.2.0 IS the runtime that packages), app/package.json:66 `"dompurify": "3.4.5",` in `dependencies`. A4 confirms electron high / fix=electron@42.11.2 major=False, dompurify moderate / fix=dompurify@3.4.14 major=False, and confirms `npm audit fix` would propose the @electron-forge → 6.4.2 major downgrade, so the "do NOT run audit fix" caveat is correct. The verify_hint also holds: js-yaml is dev-only in practice (its sole import is eval/runner/loader.ts:4, the BYOA eval harness, never src/), and nothing else in `dependencies` (better-sqlite3, marked, pdfjs-dist, turndown, chokidar, simple-git, @github/copilot-sdk, fontsource) appears in A4. The dompurify de-rating is also correct: the ONLY `sanitize(` call site in the whole tree is askView.ts:26 `return DOMPurify.sanitize(marked.parse(md, { async: false }) as string);` — string in / string out, never IN_PLACE and never RETURN_DOM, so neither advisory is reachable.

Two parts of the stated mechanism do NOT hold and should be reworded:

(1) The named advisory is inapplicable to this app. "ProtocolResponse.url reuses the default session cache instead of the registering session" requires a custom protocol handler registered against a non-default session. A grep across src/, forge.config.ts and the vite configs for `registerSchemesAsPrivileged`, `protocol.handle`, `registerFileProtocol`, `registerStreamProtocol`, `registerBufferProtocol`, `fromPartition` and `defaultSession` returns ZERO hits — the app registers no protocols and uses no partitioned session. So the concrete flagged CVE cannot fire here; the argument reduces entirely to the unenumerated Chromium rollups between 42.2 and 42.11, which the finding asserts but does not evidence (and cannot, offline, from this repo).

(2) "in an app that renders fetched web content" overstates the exposure. No BrowserWindow ever navigates to a remote origin: src/main.ts loads `loadFile(.../renderer/${MAIN_WINDOW_VITE_NAME}/index.html)` and src/main/quickCaptureElectron.ts:112 does the same with `{ hash: 'qcap' }`; the only `loadURL` calls are guarded by `MAIN_WINDOW_VITE_DEV_SERVER_URL`, i.e. dev-server only. Fetched web bytes are turndown'd to markdown into the vault and later re-rendered through marked→DOMPurify, so untrusted content does reach Chromium's HTML/CSS parsers — but as sanitized static markup with no script execution and no live web origin. The Chromium-CVE attack surface is materially narrower than "renders fetched web content" implies.

Minor: "nine patch releases of Chromium fixes behind" is inference from the version string (42.2.0 → 42.11.2 is nine increments of the third component; npm audit says major=False so the bump is safe), not something verifiable in-repo. Also note A4's own vulnerable range for electron is `42.0.0-alpha.1 - 42.5.0` while the listed fix is 42.11.2 — 42.2.0 is in range so the flag stands, but the fix version overshoots the advisory's range, i.e. 42.11.2 is "current stable", not "the minimum patched build".

Corrected claim: the shipped Electron runtime is pinned at a version carrying a published high advisory with a non-major fix available (42.11.2), and the tree has been dormant seven weeks, so an rc cut today ships a stale Chromium. The specific advisory is not exploitable in this codebase (no custom protocol/session) and the app never loads remote origins, so this is release hygiene on an unproven-exploitable stale runtime rather than a demonstrated vulnerability — P2, still worth clearing before a first public rc because the fix is a two-line patch bump plus a build-check re-run. The recommendation (bump both, add a scheduled audit gate scoped to the shipped closure = `dependencies` + electron, never `npm audit fix`) is sound and implementable as written.

Both cited quotes are exact and at the cited lines, and the version facts hold: app/package.json:50 pins `"electron": "42.2.0"` (package-lock.json:5459 confirms the resolved 42.2.0), which falls inside A4's vulnerable range `42.0.0-alpha.1 - 42.5.0` with `fix=electron@42.11.2 major=False`; dompurify is 3.4.5 at line 66. The finding's honest-scoping claims also check out: js-yaml is imported ONLY by app/eval/runner/loader.ts (dev harness), so nothing else in `dependencies` is flagged, and askView.ts:26 uses string-mode `DOMPurify.sanitize(marked.parse(...))` — never IN_PLACE — so both dompurify advisories are genuinely inapplicable.

What is overstated is the concrete mechanism and therefore the severity. (1) The named advisory — "ProtocolResponse.url reuses the default session cache instead of the registering session" — is UNREACHABLE in this codebase. Grepping all of app/src for `protocol.handle`, `registerFileProtocol`, `registerSchemesAsPrivileged`, `ProtocolResponse`, `defaultSession`, `fromPartition` and Electron `session.*` returns zero prod hits (the only `protocol.` matches are git config flags in kb/codeGit.ts:40-41, and every `session.` hit is the Copilot SDK's own session object in kb/recallAgent.ts / mediaExtract.ts). The app registers no custom protocol on any session, so the advisory's precondition cannot be met. (2) "in an app that renders fetched web content" overstates the Chromium attack surface: the only window loads a LOCAL file (main.ts:66 `mainWindow.loadFile(...)`, dev-server URL otherwise), there is no `<webview>`, no BrowserView, no remote navigation, and webPreferences sets only `preload` — so contextIsolation and sandbox stay at Electron's secure defaults. forge.config.ts:140-145 further hardens the bundle (`RunAsNode: false`, `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments: false`, `EnableEmbeddedAsarIntegrityValidation: true`, `OnlyLoadAppFromAsar: true`). The residual exposure is real but narrow: remotely fetched intake content (kb/intakeRun.ts:113 `items = await deps.fetch(c, { maxItems })`) lands in the vault and is later rendered through marked + DOMPurify into innerHTML, so attacker-influenceable text does reach Chromium's parser — inside a sandboxed, context-isolated, local-origin renderer.

Corrected claim: this is not a live exploitable advisory in the shipped configuration; it is runtime patch-drift — a shipped Chromium ~9 releases behind on a tree dormant seven weeks, with a published (but here unreachable) advisory as the audit signal. That is P2 dependency hygiene, not a P1 engineering risk. I still keep release_blocking=true: it is an S-effort patch bump with no API change, and cutting a public v0.1.0-rc.1 on a runtime with a known open advisory is not defensible when the fix is a lockfile line. Two additions the finding should carry: electron sits in `devDependencies` (line 50), not `dependencies`, so the proposed audit gate must special-case it (the recommendation already says "`dependencies` + electron" — good), and there is currently NO audit job and no dependabot config anywhere in .github/ (only .github/workflows exists), so the gate is fully net-new rather than a tweak.

The dependency facts are exactly right and NOT stale — but the exploitability framing in the scenario is overstated on two points, and the finding should be re-argued as prophylactic patch hygiene rather than as an exposed CVE.

(1) The named advisory is not reachable in this app. A4:41 describes "Electron: ProtocolResponse.url reuses the default session cache instead of the registering session" — that requires a custom protocol handler registered against a non-default session. `grep -rn "protocol\.|registerSchemesAsPrivileged|ProtocolResponse" app/src` returns exactly one hit, and it is a git config flag in an unrelated file (app/src/kb/codeGit.ts:41 `'-c', 'protocol.fd.allow=never',`). The app registers zero custom protocols. So the specific advisory npm audit flags has no attack path here; the remaining case is the generic "~9 stable increments of rolled-up Chromium fixes unapplied," which is a real but weaker argument.

(2) "in an app that renders fetched web content" is imprecise. The renderer never navigates to a remote origin: the only loads are `MAIN_WINDOW_VITE_DEV_SERVER_URL` (dev) or a local packaged `loadFile` (app/src/main/quickCaptureElectron.ts:110-112), there is no `setWindowOpenHandler`/`will-navigate` handling of remote URLs anywhere in app/src, and fetched web pages are converted to markdown in the node/main process (researchFetch, turndown) before reaching the renderer as marked+DOMPurify-sanitized HTML. Chromium's remote-content attack surface is much smaller than a browsing app's — non-zero (untrusted text, images, pdfjs) but not what the wording implies.

Everything else holds and should be kept verbatim: electron 42.2.0 is confirmed in package.json (line 50), package-lock.json:5459, and node_modules/electron/package.json; the fix is non-major (A4:40 `fix=electron@42.11.2 major=False`); dompurify 3.4.5 (line 66) with `fix=dompurify@3.4.14 major=False`; and the finding's honest scoping of dompurify as hygiene is correct — both dompurify advisories are IN_PLACE-mode-specific (A4:38-39) and `grep -rn "IN_PLACE|RETURN_DOM" app/src` returns zero hits, with askView.ts:26 using string-mode `DOMPurify.sanitize(...)`.

The "only these two reach the shipped bundle" scope claim also survives an independent check I ran: of the 13 entries in `dependencies`, only dompurify appears in A4; js-yaml is a devDependency with zero references anywhere under app/src; and every flagged transitive resolves to a build/dev chain, not the runtime closure (undici←node_modules/electron/node_modules/@electron/get, tar←@electron/node-gyp|@electron/rebuild|@mapbox/node-pre-gyp|cacache, @mapbox/node-pre-gyp←canvas, nanoid←postcss, @xmldom/xmldom←plist, ip-address←socks, fast-uri←ajv). The `npm audit fix` warning in the recommendation is also correct: the electron-forge chain's suggested remediation really is `fix=@electron-forge/cli@6.4.2 major=True` (A4:2).

Staleness lens finds nothing: `git log -S'"electron": "42' -- app/package.json` returns a single commit, a8a538c "Foundation: product specs, Electron shell, ..." (#1) — the pin has never been bumped since the repo's first commit on 2026-05-30. dompurify's pin traces to one commit, 919c93a (#93). package.json was last touched 2026-07-12 (50db509, #530/#541). There is no dependabot.yml or renovate.json (.github/ contains only workflows/{ci,nightly,release}.yml) and no audit step in any workflow — the gap is a known, explicitly-open spec item, SPEC-0011 line 48: "surface. Future: automate via a CI dependency-review / `npm audit` gate (ENG-5 none-yet)." None of the #505-#531 deep-review closures touched this. Nothing is fixed, mitigated, or test-covered.

Recommendation and effort stand unchanged (two patch-level pins + re-run package build-check + a shipped-closure-scoped audit job); one addition worth making explicit for the implementer: the audit gate must treat `electron` as shipped even though it lives in devDependencies, since electron-forge bundles it from there — a naive "`dependencies` only" filter would miss the one advisory that matters.

(1) The named advisory is not reachable in this app. A4:41 describes "Electron: ProtocolResponse.url reuses the default session cache instead of the registering session" — that requires a custom protocol handler registered against a non-default session. `grep -rn "protocol\.|registerSchemesAsPrivileged|ProtocolResponse" app/src` returns exactly one hit, and it is a git config flag in an unrelated file (app/src/kb/codeGit.ts:41 `'-c', 'protocol.fd.allow=never',`). The app registers zero custom protocols. So the specific advisory npm audit flags has no attack path here; the remaining case is the generic "~9 stable increments of rolled-up Chromium fixes unapplied," which is a real but weaker argument.

(2) "in an app that renders fetched web content" is imprecise. The renderer never navigates to a remote origin: the only loads are `MAIN_WINDOW_VITE_DEV_SERVER_URL` (dev) or a local packaged `loadFile` (app/src/main/quickCaptureElectron.ts:110-112), there is no `setWindowOpenHandler`/`will-navigate` handling of remote URLs anywhere in app/src, and fetched web pages are converted to markdown in the node/main process (researchFetch, turndown) before reaching the renderer as marked+DOMPurify-sanitized HTML. Chromium's remote-content attack surface is much smaller than a browsing app's — non-zero (untrusted text, images, pdfjs) but not what the wording implies.

findings.title: Hand-rolled frontmatter regex is LF-only — Git-for-Windows' default autocrlf makes every source's frontmatter invisible to the pipeline
findings.scenario:
Verified in-session: `"---
title: Hi
---
"`.match(/^---
([\s\S]*?)
---/) returns null. The app writes vault files with `
`, but the vault is a real git repo checked out into a staging worktree, and Git for Windows' installer defaults `core.autocrlf=true` globally. The app writes only user.email/user.name via ensureGitIdentity and ships no `.gitattributes`, so on Windows every checkout materializes CRLF — at which point deriveSourceTitle sees no frontmatter (falls back to first-body-line or 'Untitled source'), applySensitivityOverrideToSourceMd's `/^sensitivity: .*$/m` silently no-ops, and composeDoc's `md.startsWith('---')` branch reads a body that includes the whole frontmatter. Windows is a declared target: MakerSquirrel is configured and nightly.yml runs a windows e2e leg. Only `richText.ts:61` normalizes CRLF anywhere in the codebase.
findings.recommendation: Write a `.gitattributes` containing `* -text` (or `*.md text eol=lf`) at vault init/ensure, so the app's own repo never CRLF-converts regardless of the user's global git config — and make every frontmatter regex CRLF-tolerant (`/^---\r?\n([\s\S]*?)\r?\n---/`) as belt-and-braces, since a user or Obsidian plugin can still introduce CRLF. Add a fixture test with a CRLF source.md through deriveSourceTitle and applySensitivityOverrideToSourceMd.

([\s\S]*?)
---/))" → null. Then grep -rn 'autocrlf\|gitattributes' app/src → no matches, and ls .gitattributes at the repo root → absent.
corrections:
Mechanism and impact hold as claimed, with one minor citation slip: the `fmMatch` line is cited as line 43 but is actually at line 41 (the `stored` citation at line 45 is exact). Verified beyond the cited evidence: (1) the CRLF-null regex behavior reproduces exactly as stated (`node -e` check returns null); (2) `applySensitivityOverrideToSourceMd`'s `/^sensitivity: .*$/m` also fails to match a CRLF-terminated `sensitivity:` line (JS `.` excludes ``, and multiline `$` requires the position to sit immediately before `
`, not `
`), confirming the "silently no-ops" claim; (3) `composeDoc.ts:95` does have `if (md.startsWith('---'))`, matching the scenario; (4) critically, all read call sites (`sourceTitleRead.ts:20`, `composeStage.ts:226`, `connectStage.ts:163` and `connectStage.ts` `readSourceCard`) use `fs.readFile(path, 'utf8')` directly against the git worktree on disk — not `git show`/`git cat-file` — so they are genuinely exposed to git's checkout-time line-ending conversion rather than reading LF-normalized blob content, which is the load-bearing fact that makes the Windows-autocrlf mechanism actually reach the app instead of being neutralized by git internals. `readSourceCard` in connectStage.ts has its own near-identical `/^---
([\s\S]*?)
---/` frontmatter regex (also used to extract `scope:`), so the blast radius is slightly larger than stated (scope resolution breaks too, not just title/sensitivity). No `.gitattributes` file and no `autocrlf` reference exist anywhere in the repo (confirmed via grep/find), and `richText.ts:61` is confirmed as the only CRLF-normalizing line in the codebase relevant to this path (a couple of unrelated `?
` splits exist in research-note parsing, which already tolerate CRLF and are not part of this bug). MakerSquirrel (Windows installer) and a windows-latest nightly e2e leg confirm Windows is a real declared target, not a hypothetical one. The scenario's claim about Git for Windows defaulting to `core.autocrlf=true` on install is standard, well-documented git-for-windows behavior and is not falsifiable from this repo alone, but is consistent with the installer's default recommended option.

The core claim holds and reachability is real, but two of the three downstream consequences in the scenario are wrong, and the blast radius is actually broader than cited (understated, not overstated).

1) Evidence line off-by-2: the `fmMatch` quote is real but sits at sourceDoc.ts:41, not line 43 (line 43 is a comment). The line-45 quote and vault.ts:113 quote are exact.

2) Title-derivation claim CONFIRMED by direct test: `deriveSourceTitle()` on a CRLF doc with `title: My Real Title` returns the literal string `"---"` (even worse than the finding's "falls back to first-body-line or 'Untitled source'" — the frontmatter delimiter itself gets swallowed as the first body line because the body-stripping regex on sourceDoc.ts:51 also requires literal `\n`).

3) The `applySensitivityOverrideToSourceMd` claim is WRONG on mechanism: JS regex `$` in multiline mode treats `\r` as a line-terminator boundary too, so `/^sensitivity: .*$/m` (sourceDoc.ts:110) actually DOES match and replace correctly on CRLF — verified by direct test. The REAL bug in that function is different: the old `/^sensitivityMeta:\n(?: {2}\S.*\n)*/m` strip regex (sourceDoc.ts:105) requires literal `\n` and fails on CRLF, so the stale `sensitivityMeta:` block is never removed — the result is a DUPLICATE/stale sensitivityMeta block appended after a fresh one, not a "silent no-op."

4) The composeDoc.ts `md.startsWith('---')` claim is REFUTED: I traced `proseStart()` (composeDoc.ts:88-101) end-to-end on a CRLF entity doc and it correctly locates the post-frontmatter body start — `md.indexOf('\n---', 3)` and `md.indexOf('\n', ...)` are substring searches that still find the `\n` inside a `\r\n` sequence, so this path is not actually broken by CRLF.

5) "Only richText.ts:61 normalizes CRLF" is slightly overstated: researchCodeAgent.ts:139 and researchWebAgent.ts:123 also do CRLF-tolerant `\r?\n` splits (irrelevant to reachability since they're not in the frontmatter path).

6) Blast radius is actually BROADER than cited: the identical LF-only frontmatter regex also lives in connectStage.ts:179 (`readSourceCard`, uncited) — meaning the Connect stage's curated `scope:` and `sensitivity:` properties written onto entity nodes are ALSO silently dropped for every CRLF source, not just the title. healthPanel.ts:75 has the same pattern too. This strengthens the finding's overall thesis even though two specific downstream claims in the scenario were wrong.

Net: severity P1 is right (degrades data quality broadly across title/scope/sensitivity for every source, on the historically common Git-for-Windows autocrlf=true default) but is not P0 — no crash, no data corruption/loss (the underlying markdown bytes are untouched; only derived read-side values degrade), and reversible by re-deriving once fixed. release_blocking=false is reasonable today only because the product has never shipped a real build to any user (0 releases, release.yml failed once, no Windows package has ever succeeded) — but this must be fixed before any actual Windows release ships, given how commonly autocrlf=true is chosen.

---', 3)` (a raw substring search, not an anchored regex), and since "
---" contains the literal substring "

The real bug is one line earlier, uncited: line 105's `content.replace(/^sensitivityMeta:
(?: {2}\S.*
)*/m, '')` uses the same literal-`
` pattern as the frontmatter-delimiter regex, so under CRLF it fails to strip the OLD `sensitivityMeta` block, leaving a stale/duplicate `sensitivityMeta:` block appended after the new one — i.e. frontmatter corruption (duplicate keys), not a no-op. This is arguably a worse consequence than described but a different mechanism at a different, uncited line. (3) "Only richText.ts:61 normalizes CRLF anywhere in the codebase" is inaccurate — `researchCodeAgent.ts:139` and `researchWebAgent.ts:123` also split on `/?
/`. (4) `related_prior: [ENG-15, ENG-16]` is a mismatched citation — the actual prior-review ENG-15/ENG-16 (specs/research/2026-07-12-deep-review/04-engineering-health.md:31-32) are about e2e fixed-sleep flake and a stale renderer.ts string surviving a rename scrub, unrelated to CRLF/frontmatter; that citation appears to have confused those with an in-code comment tag reuse and should be dropped or left blank. None of this changes the core verdict: `deriveSourceTitle`'s `/^---
([\s\S]*?)
---/` (sourceDoc.ts:43, exact quote confirmed) genuinely returns null on CRLF input (reproduced exactly as the finding's verify_hint states), the vault's own git repo is never given `core.autocrlf`/`.gitattributes` protection (vault.ts only ever writes `.gitignore`/`README.md` via `writeIfAbsent`, confirmed by reading lines 117-187), `git worktree add` (the real checkout mechanism, confirmed in canonicalAdvance.ts:124/127, connectStage.ts:455, jobStage.ts:138, stagingWorktree.ts:51) is exactly where autocrlf conversion would bite, and Windows is a genuinely shipped target (MakerSquirrel unconditional in forge.config.ts:102, windows-latest in both nightly.yml:56 and release.yml:79). Severity/scope/release_blocking/well_scoped judgements in the original finding are all reasonable as-is; only the scenario narrative needs the three corrections above.

findings.title: `scalar()` under-quotes frontmatter — an ordinary filename like `[draft] notes.md` emits YAML that a real parser rejects, breaking Obsidian's Properties panel
findings.scenario: scalar() quotes only on `:`, `#`, quote chars, newline, or edge whitespace — it ignores every other YAML indicator. Verified against the repo's own js-yaml 4.1.0: `title: [draft] notes.md` throws 'bad indentation of a mapping entry'; `title: *ref` throws 'unidentified alias'; `title: - item` throws. Silent mis-typing is just as bad: `title: [draft, notes]` parses as an array, `title: {a}` as a map, `title: null` as null, `title: !!str hi` applies a tag. `title`/`originalName` come straight from user-controlled filenames (drag-drop, watched-folder drops), and PRIN-24 exists precisely so the note is 'self-describing IN Obsidian (the file's Properties panel)' — which is the surface that breaks. A throwing case means Obsidian shows a frontmatter parse error and no properties at all for that note.
findings.recommendation: Invert scalar()'s policy from deny-list to allow-list: emit unquoted only for strings matching a safe plain-scalar pattern (e.g. /^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9 ._\-\/()]*$/ that is not one of YAML's boolean/null/number words), and JSON-quote everything else. Add a property/table test that round-trips every emitted frontmatter through js-yaml (already a devDependency) and asserts the parsed value is the exact input string — that test is what makes this class stay fixed.
findings.verify_hint: cd app && node -e "const y=require('js-yaml'); for (const c of ['title: [draft] notes.md','title: [draft, notes]','title: *ref','title: null']) { try { console.log(c,'=>',JSON.stringify(y.load(c))) } catch(e){ console.log(c,'=> THROW',e.message.split('\n')[0]) } }"
corrections:
none — the mechanism, evidence, and impact all hold as stated. All three cited quotes match current main verbatim at the cited lines. Confirmed against the repo's own js-yaml@4.1.0: `title: [draft] notes.md` → THROW "bad indentation of a mapping entry (1:16)"; `title: *ref` → THROW "unidentified alias "ref" (1:12)"; `title: - item` → THROW "bad indentation of a mapping entry (1:8)"; plus silent mis-typing confirmed too: `title: [draft, notes]` → parses as an array `["draft","notes"]`, `title: {a}` → parses as `{"a":null}`, `title: !!str hi` → tag-coerced to `"hi"`. Traced originalName to its source: app/src/kb/ingest.ts:150 (`originalName: p.name`, drag-drop) and :260 (`originalName: e.name`, folder-drop/watched-folder) both pass the raw OS filename through unsanitized into CapturedMeta, which renderSourceMd (sourceDoc.ts:124-127) feeds straight into `scalar(title)` inside the `---
...
---
` block (sourceDoc.ts:177). The app's own read path (deriveSourceTitle) is regex-based, not YAML-based, so the app itself tolerates the malformed output — the breakage is scoped exactly to any real YAML consumer (Obsidian's Properties panel) as claimed, not to internal app function, so it doesn't cause data loss. Existing test coverage (sourceDoc.test.ts:135) exercises only the colon-quoting case ('originalName: "a: b.png"') — no test covers brackets/asterisk/leading-dash/braces, confirming this class is genuinely uncaught today. findings.title: Every worktree/branch cleanup call is `.catch(() => {})` — the 3.3 GB leak produced zero log lines for three months
findings.scenario: withEphemeralWorktree's `finally` runs four cleanup steps — `worktree remove --force`, `fs.rm`, `branch -D`, `worktree prune` — and swallows all four. reapEphemeralWorktrees does the same and only logs on SUCCESS (`if (worktrees > 0 || branches > 0) log.info('worktree.reaped-leaked')`). The intent is right (teardown must never throw into the pipeline), but the implementation means a persistently failing teardown is indistinguishable from a clean one. Result: 185 directories and 3.3 GB accumulated across three months with not a single warn in the vault's pipeline.log, and reapEphemeralWorktrees reported 'nothing to reap' every boot because compose never matched its regex.
findings.recommendation: Keep swallowing the throw but not the signal: capture each cleanup rejection and emit one `log.warn('worktree.cleanup-failed', { stage, wt, step, err })` per failure. Add a boot-time size/count check under `.kb/cache/worktrees/` that warns (and surfaces in the Health view) when the directory exceeds a threshold or holds entries the reaper does not recognize — an unrecognized worktree name is exactly the signal that would have caught this on day one.
findings.verify_hint: Read app/src/kb/canonicalAdvance.ts lines 176–184 and 205–226 — every git call ends in `.catch(() => {})`; then grep the live vault's log for the class: grep -c 'worktree' ~/kb-test-1/.kb/cache/logs/pipeline.log.
corrections: Essentially none — the mechanism, root cause, and even the exact empirical numbers (185 directories, ~3.4G) check out against the live vault. One tiny wording nit: the scenario says reapEphemeralWorktrees "reported 'nothing to reap' every boot" — in fact pipeline.log shows one successful `worktree.reaped-leaked` (worktrees:8) on 2026-06-29, after which it never fired again while ~177 more compose-<ULID> dirs silently piled up (because `compose` isn't in `EPHEMERAL_STAGES`). So it wasn't literally silent from day one, but the substantive claim — that the ongoing/majority leak produced zero diagnostic signal — holds.

findings.title: The app-level log is 99.84% memory-sampler noise, so real boot/crash breadcrumbs get rotated out by telemetry

evidence.quote: return createDevLog({ ...opts, eager: true, dir: path.join(userDataDir, 'logs'), file: 'app.log' });

findings.scenario: createAppDevLog's whole stated purpose is 'errors BEFORE a vault is open — setup / worktree-provision failures on boot that would otherwise vanish (OBS-2)', created eagerly because forensics found the dir absent in a live install. But startTelemetry points the 60s memory sampler at that same sink at level 'info'. Measured on the installed instance: 36,037 `mem.sample` + 57 `mem.leak-suspected` = 36,094 of 36,094 lines, 5,215,838 bytes — 99.5% of the 5 MB rotation threshold, with zero boot, crash or error events present. Once rotation kicks in (imminently), a boot failure from ~5 MB of samples ago is gone; at 5 files that is roughly the last four days of sampling and nothing else. The sink built for forensics is being consumed by routine telemetry.
findings.recommendation: Either drop `mem.sample` to level 'debug' (the option already exists — pass `level: 'debug'` from startTelemetry, keeping `mem.leak-suspected` at warn), or give the sampler its own sink file (`metrics.log`) so app.log stays reserved for boot/crash/error. The second is preferable: it keeps the trend data while making app.log's retention meaningful.

findings.title: researchFetch never follows redirects despite its comment claiming otherwise — a 301/302 yields an empty body and a silent no-finding

evidence.quote: // Agent makes for this researcher, incl. redirects handled at this layer.
const req = lib.request(url, { method: 'GET', agent, timeout: timeoutMs }, (res) => {

findings.scenario: `http(s).request` does not follow redirects, and there is no Location handling anywhere in the module (grep for 'location'/'redirect'/'301' finds only the comment). A researcher fetching any URL that redirects — http→https, bare-domain→www, trailing-slash normalization, or a news site's canonical redirect, i.e. a large fraction of the public web — gets `{status: 301, text: '', truncated: false}`. The caller sees a successful fetch with an empty page, spends a retrieval-budget slot, and converges on a thin or no finding. Because the gate is designed to fail closed on refusal but this path resolves successfully, the failure is invisible: it looks like the page had nothing to say. Two smaller issues sit in the same function: no User-Agent header (some hosts 403 the default), and `if (text.length > maxBytes) text = text.slice(0, maxBytes)` compares UTF-16 code units against a byte budget.
findings.recommendation: Implement bounded redirect following (cap at 3–5 hops) that re-runs BOTH gates on every hop — `isAllowedUrl` on the Location target plus the same SSRF Agent — since a redirect to a private address is the classic bypass. Reject on exceeding the hop cap. Send a descriptive User-Agent. Cap on Buffer length rather than string length. Add a unit test with a fake server that 302s to an allowed host and a second that 302s to 127.0.0.1 (must be refused).

findings.title: The process-wide Copilot RecallClient is created once and never health-checked or restarted — one dead CLI server bricks Ask until app restart
findings.scenario: #514 correctly fixed a per-question server leak by hoisting one client to module scope, but the replacement has no lifecycle beyond `will-quit`. The `copilot` CLI server is a child process: it can die on macOS sleep/wake, be killed by memory pressure, be replaced by a CLI upgrade under it, or wedge on an expired GitHub auth token. Because `getRecallClient()` only rebuilds when `recallClient` is null and nothing ever nulls it on failure, every subsequent `kb:ask` fails against a dead handle for the rest of the app's lifetime — and the app is deliberately long-lived (QCAP-8 keeps it alive with no window on macOS). `cliPath` is likewise resolved exactly once, so installing copilot after launch has no effect until restart.
findings.recommendation: On a recall failure that indicates a dead/unreachable session (transport error, ECONNREFUSED, EPIPE, spawn failure — as distinct from a model/content error), null out `recallClient` and let the next ask rebuild it, with a single in-request retry. Optionally register an Electron `powerMonitor` 'resume' handler that proactively disposes the client. Add a unit test around a getRecallClient wrapper with an injected client that throws a transport error, asserting the second call gets a fresh instance.

findings.title: The only LLM egress SDK is pinned at a pre-1.0 beta (`1.0.0-beta.7`) and loaded by dynamic import, so a breaking change surfaces only at runtime in the packaged app

findings.scenario: @github/copilot-sdk is the app's single point of LLM egress (BYOA), locked at 1.0.0-beta.7 in package-lock.json while GA is 1.0.11. It surfaces as a runtime failure in the shipped app, and the app additionally drives a user-installed `copilot` CLI whose version is unconstrained (the probe's own comment notes the accepted model set differs between 0.0.373 and 1.0.62). Keep the exact pin, but schedule the upgrade rather than leaving a beta in a shipped artifact.

findings.title: The forge `ignore` allowlist, the vite `external` list and the CI unpack assertions are three hand-maintained lists that must agree — a new native dep silently resolves to nothing at runtime
findings.scenario: Shipping a native or optional dependency correctly requires three coordinated edits: add it to vite.main.config's `external`, add it (and its transitive closure — note `bindings` and `file-uri-to-path` are listed manually for better-sqlite3) to forge.config's RUNTIME_NATIVE_DEPS, and add a `find out -path '*/app.asar.unpacked/*<name>*.node'` assertion to ci.yml. Miss the second and the module is simply absent from the package: the `require()` resolves to nothing and the feature degrades silently (exactly #540's fsevents-to-polling failure). The CI assertions are per-name, so they verify the two natives someone remembered — they do not generalize. The transitive-closure listing is the sharpest edge: better-sqlite3's `bindings` chain was found by hand, and nothing checks it stays complete.
findings.recommendation: Replace the per-name CI assertions with a generic one: after packaging, walk `dependencies` in package.json for any package containing a `.node` binary or a `binding.gyp`, and assert each appears under app.asar.unpacked. Better still, derive RUNTIME_NATIVE_DEPS programmatically from the installed tree (native packages plus their runtime closure) instead of maintaining the list by hand, so adding a dep cannot silently skip the copy path.
findings.verify_hint: Compare app/vite.main.config.ts's `external` array against forge.config.ts's RUNTIME_NATIVE_DEPS (canvas/path2d are externalized but deliberately NOT copied) and against the two `find out -path '*/app.asar.unpacked/*'` steps in .github/workflows/ci.yml.
corrections: Mechanism and all three evidence quotes verified verbatim on current main. Minor nuance: canvas/path2d being absent from RUNTIME_NATIVE_DEPS is not itself an instance of silent failure — forge.config.ts documents (lines 68-77) that this is deliberate because pdfjs's canvas import is a dead code path (never executed, caught in try/catch). The real risk is prospective: the NEXT native dep added to vite's `external` list without a matching forge.config entry gets silently dropped, with no CI assertion generalizing to catch it (confirmed: ci.yml has exactly 3 named asserts — 2x better-sqlite3, 1x fsevents — no generic check). findings.title: The nightly `report-red` auto-filer cannot start — no checkout step under a workflow-level `working-directory: app` — so seven weeks of red nights filed nothing
findings.scenario: nightly.yml sets `defaults.run.working-directory: app` at the workflow level, which applies to every `run:` step in every job. The report-red job has no `actions/checkout` step (it only needs the gh CLI and the needs-results), so `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/app` does not exist and the runner fails to start the process: 'An error occurred trying to start process /usr/bin/bash with working directory /home/runner/work/Vellum-KB/Vellum-KB/app'. This is the safety net for every other finding in this domain — the mechanism that was supposed to make a dormant repo's rot visible. It has never fired. The nightly has been red every day since its first run on 2026-07-13 and no `nightly-red` issue exists.
findings.recommendation: Give report-red a step-level `working-directory: ${{ github.workspace }}` (the pattern the `secrets` job in ci.yml already uses) or add an `actions/checkout@v4` step. Then verify by dispatching once with a forced-red input. Consider moving the workflow-level default onto the jobs that actually need it, so a job without a checkout can never inherit a nonexistent cwd again.

findings.title: The SQLite library index runs WAL inside the vault, and store handles are never closed on vault switch
findings.scenario: The index lives at `<vault>/.kb/cache/library.db` in WAL mode. Obsidian vaults very commonly live in iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive or on an SMB/NFS share — environments where SQLite WAL is documented as unsupported (shared-memory/mmap requirements) and where a sync client copying the .db and -wal files out of step is a corruption vector. The measured index is already 21 MB after 336 sources. Separately, libraryIndexRuntime's `openStores` map keeps a store per root open until process exit (documented as an accepted tradeoff and a tracked fast-follow), so switching vaults leaks a handle and keeps the old DB's WAL live. Recovery is cheap by design — the file is a rebuildable cache, and `quick_check` runs on open — but a user on iCloud would hit repeated rebuilds without ever being told why.
findings.recommendation: Detect a non-local filesystem for the vault root at index-open time and fall back to `journal_mode = DELETE` (or relocate the index to userData keyed by vault path, which also stops the vault carrying a 21 MB binary). Wire store open/close into the vault-switch lifecycle so the handle map cannot grow. Log the quick_check-failure/rebuild path at warn so repeated corruption is visible rather than silently absorbed.

findings.title: `ensurePath()` runs the user's interactive login shell on every boot, and has no Windows equivalent
findings.scenario: On every app-ready, the main process spawns `$SHELL -ilc` — an INTERACTIVE login shell — which sources the user's full rc chain (nvm, pyenv, conda, direnv, oh-my-zsh plugins, and anything else they have). This is a defensible fix for the GUI-PATH problem and it is bounded (4s timeout, failure falls back to a static list), but it means arbitrary user shell configuration executes at app startup, and on a heavy rc it costs up to 4 seconds of the launch path before initPipeline. On Windows the function returns immediately, so `copilot`, `git` and `workiq` discovery relies entirely on the inherited process PATH — with no fallback directory list at all, and no equivalent of the macOS `/opt/homebrew/bin` recovery. Combined with the absence of any 'git binary not found' user-facing state, a Windows or minimal-Linux user without git on PATH gets an opaque failure.
findings.recommendation: Prefer `$SHELL -lc` (login, non-interactive) over `-ilc` — it still sources profile files that set PATH without running interactive-only plugin chains — and cache the resolved PATH in userData so subsequent boots skip the spawn (revalidating in the background). For Windows, add explicit probe locations (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\\Programs`, `%ProgramFiles%\\Git\\cmd`, npm global prefix) and a clear needs-setup state when `git` or `copilot` cannot be resolved on any platform.

findings.title: No `engines` field or .nvmrc: CI runs Node 22, local dev runs Node 24.18 / npm 11 — the lockfile-drift class has no guard
findings.scenario: package.json has no `engines` block and there is no .nvmrc/.node-version in the tree, while the CI quick job pins Node 22 and this machine runs Node 24.18.1 with npm 11.16.0. That is the exact configuration that produced the previously-recorded 'knip/emnapi trap' (#536/#541), where a local `npm install` under a different npm major wrote a lockfile that resolved fine locally and then failed `npm ci` on CI. The failure is asymmetric and confusing: it passes every local gate and only breaks in CI, or (worse for a release) produces a package built against a different Node ABI than CI validated — which matters here because better-sqlite3 is a native module rebuilt for Electron.
findings.recommendation: Add `"engines": { "node": ">=22 <25", "npm": ">=10" }` and a .nvmrc pinning the CI Node major, and set `engine-strict=true` in .npmrc so a mismatched local install fails loudly instead of silently rewriting the lockfile. Add a CI step that asserts `git diff --exit-code package-lock.json` after `npm ci`.

findings.title: No CRLF normalization anywhere: Windows checkouts with the common core.autocrlf=true git config would break the entity/claim frontmatter parsers

evidence.quote: if (!id || !kind || !name) throw new Error('connect: entity node missing id/kind/name');
await git.raw('worktree', 'add', wt, STAGING_BRANCH); // checks out `staging` here

findings.scenario: A Windows user with Git for Windows' own recommended/default `core.autocrlf=true` (convert CRLF→LF on commit, LF→CRLF on checkout) runs the pipeline. `ensureStagingWorktree`'s `git worktree add` performs a real checkout of the `staging` branch — the pipeline's own operational root, per its own comment 'every stage reads/writes staging' — which smudges every already-committed markdown file to CRLF line endings, since no `.gitattributes` exists anywhere (neither in this app repo nor written into a newly-scaffolded vault by vault.ts, which writes `.gitignore`/README but never `.gitattributes`). I verified directly (`node -e`) that `"id: 123\r".match(/^id:\s*(.+)$/)` returns `null` — JS's `.` excludes CR as a line terminator, so the capture can never reach `$`. The same non-multiline `key:\s*(.+)$` idiom recurs in claimsStage.ts (kind/name/subject/status/confidence), connectStage.ts, mergeNodes.ts, and recallTools.ts. Result: parseEntityNode throws 'entity node missing id/kind/name' (id/kind/name are all required) on any pre-existing entity re-read from a CRLF-converted worktree — the same class of failure hits claim re-parsing. This is silent-cause (the error message gives no hint it's a line-ending issue) and would present as the pipeline mysteriously breaking on every re-run that touches existing entities/claims on Windows.
findings.recommendation:
Two independent, cheap mitigations, both worth doing: (1) ship a `.gitattributes` (`* text=auto eol=lf` or scoped to `*.md text eol=lf`) at vault creation time in vault.ts, alongside the existing `writeIfAbsent(.gitignore)` call — this makes line-ending normalization independent of the user's global git config. (2) Defense in depth: strip `` immediately after every markdown `fs.readFile` in a shared helper (or `.replace(/
/g, '
')` before any `.split('
')`), so even an externally-introduced CRLF file (e.g. a user editing in a CRLF-default Windows editor) never reaches the line-based parsers.

findings.title: No requestSingleInstanceLock — a double-launch runs two uncoordinated processes against the same vault, and the canonical-writer lock is explicitly in-process-only

evidence.quote: // In v1 the engine runs in-process, so a single shared `Mutex` instance — injected into

app.on('activate', () => {
  showMainWindow(); // restore/focus the tracked main window (or create one) — never a stray duplicate

findings.scenario: grep for requestSingleInstanceLock across app/src returns zero hits. Combined with QCAP-8 (the app never quits on window-all-closed on macOS — it stays alive as a Dock app + persistent tray agent with the background pipeline running) and stageLock.ts's own documented assumption ('the engine runs in-process, so a single shared Mutex instance... IS that serialized writer'), a second launch of the app (double-click while already running headlessly in the tray, a stuck previous instance during a slow relaunch, etc.) starts a fully independent process with its own in-memory Mutex, its own tray icon, and its own copy of the pipeline/orchestrator — both processes can concurrently attempt canonical git advances (staging worktree writes, promote commits) against the exact same vault repo with no cross-process coordination, risking interleaved/corrupted commits or git index.lock contention beyond what the existing stale-lock self-heal (canonicalLockHeal.ts) was designed to recover from (that heals a single wedged process, not two live ones).
findings.recommendation: Call `app.requestSingleInstanceLock()` at startup; on failure (`false` returned), `app.quit()` immediately. Wire the `second-instance` event to call the existing `showMainWindow()` so a user's second launch attempt just surfaces the running instance instead of silently no-op'ing or racing. This is standard ~10-line Electron boilerplate that's simply absent.

findings.title: Entity-filename collision guard is case-sensitive; two entities differing only by case silently overwrite each other on both shipped platforms' default filesystems

evidence.quote: export function entityFileRel(kind: string, name: string, id: string, taken: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set()): string {

findings.scenario: entityFileRel builds `entities/<kind>/<Human Name>.md` and only disambiguates a collision when `taken.has(base)` — an exact, case-sensitive string comparison — is true. Two entities whose human names differ only by case (e.g. Connect resolving 'Apple' from one source and 'apple' from another before they're merged, or any two genuinely distinct people/orgs that happen to share a name in different casing) produce base paths 'entities/organization/Apple.md' and 'entities/organization/apple.md' — different strings, so `taken` never flags them as colliding and no id-suffix disambiguation kicks in. But macOS's default APFS volume and Windows' default NTFS are both case-insensitive-but-case-preserving: on disk these resolve to the SAME file, so the second entity's write silently overwrites the first's evergreen node (and/or desyncs git's case-sensitive index from what the case-insensitive working tree actually holds — a well-known class of git-on-case-insensitive-FS corruption). Linux ext4 is case-sensitive and would not exhibit this, making it a real cross-platform-consistency gap exactly matching the review brief's callout. connectDoc.test.ts has no test for this case (only exact-duplicate-name collision is tested, connectDoc.test.ts:184-188).
findings.recommendation: Case-fold (and ideally also compare accent/diacritic-normalized, though case is the concrete proven risk) when checking `taken.has(base)` — either store `taken` entries lowercased and compare `base.toLowerCase()`, or maintain a parallel case-insensitive Set. Add a regression test with two names differing only by case landing in the same `taken` collection.

findings.title: entityFileName has no guard against Windows reserved device names (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9)

evidence.quote: * cap length. Case is **never** folded (so `iPhone`, `NASA`, `von Neumann` survive). Empty → `Unnamed`.

findings.scenario: entityFileName's doc comment explicitly calls out 'Windows hazards' for leading/trailing dots and spaces, but the function has no check for the Windows reserved base filenames (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-COM9, LPT1-LPT9, case-insensitive, with or without an extension). An entity legitimately named 'Con' (a person's nickname), or an organization whose name strips down to 'Com1' after character-cleaning, produces `entities/<kind>/CON.md` or `entities/<kind>/Com1.md` — filenames the Windows filesystem refuses to create at all (not merely rename-hostile, outright uncreatable), causing a hard write failure the surrounding pipeline code has no specific recovery path for beyond a generic error.
findings.recommendation: Add a reserved-name check to entityFileName (case-insensitive match against the CON/PRN/AUX/NUL/COM1-9/LPT1-9 set on the base name before the extension) and append a suffix (e.g. a trailing space-safe marker or fold into the existing id-suffix disambiguation path) when it matches. Small, well-understood fix; add a test case alongside the existing dots/spaces/Windows-hazard tests.

findings.title: Linux deb/rpm makers have never been invoked by any CI workflow, ever
findings.scenario: forge.config.ts registers MakerDeb and MakerRpm (implying Linux distributable support), but grepping every workflow for 'npm run make' shows it is used only in release.yml, whose build job matrix is `[macos-latest, windows-latest]` — Linux is absent. nightly.yml has no Linux job of any kind. So `electron-forge make` (the command that actually runs the deb/rpm makers, as opposed to `npm run package`, which only produces the raw unpacked app and is what the ubuntu-latest per-PR/nightly jobs run) has never executed on Linux in this project's history. Any first-time issue in that path — e.g. maker-rpm requiring `rpmbuild` to be installed, which is not guaranteed present on a stock ubuntu-latest runner — has never been caught.
findings.recommendation: Add a Linux leg to release.yml's build matrix (`ubuntu-latest`) running `npm run make`, or at minimum a periodic nightly/dispatch job that runs `electron-forge make` on ubuntu-latest and asserts a .deb and .rpm artifact exists, mirroring the existing macOS/Windows artifact assertions. If Linux is intentionally out of scope for v1 shipping, consider removing MakerDeb/MakerRpm from forge.config.ts rather than carrying an unverified promise, or explicitly document Linux as best-effort/unsupported.

findings.title: The one CI path meant to verify a real Linux boot (xvfb snapshot regeneration) has itself never been run

evidence.quote: workflow_dispatch   — manual, on demand (excludes the update_snapshots dispatch, which is
run: xvfb-run -a npm run test:e2e -- e2e/showcase.e2e.ts --update-snapshots

findings.scenario: ci.yml's `snapshots` job is the only CI path that packages the app and launches it under xvfb on Linux (the mechanism that would prove the app actually boots and renders on Linux). It only runs on `workflow_dispatch` with `update_snapshots: true`. findings.title: userData directory naming drift (kb-app/KB-App/vellum/Vellum) has no migration path and would be guaranteed-distinct (not filesystem-luck-dependent) on Linux
findings.scenario: package.json carries both `name: "kb-app"` (used by Electron for the dev-mode/default userData path) and `productName: "Vellum"` (used for packaged builds) with no `app.setName()` call anywhere and no migration code (grep for 'migrat' near userData/appData/rename turns up nothing relevant). This session's own observed instance already shows the resulting drift on disk (~/Library/Application Support/ carrying separate Vellum, vellum, and kb-app/KB-App directories from the product's rename history). On macOS this is partly an accident of the volume's case-insensitive-but-case-preserving APFS default; on Linux, `~/.config/<name>/` sits on a strictly case-sensitive filesystem by default, so every one of these variants (and any future rename) would deterministically become its own permanently orphaned config/userData directory with zero chance of accidental coalescing and no migration to reconcile them.

findings.scenario: A large capture (a long meeting transcript, a big pasted document) is fed whole into decompose's `copilot -p <prompt>` invocation as a single execFile argv argument — no stdin/temp-file path and no byte cap exist anywhere in the six thin deciders. A sufficiently large source can exceed OS argv limits or flood the model's context window, and recall's readSource/readNode tools return whole files via an untruncated cache with the same risk on the Ask side.
findings.recommendation: Implement the two still-open #514 acceptance criteria: route decider prompts through stdin or a temp file instead of argv, and add a byte cap (with a truncation marker) to readSource/readNode/grep tool results, mirroring the windowing already shipped for recall's conversation history (MAX_HISTORY_TURN_CHARS=2000).
corrections:
The decider-argv mechanism is real and confirmed, but the finding's title and half its evidence are wrong, and the severity is overstated as a result.

CONFIRMED half: all six thin deciders (archivist/decompose/claims/compose/connect/reflect) funnel through the single `makeDefaultCopilotRunner` in app/src/kb/deciderScaffold.ts:61, which still does `exec('copilot', ['-p', prompt, ...launchFlags(model)], ...)` — the full source text is embedded in `prompt` (via `buildDecomposePrompt`/`buildClaimsPrompt`, which fall back to a placeholder only when `input.text` is null) and passed as a single execFile argv element, with no stdin/temp-file routing and no upstream byte cap on source text (ingest.ts:201 only caps raw file drops at 2GiB). This part of the mechanism is real and unaddressed.

REFUTED half: the claim that "recall's readSource/readNode tools return whole files via an untruncated cache with the same risk on the Ask side" is false on current main. PR #543 (merged, closing #514) added `windowToolResult()` in app/src/kb/recall.ts (MAX_TOOL_RESULT_BYTES = 32*1024, 12KB head+tail with an honest truncation note), which wraps every retrieval tool's result — including readSource and readNode — before it reaches the model. The code comment at recall.ts:440-443 explicitly names this as the #514 fix: "no single tool result reaches the session over this bound — readSource/readNode could return a whole (possibly multi-MB) file verbatim into context." So recommending "add a byte cap to readSource/readNode/grep" is asking for something functionally already shipped at the call-wrapper layer.

Framing correction: I read #514's actual acceptance-criteria checklist (via `gh issue view 514`). Its 5th (and only prompt-size-related) formal AC was "Per-turn prompt bytes bounded by a constant independent of conversation length; no single tool result >32KB reaches the session" — this is Ask-specific and DID land in PR #543 (history capped to last-10-turns + MAX_HISTORY_TURN_CHARS=2000, tool results windowed at 32KB). The decider-argv-passing risk was mentioned only in the issue's Problem/Suggested-approach prose ("Background one-shot deciders separately still pass whole sources as argv — claimsAgent.ts:68 et al." / "move background decider prompts from argv to stdin/temp-file"), never promoted into the enumerated acceptance criteria. So the title "#514's prompt-size-bound acceptance criteria were closed without landing" overstates: the actual AC landed; what's outstanding is a suggested-approach line item that was always scoped as a separate, non-AC concern.

Net: keep the decider-argv finding (it's real, well-scoped, and worth an issue), but retitle it as its own gap rather than an unmet #514 AC, drop the readSource/readNode/recall-side evidence and recommendation (already shipped), and downgrade to P2 — this is a latent risk with no observed incident (spans.jsonl's decompose errors are 'no JSON object in output' / timeouts, not argv-limit failures) rather than a demonstrated P1 correctness break. Minor citation note: decomposeAgent.ts's quoted line is actually 41, not 39 (claimsAgent.ts:49 and recallTools.ts:354 are exact).

The finding's central premise — "#514's prompt-size-bound acceptance criteria were closed without landing" — is wrong for the half that matters most (the Ask/interactive side). #514 was closed by a MERGED PR (#543, merged 2026-07-13T02:04:23Z, commit 86ce762 / 2e40258). That PR's diff explicitly implements the two Ask-side prompt-size ACs from #514's checklist: (1) `MAX_HISTORY_TURN_CHARS`/`MAX_HISTORY_TURNS` history capping (recall.ts:422-436) and (2) a generic 32KB head/tail `windowToolResult()` applied to EVERY retrieval tool's result before it reaches the SDK session (recall.ts:445-490, inside the `retrieval()` wrapper that `buildRecallToolDefs` applies uniformly). Because `readSource`/`readNode` are two of the tools wrapped by that same `retrieval()` factory, the finding's claim that "recall's readSource/readNode tools return whole files via an untruncated cache with the same risk on the Ask side" is REFUTED as stated: `recallTools.ts`'s `cachedRead` itself has no cap (true), but the caller that turns its output into what the model actually sees (`recall.ts`) already truncates it — the finding cites the inner function and misses the outer wrapper that was added for exactly this reason (comment at recall.ts:441-443: "`readSource`/`readNode` could return a whole (possibly multi-MB) file verbatim into context" — the PR that fixed it).
