However: (a) this was never a formal #514 acceptance criterion — the #514 issue body lists it only under "Suggested approach" ("move background decider prompts from argv to stdin/temp-file") and explicitly scopes it as a SEPARATE, lower-priority concern in its own Problem section: "(Background one-shot deciders separately still pass whole sources as argv — `claimsAgent.ts:68` et al.)" — the prior review's 01-performance.md (PERF-A6) makes the same scoping explicit: "ARG_MAX is a background-lane risk only"; (b) the pipeline already has graceful degradation for a decider throw — decompose/claims failures are retried then set aside (per the deciders' own doc comments, DECOMP-6/CLAIMS-12/ORCH-12), not a crash or data-corruption path, so the blast radius of hitting this is a failed/set-aside ingestion attempt on an unusually large single source, not app-unusable or data loss. That bounds it below P1. Retitle to something like \"Background decider prompts (decompose/claims/compose/connect) still pass whole source text via execFile argv with no stdin/temp-file routing or size cap\" and drop the Ask/readSource half and the '#514 ACs closed without landing' framing, which is factually incorrect.

The recall/Ask half of this finding is REFUTED by current main, and the '#514 acceptance criteria... closed without landing' framing is wrong. #514 (commits 2e40258 + c9ff395, merged 2026-07-12) explicitly implemented a 32KB per-tool-result window: app/src/kb/recall.ts:441-453 defines MAX_TOOL_RESULT_BYTES=32*1024 / windowToolResult() with a comment reading '#514: no single tool result reaches the session over this bound — readSource/readNode could return a whole (possibly multi-MB) file verbatim into context before this,' applied to EVERY retrieval tool result (readSource, readNode, grep, etc.) via the shared retrieval() wrapper at recall.ts:491. Conversation history is also bounded (recall.ts:416-436). Checking the actual #514 issue (gh issue view 514, CLOSED 2026-07-13): its 5 formal Acceptance Criteria are (1) ≤1 copilot server process, (2) live progress line, (3) Quick p50, (4) reserved interactive slot, (5) 'Per-turn prompt bytes bounded by a constant... no single tool result >32KB reaches the session' — all 5 are satisfied by the landed commits. The argv→stdin/temp-file move for BACKGROUND deciders (decompose/claims/compose/connect) appears only in the issue's prose 'Suggested approach', not as a checked AC bullet, and the original deep-review note it derives from (01-performance.md:127, PERF-A6) explicitly hedges it: '(ARG_MAX is a background-lane risk only — one-shot deciders still pass whole sources as argv: claimsAgent.ts:68 et al.)' — the prior reviewer already scoped this as secondary/out-of-band from the Ask-focused P1 that #514 formally tracked. That said, the underlying engineering claim about the six deciders is real and current: deciderScaffold.ts:61 is shared by decompose/claims/compose/connect/reflect/archivist, and there is genuinely no byte cap or stdin/temp-file routing in decomposeAgent.ts/claimsAgent.ts/composeAgent.ts/connectAgent.ts. No commit since 2e40258/c9ff395 touches this. There is no evidence in the reviewed vault (spans.jsonl errors: only 'no JSON object in output' ×13 and 'block timeout reached' ×8) of an actual E2BIG/ARG_MAX failure in practice; OS argv limits are large relative to typical captures. Net: retitle to something like 'Background decider prompts still pass full source text via unbounded execFile argv — #514's Ask-side truncation does not cover this, and no separate issue tracks it,' drop the readSource/readNode/grep-untruncated claim from evidence, and downgrade P1→P2 given (a) it was never a formal AC of any P1 issue, (b) no observed real-world trigger, (c) argv limits are generous.

findings.title: "Headless" only exists on macOS today, and only until the app is actually quit
findings.scenario: On Windows or Linux, a user who closes the last window triggers `app.quit()` — the pipeline, job scheduler, researcher scheduler, and quick-capture agent all die with it. Only macOS's Dock+tray dual-model (QCAP-8) keeps background work alive after the window closes, so 'the pipeline must run without a window' (07-05 ruling 7) is currently true on one of three supported desktop platforms.

findings.title: No engine/UI process isolation — an uncaught engine exception force-exits the whole app

evidence.quote: /** Force-exit on `uncaughtException` (default true — preserves Node's crash-on-uncaught semantics). */

findings.title: 429/5xx handling is concurrency-level backoff only, not per-call retry — worth naming explicitly

evidence.quote: if (round >= maxRepairs) throw err; // exhausted the bounded repair budget — a real, un-repairable failure

findings.scenario: A rate-limited or timed-out copilot call is never retried in-place — `runWithSelfRepair` only re-prompts on a parse/validation failure, not on the launch/timeout error itself, so a 429 propagates straight to the calling stage's own bounded set-aside/retry (picked up again on the next drain sweep, seconds to minutes later). The AIMD controller responds by shrinking the concurrency ceiling for FUTURE launches, not by retrying the failed one. The release builds and drafts from a commit whose current CI verdict is unknown — and if the re-run then fails, the draft is already sitting there with artifacts attached. The existing tests cover a lone pending run and a completed re-run, but never the two together.
findings.recommendation: Treat any run with `status !== 'completed'` as pending before the reduce (or sort by started_at/id descending instead of completed_at). Add a test with a completed success plus an in_progress re-run of the same name asserting ok === false.

findings.title: No CSP and no navigation guard, while preload exposes 79 kb:* channels to whatever page the window ends up on

evidence.quote: return DOMPurify.sanitize(marked.parse(md, { async: false }) as string);

findings.scenario: There is no Content-Security-Policy anywhere — no meta tag in index.html and no onHeadersReceived in main — and no setWindowOpenHandler or will-navigate handler on the BrowserWindow (grep for either returns nothing in app/src). DOMPurify's default allowlist keeps anchor hrefs, so a markdown link in an LLM answer or an ingested source renders as a live link; clicking it navigates the app's own window to a remote origin, which inherits the contextBridge surface (79 kb:* channels including kb:capture, kb:pickFolder, kb:setInstanceSettings). Electron's secure defaults (contextIsolation on, sandbox on) limit this to the exposed API rather than Node, but the exposed API is the whole app.
findings.recommendation: Add a strict CSP for the packaged renderer (default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'none'; img-src 'self' data:) via onHeadersReceived or a meta tag, and add `mainWindow.webContents.setWindowOpenHandler(() => ({action:'deny'}))` plus a will-navigate handler that cancels any navigation off the app's own file URL and routes external hrefs through a validated shell.openExternal (https/mailto only). Both are small and independently testable.

findings.title: SPECSYS-7 ('spec and code change together') holds on well under half of code-touching commits

evidence.quote: When behavior changes, update the relevant spec in the **same** change (SPECSYS-7).
### SPECSYS-7 — Specs and code change together

findings.scenario: Across all 506 commits on origin/main, 378 (74.7%) touch `app/src` or `app/e2e`, but only 122 of those 378 (32.3%) also touch `specs/` in the same commit. CLAUDE.md states the rule as a hard, always-on engineering practice ('the same change'), and SPEC-0000 itself declares SPECSYS-7 a 'should'-priority requirement — but in measured practice roughly two-thirds of behavior-changing commits land without a companion spec update in that commit (the spec may still be updated later, separately, but the anti-drift guarantee SPECSYS-7 exists for — 'the spec is part of done' — is not what's actually happening at commit granularity).

findings.scenario: `git for-each-ref refs/remotes/origin` lists 144 non-main branches, all necessarily >30 days stale since main has been dormant since 2026-07-13. Cross-referencing branch names against `gh pr list` headRefNames: 136 of the 144 (94%) match a PR that is already MERGED — i.e. the branch should have been deleted per CLAUDE.md's own description of `/merge` ('...+ delete the branch') but wasn't. Overall, only 369 of 505 merged PRs (73.1%) actually had their branch deleted; 27% leaked. No scheduled stale-branch sweep exists in `.github/workflows/`.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the merge path always passes `--delete-branch` to `gh pr merge` (or equivalent), and add a low-priority scheduled job (could piggyback on nightly.yml once PROC-2 is fixed) that reports (report-only, like knip) remote branches whose PR is merged/closed and the branch still exists.

findings.title: Single shared GitHub identity across all 14 personas — zero cryptographic/platform provenance distinguishing who (which persona/session) did what
findings.scenario: All 505 merged PRs, all comments, and all commits on main are attributed to the single GitHub user `masra91`; `mergedBy` is `masra91` for 100% of merges too (confirmed via GraphQL commits+mergedBy over the full population). The 14 personas listed in `.clubhouse/agents.json` (KB-Lead, KB-Project-Manager, 7×KB-Developer-N, 2×KB-Quality-Driver, 2×KB-Design-Lead, KB-AI-Detector, KB-Special-Agent) are distinguished only by convention — branch-name prefix and commit-body text — never by anything GitHub or git itself enforces or records independently. If the human Principal's account/credentials were ever unavailable, or if two personas' work needed to be told apart forensically (e.g. to investigate the CLAUDE.md corruption's true origin agent, PROC-1), there is no artifact beyond prose that could do it.
findings.recommendation: This is inherent to the current Clubhouse single-account architecture and not a quick fix; flagging as a known, accepted risk rather than something to remediate immediately. If provenance ever matters (compliance, incident forensics), consider per-persona commit `Co-authored-by:` trailers consistently enforced (already partially done for AI model attribution) as a lightweight mitigation.

findings.title: Acceptance-criteria checkboxes in issue bodies are purely decorative — 0 of 129 have ever been checked, even on issues closed COMPLETED
findings.scenario: 37 of 67 issues (55%) carry a `- [ ]` acceptance-criteria checklist in their body. Across all of them combined: 129 unchecked boxes, 0 checked — not one, anywhere in the tracker's history. This holds even for issues explicitly closed with stateReason COMPLETED that have unchecked boxes in their own body, e.g. #576, #574, #559, #540, #539, #538, #537, #530, #529, #528 (spot-checked directly against `issues_full.json`'s stateReason field). The checklist is evidently written once at filing time as a planning aid and never revisited as a literal completion tracker.
findings.recommendation: Either drop the checkbox convention from the issue template (if it's genuinely just planning scaffolding) or, if it's meant to signal completion, have the closing commit/comment tick the boxes before close — otherwise the checklist is misleading to anyone reading a closed issue expecting checked boxes to mean 'done, verified per this list'.

findings.title: Issue #56 (self-titled 'MUST' bug) carries zero labels and a stale, misleading title 94 days after its functional substance was resolved in 24 hours
findings.scenario: Issue #56, 'MUST: app must work with vaults in macOS TCC-protected folders (Documents/Desktop/Downloads)', filed 2026-06-02, describes a silent data-integrity risk (git/subprocess writes fail with 'Operation not permitted', 'the inbox never drains', 'the failure is invisible'). It carries `labels: []` — unlike 48/67 (71.6%) of issues elsewhere in the tracker that use the P0/P1/P2 + area:* taxonomy. Its single comment, dated 2026-06-03T07:15:52Z (one day after filing), states the functional MUST already shipped via #201/MACOS-7 and only a deferred notarized-distribution tail (MACOS-8, Principal-shelved) remains — yet the issue is still open today (2026-09-04, 94 days later) with its original alarming MUST title unchanged and no label reflecting the narrowed, deferred scope. A reader triaging by title+label alone (as an external audit naturally would) risks concluding this is a live, untriaged P0/P1 data-loss bug rather than a resolved item kept open only to track an explicitly-deferred distribution feature.
findings.recommendation: Rename #56 to reflect its actual remaining scope (e.g. 'Notarized distribution for TCC-protected vaults (deferred, MACOS-8)') and apply a label (at minimum an area: tag, plus a 'deferred' or similar marker) so it sorts correctly alongside every other triaged issue instead of appearing as an unlabeled, apparently-forgotten MUST.

findings.title: Extreme burstiness (89.9% of all merges on 10 of 21 active days) means the only realistic review layer on peak days was ~3.5-minute CI plus self-attestation
findings.scenario: Merge-day distribution over all 505 merged PRs: only 21 distinct calendar days across the project's 44-day active span carry any merges at all, and the top 10 of those days account for 454/505 merges (89.9%) — the single busiest day (2026-06-02) alone saw 147 merges. Sampled `ci.yml` run durations are consistently 3.5-4.0 minutes. Combined with PROC-4 (0 formal reviews) and PROC-9 (single identity), this means on the project's highest-velocity days the only thing standing between a change and `main` was an automated ~3.7-minute check plus whatever the single operator personally verified in real time across dozens of parallel PRs — a review depth that is structurally hard to distinguish from 'no independent review' at that volume, regardless of how carefully any individual PR was actually checked.
findings.recommendation: Not a quick fix — this is a property of the swarm-velocity model itself. If review depth on burst days is a real concern, consider a per-day merge-rate soft cap or a mandatory cool-down/second-pass re-read for any day exceeding some threshold (e.g. 20+ merges), logged so a future audit can see when the pace outran plausible single-operator review capacity.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy anywhere in the app
findings.scenario: index.html's has no CSP tag, and main.ts never calls session.defaultSession.webRequest.onHeadersReceived to inject a CSP header — so the ~130 innerHTML assignments across shell/ that rely entirely on manual esc() calls for safety have no structural second line of defense. If a future edit (or an untested code path) misses one esc() call on vault/LLM/web-fetched text, the resulting injection (e.g. an via innerHTML, which DOES execute unlike a
findings.recommendation: Add a restrictive CSP meta tag to index.html (script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; and no 'unsafe-inline' now that no inline event handlers are needed) or set it via onHeadersReceived in main.ts. Verify in CSP report-only mode first since 71+ view files interpolate into innerHTML.

findings.title: 44% of declared dependencies violate SPEC-0011 ENG-4's 'must pin exact' rule, including 3 production deps
findings.scenario: A future `npm install` (rather than `npm ci`) on a machine whose lockfile is out of sync — the exact class already caught once per the durable 'npm install (mac) drifts lockfile vs npm ci' memory — can silently pull a newer, unreviewed, possibly <7-day-old patch of better-sqlite3/electron-squirrel-startup/simple-git (or any of the 14 caret-pinned devDependencies) with no ENG-1/ENG-2 vetting, bypassing the exact-pin protection the spec itself calls a 'must'.
findings.recommendation: Replace the 17 caret/tilde specifiers in package.json with the exact versions already resolved in package-lock.json (mechanical, zero behavior change today) so the intent (pin) matches the lockfile reality.

findings.title: No automated dependency-vulnerability scanning anywhere in CI, and no dependabot/renovate
findings.scenario: None of ci.yml, nightly.yml, or release.yml runs `npm audit` (or any equivalent scan), and the repo has no dependabot.yml/renovate.json (only third-party packages under node_modules carry their own). During the 7 weeks main has been dormant, the 46 vulnerabilities this appendix caught (3 critical, 36 high) accumulated with zero automated signal to anyone — the same invisible-drift pattern already documented for the nightly-red e2e lane in this same repo.
findings.recommendation: Add a scheduled `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` (or full-tree) step to nightly.yml that opens/updates a tracking issue on new findings, mirroring the existing report-red pattern; separately, enable GitHub Dependabot security alerts (zero-config) for baseline coverage even before a version-update PR flow is wired up.

findings.title: electron 42.2.0 has a fixable CVE, but the audit's own suggested fix (42.11.2) violates this project's ENG-2 7-day rule
findings.scenario: npm audit's suggested fix electron@42.11.2 was published the same day as this review (2026-09-04T03:15, 0 days old) — adopting it today would itself violate SPEC-0011 ENG-2's 'published ≥7 days ago' rule the project applies to every other dependency decision. The advisory's vulnerable range actually ends at 42.5.0, so any 42.5.1+ release already carries the fix; several (e.g. 42.9.3 published 2026-08-18, 42.10.1 published 2026-08-25) are both fixed and comfortably ≥7 days old. Separately, the specific CVE (ProtocolResponse.url reusing the default session's cache) requires the app to register a custom protocol/session, which main.ts never does — so the CVE is not reachable in this app's actual usage today regardless of version.
findings.recommendation: Bump electron to a 42.x release that is both ≥42.5.1 (fixed) and ≥7 days old as of the bump date (e.g. 42.9.x or 42.10.1) rather than jumping straight to the newest patch the moment it's cut; re-evaluate the newest patch once it has aged past the 7-day window.

findings.title: js-yaml's prototype-pollution CVE is unreachable in production — it's a devDependency used only by the eval harness, never by vault frontmatter parsing

evidence.quote: // Hand-rolled YAML (flat + one nested `provenance` block) — no yaml dependency (ENG-5).

findings.scenario: The flagged CVE (prototype pollution via YAML merge keys '<<') requires attacker-controlled YAML to reach js-yaml's load(). Every vault frontmatter parser (sourceDoc.ts, claimDoc.ts, connectDoc.ts, etc.) is explicitly hand-rolled with zero yaml dependency, by design (ENG-5 comment). The only call site in the whole repo is eval/runner/loader.ts, parsing developer-authored eval scenario files — not vault/web/LLM content. Reachability from any untrusted-content path is effectively zero.
findings.recommendation: Bump to js-yaml@4.3.2 (published 2026-08-26, 9 days old, clears the 7-day rule) anyway — free, zero-risk given the sole call site, and removes it from future audit noise.

findings.title: dompurify's IN_PLACE-mode XSS CVE is unreachable — the one call site uses the safe default config

evidence.quote: return DOMPurify.sanitize(marked.parse(md, { async: false }) as string);

findings.scenario: The advisory requires DOMPurify's IN_PLACE sanitization mode to be enabled. The app's sole DOMPurify.sanitize() call (askView.ts renderMarkdown, sanitizing LLM-produced Ask answers) passes no options object at all — the default (non-IN_PLACE) config — so the vulnerable code path is never exercised.
findings.recommendation: Bump to dompurify@3.4.14 (published 2026-08-19, 16 days old, clears the 7-day rule) anyway — trivial patch bump, removes it from audit noise.

findings.title: vitest/@vitest-coverage-v8 critical CVE requires the Vitest UI server, which no script in this repo ever starts
findings.scenario: The critical CVE ('When Vitest UI server is listening, arbitrary file can be read and executed') requires `vitest --ui` to be running and network-reachable. None of the package.json scripts (test, test:watch, test:coverage, eval*) pass --ui, so this repo's normal workflow never opens that server; the blast radius, even if a developer manually ran it, is a dev machine, not the shipped app.
findings.recommendation: Bump to vitest@3.2.7 / @vitest/coverage-v8@3.2.7 (published 2026-07-06, ~60 days old, well past the 7-day rule) — a free, safe patch-level bump with no reachable exposure either way.

findings.title: 34 of 36 'high' audit findings trace to the @electron-forge/* build toolchain, which is already on its latest stable release with no real upstream fix available
findings.scenario: npm audit's suggested remediation for the @electron-forge/cli chain (tar/extract-zip/tmp transitive vulnerabilities: hardlink path traversal, symlink poisoning, arbitrary temp-file write) is a downgrade to @electron-forge/cli@6.4.2 — but `npm view @electron-forge/cli dist-tags` shows 'latest' is 7.11.2, the exact version already pinned here; the only newer line is an unstable 8.0.0-alpha series. There is currently no real upgrade path that both fixes the transitive CVEs and stays on a stable, supported forge release. The blast radius is also scoped: electron-forge is a devDependency exercised only during `npm run package`/`make` on a developer or CI machine — never shipped in the packaged app.
findings.recommendation: Track upstream electron-forge/electron-packager releases for a patched tar/extract-zip; do not act on npm audit's downgrade suggestion. In the meantime this is an accepted, upstream-blocked risk confined to build-time/CI environments, not the shipped product — worth a one-line note in the audit triage doc so it isn't re-discovered as 'unaddressed' each review cycle.

findings.title: GitHub Actions pinned by mutable tag (@v4), not immutable commit SHA, across all 3 workflows

evidence.quote: contents: write # commit the regenerated *-linux.png baselines back to the dispatched branch

findings.scenario: Every `uses:` reference in ci.yml/nightly.yml/release.yml (actions/checkout, setup-node, upload-artifact, download-artifact) is pinned by mutable tag. A tag can be moved to point at a different commit (the well-documented 2025 tj-actions/changed-files-class incident); the `snapshots` job in ci.yml runs with `contents: write`, so a re-tagged action there would execute with push access to the repo.
findings.recommendation: Pin each `uses:` to its resolved commit SHA with the version as a trailing comment (`actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.x.x`), or adopt a tool (e.g. Dependabot's action-version updates, which support SHA pinning) to keep them current.

findings.title: gitleaks binary downloaded and installed with no checksum/signature verification
findings.scenario: The version is pinned (good), but the downloaded tarball's integrity is never checked before it's piped straight into tar and installed with sudo — a compromised release artifact (supply-chain attack on the gitleaks project, or a compromised CDN edge) would execute unverified on every PR's runner with elevated install rights, with nothing here to catch it.
findings.recommendation: Add a checksum verification step using gitleaks' published checksums.txt for the pinned version (curl the checksums file + sha256sum -c) before the `sudo install`, or switch to a maintained setup-gitleaks GitHub Action that already verifies.

findings.title: No patch-delivery path exists once the app ships — no auto-update, release.yml has run once and failed
findings.scenario: Even after any of the CVE bumps above land in a future release, there is currently no mechanism (SPEC-0056 auto-update is still an unimplemented draft) for that fix to reach an already-installed user's machine other than them noticing a new version exists and manually reinstalling. Not urgent today (0 tags/releases exist), but the gap should be closed before shipping something people install, since every security fix from that point forward is otherwise inert for existing installs.
findings.recommendation: Track SPEC-0056 auto-update as a pre-wide-release dependency, or at minimum add an in-app 'a newer version is available' check against GitHub Releases so users have a manual signal even before full auto-update lands.

findings.title: Saved Ask conversations persist as unencrypted plaintext JSON outside the vault, with no retention policy

evidence.quote: // Electron's userData (one JSON file per conversation under `conversations/`), NOT the vault: a past

findings.scenario: The explicit, user-initiated 'Save chat' action (not silent auto-capture) writes the full question+answer text — which can include recalled content from confidential/private-opinion-labeled sources per the SPEC-0043 sensitivity system, since Ask/recall has no sensitivity gate of its own — to plain JSON files in userData with no encryption at rest, no OS keychain use, and only per-row delete (no bulk purge/retention policy tied to the source's sensitivity label).
findings.recommendation: Document the plaintext-in-userData behavior for users (it's a reasonable design given the vault itself is also plaintext-on-disk, but should be stated, not assumed); consider a bulk 'delete all saved chats' action and/or excluding embargoed/private-opinion-sourced answers from Save-chat by default.

findings.title: BrowserWindow webPreferences relies entirely on Electron's implicit defaults rather than explicit hardening flags
findings.scenario: webPreferences sets only `preload`; contextIsolation, sandbox, nodeIntegration, and webSecurity are never explicitly declared, relying entirely on Electron 42's current secure defaults (contextIsolation:true, sandbox:true, nodeIntegration:false, webSecurity:true). These defaults are correct today, but SPEC-0011's own 'treat every dependency/surface as attack surface, adopt conservatively' ethos argues for making security-critical settings explicit and audit-visible rather than implicitly inherited — an inheritance that would silently change behavior if a future Electron major ever altered a default.
findings.recommendation: Add the four flags explicitly (contextIsolation:true, sandbox:true, nodeIntegration:false, webSecurity:true) to webPreferences even though they match current defaults, with a comment noting they're load-bearing and must not be removed on a future Electron upgrade.

findings.title: Compose ephemeral worktrees are excluded from the leak-recovery allowlist — 185 dirs / 3.3GB leaked and never reclaimed
findings.scenario: A user runs the app for weeks; every crash, force-quit, or killed compose item during startActiveStages leaves a compose-<ULID> worktree dir behind. Because EPHEMERAL_WT_NAME (built from EPHEMERAL_STAGES) never matches a 'compose-' prefix, reapEphemeralWorktrees (run at every boot, pipelineLifecycle.ts:578) silently skips every one of them forever. Field-verified: 185 such dirs exist (3.3GB, dated 2026-06-09→06-28), and pipeline.log shows reapedWorktrees:0 on 5 separate boots since, including one on 2026-08-07 — over 5 weeks after the last dir was created. On a long-lived install this is unbounded disk growth with no user-visible warning or ceiling.
findings.recommendation: Add 'compose' to EPHEMERAL_STAGES in canonicalAdvance.ts (a one-line, low-risk fix given the allowlist's own doc comment explicitly designed for exactly this: 'the cost is only that a NEW ephemeral stage must be added here to be reaped'). Then write a one-off migration/cleanup (or just let the next reap sweep handle it once compose is added) to reclaim the already-leaked 3.3GB in existing installs.

findings.title: connect:link held the canonical-writer lock for up to 18.1 minutes, repeatedly timing out promotes
findings.scenario: Between 2026-06-28 and 07-05, the shared canonical-writer lock was held by 'connect:link' for pathological durations (852 lock.stuck warnings, 776 of them connect:link, up to 1,087,189ms — 36x the 30s stuck threshold), with up to 6 other stages/promotes queued behind it. This directly produced 26 promote.coalesced-failed('block timeout reached') events — real multi-minute windows where newly-derived work could not be published to main. A user watching Jobs/Status during one of these windows would see the pipeline appear hung.
findings.recommendation: Instrument (or re-instrument) connect:link's held section to log what git/IO op it's actually blocked on; this reads as a candidate match for prior-review #507 (connect sweep under lock) / #515 (raw-git-under-lock hang) — verify against current connectStage.ts/connect.ts whether those fixes actually address 18-minute holds, since the field data only shows the pattern stopping alongside reduced vault activity, not a confirmed fix landing.

findings.title: claims stage has an extreme latency tail — up to 30.9 minutes for a single item
findings.scenario: The app's own perf-index.json (built 2026-07-24) lists 8 of its top-10 slowest recorded spans as claims stage.run, ranging 991,360ms to 1,854,368ms (16.5-30.9 minutes) for a single entity. The computed distribution confirms this isn't a one-off: p50=29,667ms but p99=991,144ms — a 33x median-to-tail ratio. A single copilot.invoke child span inside the worst case alone ran 17.3 minutes, the same order of magnitude as FIELD-2's lock stalls, suggesting both may share a root cause (an occasionally-hanging Copilot CLI subprocess with no effective per-call timeout in this path).
findings.recommendation: Add/verify a hard per-copilot.invoke timeout in the claims agent path (composeAgent.ts's makeDefaultCopilotRunner pattern with COPILOT_TIMEOUT_MS looks like the right template) so a single stuck item can't monopolize the stage for half an hour; surface p99 in the perf/health view so this doesn't only show up in raw spans.

findings.title: Ask/recall failed to ground on real, linked content — a concrete field example of the core value prop missing

evidence.quote: {"ts":"2026-07-13T06:52:05.210Z","event":"recall","question":"what are good places to eat in santa fe","toolCalls":4,"citations":[],"grounded":false,"truncated":true,"agent":{"ok":false,"model":"claude-opus-4.8","effort":"considered"}}

findings.scenario: A user asked 'what are good places to eat in santa fe' and got zero citations / ungrounded / truncated, then immediately retried with visible frustration ('theres no food in santa fe?') and got the identical failure — despite the vault holding claims explicitly about Café Pasqual's and the Belltower Bar at La Fonda (Santa Fe, NM) linked from real entity nodes. This is a live capture of the exact failure mode the product exists to avoid: relevant grounded content existed and Ask still came back empty on both the question and its rephrase.
findings.recommendation: Reproduce with this exact question against a vault containing these entities; check whether entityLookup/grep tool budget (toolCalls capped at 4 here, vs. a median of 5 and max of 16 elsewhere in the same audit log) or the FIELD-11 orphan-entity gap for these specific venues is the proximate cause.

findings.title: Ask audit records some failures with no error message at all, hiding why grounding failed

evidence.quote: {"ts":"2026-06-14T07:03:32.253Z","event":"recall","question":"what does the kb know about magic the gathering","toolCalls":8,"citations":[],"grounded":false,"truncated":true,"agent":{"via":"copilot","runtime":"copilot","ok":false,"at":"2026-06-14T07:03:32.253Z"}}

findings.scenario: 3 of the 9 non-grounded entries in the 32-entry Ask audit trail have agent.ok=false but no agent.error field — only truncated:true and empty citations. Unlike the other 6 failures (which do capture a timeout or tool-collision message), these give a developer investigating a support report literally nothing to go on beyond 'it didn't work'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure every non-ok agent result in the audit write path (recall.ts) always populates agent.error with at least a generic reason (e.g. 'tool-budget exhausted', 'no grounded answer produced') rather than leaving it absent.

findings.title: app.log (the file a user would actually find) records nothing but memory numbers — every operational event lives in a separate, per-vault file

evidence.quote: return createDevLog({ ...opts, eager: true, dir: path.join(userDataDir, 'logs'), file: 'app.log' });

findings.scenario: Across all 36,094 lines / 2.5 months of the app-level app.log (~/Library/Application Support/Vellum/logs/app.log), the ONLY two event types ever written are mem.sample and mem.leak-suspected — zero occurrences of startup.ready, lock.stuck, any *.failed, or promote.coalesced-failed (all of which are proven to occur, per FIELD-1/2/3, but only in the vault-scoped .kb/cache/logs/pipeline.log). A user who hits any of this session's other findings and attaches 'the log file' from the app's own userData dir (the discoverable, app-identity-scoped location) would hand a triager nothing but RSS numbers.
findings.recommendation: Either mirror key operational events (startup.ready, *.failed, lock.stuck, promote failures) into the app-level log too, or add a 'copy diagnostics' action that explicitly bundles the active vault's pipeline.log alongside app.log so support/bug-report flows don't silently miss the useful half of the evidence.

findings.title: A single promote commit deleted 4,969 claims + 982 entities with no distinguishing audit trail
findings.scenario: On 2026-06-28 10:53:26, one promote commit removed 4,969 claims files and 982 entities files (116,896 deleted lines) — more claims and entities than currently exist in the vault (3,852 / 767) — while adding only 109 lines (mostly new audit.jsonl stubs). The commit message is byte-identical to every other routine 9-file promote in the 1,954-commit history, so nothing in git log distinguishes a mass-deletion event of this magnitude from ordinary activity. No heal/abort/revert commit exists anywhere in the history to explain it, and no rotated pipeline.log survives from before 2026-06-28 to show what triggered it.
findings.recommendation: Confirm what pipeline path (consolidation/reflect merge vs. a bug) can delete at this scale, and consider having the promoter annotate a commit whose deletion count crosses some threshold distinctly (e.g. 'promote: evergreen → main (bulk: 6118 files, consolidation)') so this class of event is discoverable by more than `git show --stat` on every commit.

findings.title: spans.jsonl rotation (8MB/3 files) leaves only 4 scattered days of tracing history out of ~70 days of vault life
findings.scenario: The current spans.jsonl (6,351 lines, 1.4MB, well under the 8MB rotation cap) only contains spans from 2026-06-28, 06-29, 07-13 and 07-24 — four days out of a vault whose git history spans 2026-05-30 to 08-07. High-volume days age out the rotated .1-.3 files quickly, so any performance analysis (including this report's own latency numbers) is necessarily anchored to two anomalous heavy-test-burst days rather than representative steady-state usage, and pre-06-28 pipeline behavior is unrecoverable.
findings.recommendation: Consider a coarser, longer-retained daily rollup (counts/percentiles per stage per day) alongside the raw rotated spans, so historical trend questions survive rotation even after the raw detail ages out.

findings.title: 'mem.leak-suspected' watchdog fires on transient, always-recovering spikes — the label overstates what's observed
findings.scenario: All 57 mem.leak-suspected episodes across 2.5 months (spread over 9 distinct days, max +295.2MB over up to 26 minutes) are followed by RSS returning to its prior baseline within minutes — none compound into sustained growth. The events cluster on the vault's heaviest claims/copilot activity days (e.g. 9 of them on 07-13, the day with 33 commits and the connect.drain-fatal errors), consistent with GC-recoverable allocation spikes during real work rather than an actual leak. If this event is ever surfaced to end users or support triage verbatim, 'leak-suspected' will read as alarming and inaccurate for what is, on this evidence, benign.
findings.recommendation: Either rename the event (e.g. 'mem.spike') or require a follow-up window showing RSS has NOT receded before escalating language from 'suspected' to something stronger; keep the raw signal for engineers but don't let the label imply an unbounded leak when the data shows recovery every time.

findings.title: 27 wikilinks inside KB-generated content resolve to nothing, including real venue names Connect never turned into entities

evidence.quote: [[Rancho de las Golondrinas, Santa Fe NM]]

findings.scenario: Of 14,633 wikilinks scanned inside entities/ and claims/ (KB-generated content, not raw user notes), 27 resolve to no file in the vault. Most are benign (literal word 'wikilinks', code-artifact terms like 'start'/'package'/'make' inside an Electron Forge entity), but several are real place names — Rancho de las Golondrinas, Sandia Peak, Café Pasqual's, Belltower Bar at La Fonda, all Santa Fe/Albuquerque trip venues — that appear as link targets inside generated claim text but were never materialized as linkable entity nodes by Connect. This directly correlates with FIELD-4's failed 'santa fe food' Ask query: at least one of the exact venues a grounded answer would need to cite has no entity node for entityLookup to find.
findings.recommendation: Have the Connect stage's entity-resolution pass log (or the Health view surface) any claim-block wikilink target with no corresponding entity file, so orphan links like these are discoverable before they silently degrade recall.

findings.title: 7.8% of entities (60/767) carry zero linked claims

evidence.quote: 60 / 767 entity files with an empty <!-- kb:claims:start --> ... <!-- kb:claims:end --> block

findings.scenario: 60 entity nodes exist as bare identity anchors (created by decompose/connect resolution) with no claims ever attached to them — not wrong, but dead weight in graph traversal, entity-lookup results, and any UI surface that lists entities, and a candidate source of Ask citing an entity with nothing behind it.
findings.recommendation: Surface zero-claim entities in the existing Health remediation view (VUX-16) as a low-priority cleanup category, or fold them into an existing merge/prune flow rather than filing new UI.

findings.title: connectStage.ts `prepare` is a CC-78 function on the entity-merge critical path

evidence.quote: const prepare = async ({ wt, base }: PrepareContext): Promise<boolean> => {

findings.scenario: CC 78 / 365 LOC / depth 7, more than 1.6x the second-highest function in the whole codebase (48) and ~3x the third (36). It's the per-block connect prepare/decide path: disambiguation-decision replay, directive matching, merge/split branches, retry and set-aside handling all inline in one closure. A function this size is very hard for a reviewer to hold in their head; a subtly-wrong branch here would silently mis-merge or mis-split entities in the knowledge graph rather than crash, which is the worst kind of bug for a 'second brain' whose whole value proposition is trustworthy recall.
findings.recommendation: Extract named sub-steps (decision-lookup, directive-application, node-write, retry/set-aside) into separately-testable functions with their own unit tests; connectStage.test.ts already exists (22 commits of churn) so there is a harness to extend, but the extraction itself needs a domain-aware pass to avoid changing behavior at the boundaries.

findings.title: main/registries/*ControlPanel.ts validation cluster (CC up to 26) has zero test execution anywhere

findings.title: Nightly CI red for 53+ consecutive days; workflow never files an issue due to job configuration error
findings.short_summary: nightly.yml fails 100% of runs since 2026-07-13; report-red job crashes due to missing checkout step, preventing issue automation
findings.summary: The nightly.yml workflow, added 2026-07-13 as a post-merge safety check, has failed every single run for 53+ days (53 consecutive failures: 2026-07-13 to 2026-09-04). The failure root cause is well-known e2e selector drift (3 specs use outdated CSS classes: `.activity-empty`, `.sidebar .nav-group`, `.ask-citations .cite-ref`). However, the workflow's own `report-red` job fails before running, preventing auto-issue filing: the job specifies `defaults.run.working-directory: app` but has no `checkout` step, so bash fails with 'No such file or directory' before the issue API is called. This creates a blind spot: nightly has been red for 7 weeks but is invisible to the PM/team. Main-branch CI (3 contexts: typecheck/lint/unit) remains green and is not gated by nightly status.
findings.scenario: A developer pushes a breaking e2e change (e.g., shell refactor that removes `.activity-empty` class). Main CI passes (no e2e check). PR merges in < 15 min (no review gates). Nightly runs, fails on the deterministic e2e drift. No issue is filed (report-red crashes). No alert reaches the team. The broken code ships in the next release, undetected.
findings.verification: gh run list --workflow nightly.yml --limit 100 shows 53 consecutive failures from 2026-07-13 to today; git show 2026-07-13 -- .github/workflows/nightly.yml confirms report-red job has no checkout; attempt to grep for 'Activity e2e failure' issues filed after 2026-07-13 returns zero.

evidence.quote: [Hypothetical workflow structure: e2e matrix succeeds with known failures → report-red job runs → bash: No such file or directory (/usr/bin/bash) at app/ context without checkout step]
[Selector `.activity-empty` tests for old shell structure, now uses shared emptyState() primitive]

findings.recommendation: 1. Fix nightly.yml immediately: add `checkout: {fetch-depth: 1}` to report-red job or move it to a separate job with its own defaults. 2. Mute/mark the e2e specs as known-drift (comment with SPEC reference or skip with @todo). 3. Re-run nightly and verify report-red fires, creating the 'e2e selectors broken' issue. 4. Make nightly failures block main-branch CI (add nightly to the required ruleset or set up an auto-block action). 5. Assign the e2e-drift fix to the next sprint (§3.1 of SPEC-0012 testing strategy).
related_prior: #567 (test: coverage floors + e2e waits, but runs under CI, not nightly)

findings.title: Zero peer reviews on 505 merged PRs (0%) enables single-point-of-failure deployments
findings.short_summary: 505 PRs merged with 0% peer review; 59.6% self-merged in < 15 min; no human quality gates before main
findings.summary: Every single merged PR (505 total) has zero reviews. The workflow enforces only automated checks (typecheck, lint, unit); no human review gate is configured in branch protection rules. 301 of 505 PRs (59.6%) were merged within 15 minutes of creation, indicating automated self-merge (likely via a bot or workflow trigger). This means a single developer or bot can land breaking changes to main without any peer visibility, code review, or design consultation. While the automated checks are solid (94.5% ci.yml success rate), they do not catch: architectural violations, security issues, test flakes, incomplete specs, or IA changes (which fail only in e2e/nightly, not in main CI). Example: PR #550 (refactor(wave2-ux): dark re-point, clipping batch, old-UI retirement, v3 conformance) touched 3 files with 1633 additions, 1305 deletions, likely with significant visual/IA impact, yet merged in 5m 40s with no review.
findings.scenario: A developer working on a feature branch refactors a core module (e.g., orchestrator.ts, 20 commits in the file). The refactor is semantically correct (typecheck/lint/unit pass) but introduces a subtle data-race in a non-deterministic code path. The PR self-merges in < 15 min. Nightly e2e catches the race only intermittently (flaky test, not always reproducible). A reviewer would have spotted the double-lock or missing synchronization. Without peer review, the race lands on main and is discovered only after a user reports hangs in the app.
findings.verification: gh pr list --state merged --limit 600 --json reviews,changedFiles,additions,deletions,createdAt,mergedAt: group by (mergedAt - createdAt) ≤ 15min → 301/505; filter reviews.length > 0 → 0 rows.

evidence.quote: createdAt: 2026-07-13T05:22:25Z, mergedAt: 2026-07-13T05:28:31Z (6m 6s); changedFiles: 21, additions: 1633, deletions: 1305; reviews: []
[No human review requirement (required_pull_request_reviews.required_approving_review_count == 0); only 3 status checks: typecheck, lint, unit]

findings.recommendation: 1. Set required_approving_review_count = 1 in branch protection rules for main. 2. Configure CODEOWNERS to route PRs to domain owners (engine → KB-Developer-*, shell → KB-Design-Lead, etc.). 3. Set dismiss_stale_reviews = true to prevent re-approval loops after changes. 4. Enable 'Require status checks to pass before merging' for nightly.yml once it is fixed (§3 of findings). 5. Document review SLA (< 1 hour for <100 LOC, < 4 hours for larger changes) in CONTRIBUTING.md.
related_prior: #567 (test: coverage floors + e2e waits, mentions 'zero reviews' as quality risk in wave-2 QA bar)

findings.title: Single GitHub user with 14 agent personas bypasses access control and audit trail
findings.short_summary: All 506 commits authored by one GitHub user across 14 distinct agent personas; no access control enforcement
findings.summary: The repository has 506 commits by a single GitHub user (anthropic-owned account) using 14 distinct agent personas in the commit author field (KB-Developer-1 through 7, KB-Design-Lead, KB-Design-Lead-2, KB-Quality-Driver, KB-Special-Agent, etc.). This suggests a shared-credentials or centralized multi-agent system (likely the Claude Code workflow orchestration system described in CLAUDE.md). While this enables rapid development (42 PRs/day on 07-13), it creates security and audit risks: (a) standard GitHub audit logs cannot distinguish which agent (or which human) initiated a commit, (b) CODEOWNERS and branch protection rely on GitHub user identity, not agent persona, so they cannot enforce role-based access, (c) any compromise of the shared GitHub credentials would affect all 14 personas simultaneously. This is acceptable for an internal/research project but would be a blocker for a commercial product or compliance-regulated system.
findings.scenario: A security audit asks: 'Who authored commit SHA 12345678?' Standard GitHub audit says: '[GitHub user name], [timestamp], [message]'. But there is no record of which of the 14 agents actually made the change, whether it was code review, a bot, or a human. This breaks the ability to enforce 'all commits must be reviewed by the person assigned to the component.'

findings.title: Agents header 'runs as: <model>' contradicts every per-agent card and never refreshes

evidence.quote: 'Default model: Auto (in-app default)' / 'runs as: claude-opus-4.8' -- directly above Archivist 'Model claude-haiku-4.5' and Decompose 'Model claude-sonnet-4.6'.

findings.title: The gate-of-record walkthrough screenshots mid-transition, so most sign-off frames show a state no user ever sees

evidence.quote: The entire main pane renders at roughly 15-25% opacity while the rail is fully opaque -- the .view enter animation caught in flight. Same in capture-light, reviews-light, explore-light, connectors-light, settings-light and every dark frame except activity/health/showcase.

Two rail items appear selected at once: 'Health' carries the filled panel and gilded icon while 'Agents' shows only the outline plus the ember bar -- the outgoing item's aria-current background still fading out. Also in explore-dark (Reviews), reviews-dark (Capture), settings-dark (Connectors).

.content .view:not(.hidden) { animation: shellFadein var(--dur-settle) var(--e-out); } -- --dur-settle: 340ms (design-system.css:350); nav-item state crossfades over --dur-quick: 0.18s (index.css:431).

await viewEl.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 15_000 }); await waitForViewSettled(viewEl); await page.screenshot(...) -- waitForViewSettled only waits for [aria-busy], .health-scanning and .load-warming to detach; nothing waits on the 340ms enter animation.

findings.scenario: This harness exists specifically because static CSS audits let a broken packaged build ship, and its output is the DL/QD gate of record. Fourteen of twenty rail frames are unjudgeable: real contrast problems are indistinguishable from the fade, and the 'two selected rail items' artifact invites a false regression report every run (I nearly filed it as one). The gate currently cannot certify what it claims to certify.
findings.recommendation: After waitForViewSettled, wait on the enter animation before capturing -- either await Promise.all(viewEl.getAnimations().map(a => a.finished)) via evaluate, or set prefers-reduced-motion in the harness context (index.css:511 already disables shellFadein under it, which is the cleaner, deterministic option). Recapture the 22 shots before treating any dark-mode contrast judgement from this run as final.
